topics.t: Economics all around us: economic activities and roles
topics.h: Walk through any sabzi mandi at 7 a.m. and you can watch economics happen live: someone grows, someone sells, someone buys, someone carries the crates for a wage.
p: Economics studies the everyday activities people carry out to earn a living and to meet their needs: buying, selling, producing, working and hiring.
A consumer buys goods and services to satisfy wants; a seller sells goods; a producer makes goods or provides services.
An employee (worker) sells labour for wages or salary; an employer hires workers and pays them.
Services are produced too: a doctor produces health services, a teacher produces education services, a taxi driver provides transport services.
Economic activities are done for money or a livelihood; non-economic activities (helping a friend, praying, playing for fun) are not done to earn income.

ex.q: At a bus stand you see: (a) a vendor selling chai, (b) a girl waiting for her bus to school, (c) a conductor issuing tickets, (d) two friends chatting. Which are economic activities?
st: Ask of each: is someone earning a living or buying/selling a good or service?
(a) The vendor sells chai to earn income: economic.
(c) The conductor works for a salary from the transport undertaking: economic.
(b) Waiting for a bus and (d) chatting earn nobody any income: non-economic.

topics.rl: When you buy a metro card you are a consumer; the Delhi Metro is a service producer; the ticket clerk is an employee; DMRC is the employer. One trip, four economic roles.

topics.t: Scarcity and choice: we cannot get something for nothing
topics.h: You have ₹500 for the month. The new cricket bat costs ₹450, the concert ticket ₹300 and the online course ₹250. Welcome to the oldest problem in economics.
p: Human wants are unlimited, but the income and resources available to satisfy them are limited. At given prices, you cannot buy everything you want.
This gap between wants and means is called scarcity. Scarcity is the root of all economic problems.
Resources have alternative uses: a plot of land can grow food crops or cash crops; a rupee can buy a book or a burger. So every use means giving up another.
Because of scarcity, individuals and society must choose which wants to satisfy and which to postpone.
Signs of scarcity are everywhere: long queues for gas cylinders, crowded local trains, shortages of seats in good colleges.

ex.q: Anjali has ₹600. She wants a book (₹400), shoes (₹500) and a movie outing (₹200). What can she afford, and what does this show?
st: Total cost of all three = 400 + 500 + 200 = ₹1,100, which is more than ₹600.
Affordable sets within ₹600: book + movie (₹600), shoes alone (₹500), book alone, or movie alone.
She must rank her wants and give up something.
ex.a: She cannot buy all three; she must choose, for example book + movie. This is scarcity forcing a choice.

topics.rl: During the 2023 tomato price spike, many families shifted to other vegetables. Limited budgets plus higher prices forced choices, exactly what scarcity means.

topics.t: Consumption, production, distribution and the definition of economics
topics.h: Every rupee of India's national income ends up in someone's pocket as wages, rent, interest or profit. Who gets what is one of economics' biggest questions.
p: Consumption: how consumers decide what to buy with their income, given prices, to satisfy their wants.
Production: how producers decide what to produce, how much, and with which inputs, given costs and market demand.
Distribution: how national income is shared among the factors of production as wages (labour), rent (land), interest (capital) and profit (entrepreneurship).
Definition: economics is the study of how people and society choose to use scarce resources that have alternative uses, to produce goods and services and distribute them for consumption.
Modern economics also studies poverty, unemployment, inequality, education, health and disasters, and these questions need statistical data.

ex.q: A sugar mill pays ₹40 lakh in wages, ₹10 lakh as rent for land, ₹15 lakh as interest on a loan, and keeps ₹35 lakh as profit. Which factor earns what?
st: Rent goes to the owner of land.
Interest goes to the supplier of capital (the lender).
Profit goes to the entrepreneur (the mill owner).
ex.a: Labour ₹40 lakh, land ₹10 lakh, capital ₹15 lakh, entrepreneur ₹35 lakh; total ₹100 lakh. This is distribution.

topics.rl: When the government debates raising the minimum wage for construction workers or tax on company profits, it is debating distribution of national income.

topics.t: Economic data, analysis and policy
topics.h: Before launching free cooking-gas connections for poor families, planners needed to know how many households still cooked on firewood. No numbers, no plan.
p: Economic facts expressed in numbers, such as rice output, prices or the number of unemployed, are called economic data.
The chain is: data → analysis (finding the causes of a problem) → policy (measures to solve it).
Without data there can be no proper analysis, and without analysis there can be no sound policy. This is why economics and statistics are linked.
Governments use data such as the Census, NSS surveys and price indices to design and review policies on food, health, jobs and education.

ex.q: The government wants to reduce child malnutrition in a district. Put the steps in order using the data-analysis-policy chain.
st: Data: survey children's height and weight and families' food intake.
Analysis: find the causes, e.g. low protein in diet, poor sanitation.
Policy: add eggs or pulses to mid-day meals and improve sanitation.
Review: collect fresh data to check whether malnutrition has fallen.
ex.a: Data → analysis → policy → review with new data.

topics.rl: The Public Distribution System uses data on household numbers and incomes to decide how much grain each state is allotted.

topics.t: Meaning of statistics and kinds of data
topics.h: 'India produced over 130 million tonnes of rice' and 'Statistics helps us compare states' use the word statistics in two different senses. Can you spot them?
p: Plural sense: statistics means numerical facts or data, e.g. statistics of exports or crop output.
Singular sense: statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.
Quantitative data are characteristics measured in numbers: income, marks, height, output of rice.
Qualitative data are attributes that cannot be measured directly in numbers: gender, beauty, honesty, skill, health. They are often described in degrees (good, average, poor).
Stages of a statistical study: collection → organisation → presentation (tables, diagrams, graphs) → summarising (averages etc.) → analysis → interpretation.

ex.q: Classify: (i) beauty, (ii) monthly income, (iii) marks in an exam, (iv) singing ability, (v) intelligence.
st: Ask: can it be measured directly as a number with a unit or count?
Income (₹) and marks (out of 100) are numbers: quantitative.
Beauty, singing ability and intelligence are attributes: qualitative.
ex.a: Quantitative: income, marks. Qualitative: beauty, singing ability, intelligence.

topics.rl: The Census of India records quantitative data (age, number of rooms) as well as qualitative data (religion, mother tongue, type of roof) about every household.

topics.t: Why statistics matters, and where it falls short
topics.h: A family of four heard the river's average depth was 3 feet, so they all waded across. The average was right; the middle was 7 feet deep. Statistics is powerful, but it needs common sense.
p: Precision: statistics states facts exactly. 'Rice output rose by 8%' says more than 'output went up a lot'.
Condensation: it reduces masses of data to a few summary figures such as averages and percentages.
Relationships: it helps find and test links between variables, e.g. price and demand, income and consumption.
Forecasting and policy: it helps estimate future values (food demand, oil imports) and check whether a policy works and what causes a problem.
Limitations: it studies aggregates, not single individuals; it can be misused or misread (e.g. averages hiding extremes); it is no substitute for common sense.

ex.q: A town's average monthly income is ₹50,000. Nine people earn ₹10,000 each and one earns ₹4,10,000. Does the average describe a typical person?
st: One extreme value has pulled the average up.
ex.a: No. The average is misleading here; common sense says most people earn ₹10,000.

topics.rl: The RBI forecasts inflation each quarter from price data before deciding interest rates: statistics used for forecasting and policy.

topics.t: Data: primary and secondary
topics.h: A student who interviews 50 chaiwalas about their earnings has primary data. The student who later reads her report has secondary data. Same numbers, different labels!
p: Data are the values of variables; each recorded value is an observation. Data help explain economic problems such as low farm income.
Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the purpose of the enquiry, e.g. through a survey or interview.
Secondary data have already been collected and processed by another agency, e.g. Census reports or RBI publications. They save time and money.
The same data are primary for the agency that collected them and secondary for anyone who uses them later.
Choice depends on purpose, time and money: primary data are original and suited to the purpose but costly; secondary data are cheap but must be checked for suitability and reliability.

ex.q: A student wants to know the average pocket money in her school. She (a) surveys 60 classmates herself, and (b) also reads a newspaper report on teenagers' spending. Classify each source.
st: (a) She collects the data first-hand for her enquiry: primary data.
(b) The newspaper collected and published the figures earlier: secondary data for her.

topics.rl: NSO publishes the Periodic Labour Force Survey. For NSO it is primary data; for a journalist writing about jobs from that report it is secondary data.

topics.t: Framing a good questionnaire
topics.h: 'Don't you think our tasty noodles are better than other brands?' That one question breaks at least two rules of survey design. Let's learn to spot them.
p: A survey collects information from individuals using an instrument: a questionnaire (filled by the respondent) or an interview schedule (filled by the interviewer).
A good questionnaire is short, clear and precise, and moves logically from general to specific questions.
Avoid: ambiguous words ('often', 'regularly'), double negatives ('Don't you not…'), leading questions that hint at an answer, and questions that need calculations.
Closed-ended questions give fixed choices: two-way (yes/no) or multiple-choice. They are easy to tabulate but harder to frame well.
Open-ended questions allow free answers ('What do you think of…?'). They give rich detail but are hard to compare and interpret.

ex.q: Improve this question: 'You don't think smoking is not harmful, do you?'
st: Problem 1: double negative ('don't… not') confuses the respondent.
Problem 2: it leads the respondent towards an answer.
Rewrite as a neutral closed question: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health?' (Yes / No / Can't say).
ex.a: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health? Yes / No / Can't say'

topics.rl: Before every big election, survey agencies frame neutral, short questions so that responses from lakhs of voters can be compared quickly.

topics.t: Modes of data collection and the pilot survey
topics.h: Want to survey tribal households in remote Bastar, college students in Pune, and shoppers at a Delhi mall? One method will not fit all three.
p: Personal interview: face-to-face questioning. Highest response, allows clarification and observation, but costly, slow, needs trained interviewers, and the interviewer may influence answers.

Mailing questionnaire (post, email, online form, SMS): cheapest, covers wide and remote areas, respondents answer privately, but response is low, no one can clarify doubts, and it needs literate respondents.
Telephone interview: cheaper and quicker than personal visits, allows some clarification, but reaches only people with phones and loses face-to-face cues like body language.
Pilot survey: a small trial survey before the main one. It tests the questionnaire's clarity, the instructions, the enumerators' performance, and estimates cost and time.

ex.q: Choose a mode: a researcher must survey 5,000 graduates across India within a week and with a small budget.
st: Personal interviews across India in a week: too slow and costly.
Telephone: possible but costly for 5,000 people in a week.
Online/mailed questionnaire: cheap, fast and graduates are literate and connected.
ex.a: An online (mailed) questionnaire, perhaps with phone follow-ups for non-response.

topics.rl: Before Census operations, enumerators run a pre-test (a pilot) in selected areas to see which questions confuse people, and the forms are revised.

topics.t: Census and sample survey
topics.h: To know if the dal is cooked, you taste one spoonful, not the whole pot. That spoonful is a sample.
p: Population (universe): all the items or units under study, e.g. all farms in a district.
Census (complete enumeration): data collected from every unit of the population. The Census of India is held every 10 years and counts every person.
Sample: a group of units drawn from the population that represents it. A good sample is representative.
Advantages of a sample survey: cheaper, quicker, needs fewer staff, allows more detailed questions, and can give reasonably accurate results.
A census is preferred when every unit matters (e.g. population count, voter lists) or when the population is small; a sample is needed when testing destroys items (e.g. testing bulbs).

ex.q: A researcher studies 50 out of 200 farms in a village to estimate average yield of wheat per acre. Identify the population, sample and variable.
st: Population = all units under study = 200 farms.
Variable = the characteristic measured = wheat yield per acre.
ex.a: Population: 200 farms; sample: 50 farms; variable: yield per acre.

topics.rl: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011, a fact known only because the Census counted everyone.

topics.t: Sampling methods: random and non-random
topics.h: Exit polls on election day interview a few thousand voters and try to predict the votes of crores. Sometimes they nail it; sometimes they miss badly. Sampling method makes the difference.
p: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. The investigator has no say in who is chosen.
Lottery method: write each unit's name on a slip, mix well, draw the required number. Random number tables or computer-generated random numbers do the same for large populations.
Sampling frame: the complete list of units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. a voters' list).

Non-random sampling: units do not have an equal chance of selection. Types: judgement/purposive (investigator's choice), convenience (easy to reach) and quota (fixed numbers from each group). Bias is likely.
The number of ways of choosing r units from N is ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!), e.g. 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways.

ex.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be drawn from a class of 10?

topics.rl: Exit polls sample voters at chosen booths. If the booths or voters chosen are not representative, or people do not answer honestly, the prediction can go wrong.

topics.t: Sampling and non-sampling errors
topics.h: Your sample says farmers in a village earn ₹600 a day on average. The truth is ₹580. That ₹20 gap has a name, and so do the much nastier errors that no sample size can fix.
p: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value (the gap is often stated as a size). It arises because only part of the population is observed.
Sampling error falls as the sample size rises; it disappears in a census.
Non-sampling errors can occur in both a census and a sample survey, are more serious, and are harder to detect and control.

Types: sampling bias (the sampling method excludes some units, e.g. a phone survey missing people without phones); non-response (people do not reply); errors in data acquisition (wrong recording, measurement mistakes, misunderstood questions, false answers).
Non-sampling errors can be reduced by careful questionnaire design, training enumerators and follow-ups, but not by simply enlarging the sample.

ex.q: Five farmers earn ₹500, ₹550, ₹600, ₹650 and ₹700 a day. A sample of two picks ₹600 and ₹700. Find the sampling error.

topics.rl: Surveys on household spending face non-response when wealthy households refuse to take part, which can understate average consumption, an error a bigger sample alone cannot fix.

topics.t: Census of India, NSSO and other data agencies
topics.h: Every 10 years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep. It is one of the largest data operations on the planet.
p: Major national agencies: Census of India, National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Central Statistical Office (CSO), Registrar General of India (RGI), Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS), and the Labour Bureau.

Census of India: the most complete source of demographic data (population size, density, sex ratio, literacy, migration). Held regularly every 10 years since 1881; the first Census after independence was in 1951.

NSSO (set up in 1950) runs nationwide sample surveys in 'rounds' on socio-economic issues such as consumer expenditure, employment, literacy and health. Results appear in reports and its journal 'Sarvekshana'. In 2019, NSSO and CSO were merged to form the National Statistical Office (NSO).
Other sources: CSO (national income), RGI (births and deaths), DGCIS (foreign trade), Labour Bureau (labour data); also the Economic Survey, RBI publications and international bodies.

ex.q: A student needs data on (i) India's sex ratio, (ii) household consumption expenditure, (iii) India's exports. Which source fits each?
st: (i) Sex ratio is demographic: Census of India.
(ii) Consumer expenditure surveys are run by NSSO (now NSO) in rounds.

topics.rl: Census 2011 was the 15th Census of India and the 7th after independence. Census data guide everything from seat allocation to planning schools and hospitals.

topics.t: Why classify data? Raw data and classification
topics.h: A kabadiwala's cart is a jumble of newspapers, bottles, tins and plastic. Within minutes he sorts it into neat heaps, because sorted scrap is easy to price and sell. Data work the same way.
p: Raw (unclassified) data are data in the form they were collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Even finding the highest value or the average is tedious.
Classification arranges data into groups or classes according to some common feature, so the data become easy to understand, compare and analyse.
Each classification must follow a clear criterion (basis), e.g. by year, by state, by gender or by income range.
Advantages: brings order, highlights similarities and differences, makes comparison possible, and prepares data for tabulation and analysis.

ex.q: Marks of 20 students are recorded in roll-number order: 47, 85, 32, 61, 75, 52, 90, 38, 64, 71, 29, 55, 83, 49, 66, 78, 41, 58, 69, 93. How many scored 60 or more? Why is this slow?
st: We had to check every value because the data are raw and unordered.
ex.a: 11 students; raw data force us to inspect every value, which classification avoids.

topics.rl: The RBI classifies bank loans by sector (agriculture, industry, services, personal loans) so it can quickly see where credit is flowing.

topics.t: Kinds of classification
topics.h: India's GDP by year, rainfall by state, workers by gender, and students by marks are four different ways to slice data. Each answers a different question.
p: Chronological (temporal): by time, such as years or months. Such data form a time series (e.g. India's population 1951–2011).
Spatial (geographical): by place, such as country, state, district (e.g. wheat output by state).
Qualitative: by attributes that cannot be measured, such as gender, marital status, religion. Classifying by several attributes at once (e.g. sex, then married/unmarried) is manifold classification.
Quantitative: by measurable characteristics such as marks, height, income, grouped into classes like 0–10, 10–20.
Relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency; it can be shown as a percentage (× 100).

ex.q: In a class of 50, the 30–40 marks class has 15 students. Find its relative frequency and percentage.

topics.rl: The Economic Survey shows exports by year (chronological), by destination country (spatial) and by commodity group (qualitative), all from the same trade data.

topics.t: Variables: continuous and discrete
topics.h: Your height can be 162.37 cm, but the number of siblings you have can never be 2.5. That difference decides how data are grouped.
p: A variable is a characteristic whose value changes from unit to unit and can be measured, e.g. income, height, marks. An attribute (like gender) is qualitative and is not measured in numbers.
A continuous variable can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age.
A discrete variable takes only certain values (usually whole numbers) and changes in jumps: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice.
Tip: if you measure it, it is usually continuous; if you count it, it is usually discrete.

ex.q: Classify: (a) area of a farm, (b) number on a rolled dice, (c) population of a city, (d) rainfall in a month, (e) age.
st: Population is a count of people: discrete.
Age can be 15 years 4 months: continuous.
ex.a: Continuous: area, rainfall, age. Discrete: dice number, population.

topics.rl: IMD reports rainfall to the nearest millimetre (a continuous variable), while Indian Railways counts passengers (a discrete variable).

topics.t: Frequency distribution: the key terms
topics.h: The marks of 1,000 board candidates fit on one small table once you group them into classes like 40–50 and 50–60. That table is a frequency distribution.
p: A frequency distribution shows how the values of a variable are spread across classes, with the number of values (frequency) in each class.
Class: a group of values such as 20–30. Class limits: the lowest (lower limit) and highest (upper limit) values of a class. Class frequency: the number of observations in the class.
Class interval (class width) = upper class limit − lower class limit, e.g. 30 − 20 = 10.
Class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit) / 2. It represents the whole class in calculations.
Range = largest value − smallest value. A frequency curve is drawn by plotting frequencies against class marks and joining the points smoothly.

ex.q: For the class 40–60: find the class width and class mark. If the data range from 12 to 97, find the range.

topics.rl: Pay commissions publish salary bands like ₹25,000–35,000; HR teams use the band's mid-point to estimate average pay.

topics.t: Building a frequency distribution
topics.h: Too few classes and you lose the shape of the data; too many and the table is as messy as the raw data. The art is choosing the right classes.
p: Decide equal or unequal classes: equal classes are usual; unequal classes suit data with a very wide range or values bunched in one area (e.g. incomes).
Number of classes is usually between 6 and 15. Number of classes = range ÷ class width (round up to a whole number).
Class limits should be clear and avoid gaps or overlaps. Open-ended classes (like 'below 10' or '90 and above') are avoided where possible because they have no mid-point.
Tally marks count frequencies in groups of five: four strokes and a fifth crossing them (𝍸).
Grouping causes loss of information: once grouped, every value in a class is treated as if it were equal to the class mark.

ex.q: Marks range from 30 to 99. You want exclusive classes of width 10. How many classes are needed, and what are they?
st: Number of classes = 69 / 10 = 6.9, round up to 7

topics.rl: Income tax slabs are a frequency-style grouping with unequal classes, because incomes are spread over a very wide range.

topics.t: Exclusive and inclusive classes
topics.h: A student scores exactly 20. Does she go in 10–20 or 20–30? The method you use decides, and getting it wrong double-counts students.
p: Exclusive method: the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next (10–20, 20–30). A value equal to the upper limit is excluded from that class and goes into the next. So 20 goes into 20–30.
Inclusive method: both limits are included in the class (10–19, 20–29). There is a gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Inclusive classes suit discrete data (like marks in whole numbers).

Adjustment: to make inclusive classes continuous, find the gap between one class's upper limit and the next class's lower limit, then subtract half the gap from every lower limit and add half to every upper limit. E.g. 10–19, 20–29 → 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
The class mark is unchanged by the adjustment, but the class width becomes the true width (10 instead of 9).

ex.q: Adjust the inclusive classes 30–39, 40–49, 50–59.

topics.rl: Census age tables use inclusive groups like 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 years, because age there is recorded in completed whole years.

topics.t: Frequency arrays and bivariate distributions
topics.h: Survey 30 families on how many members they have and the answers are just 2, 3, 4, 5, 6… Grouping them into classes like 2–4 would be silly. A frequency array is the neat solution.
p: A frequency array is a frequency distribution for a discrete variable: each value is listed with its frequency, without class intervals (e.g. household size 1, 2, 3… with number of households).
A univariate distribution deals with one variable. A bivariate (two-way) frequency distribution shows the joint frequencies of two variables in a table.
In a bivariate table, the rows are classes of one variable and the columns classes of the other; each cell shows how many units fall into both classes.
Example: companies classified by advertisement spending (rows) and sales (columns). Row and column totals give each variable's own (marginal) distribution.

ex.q: A bivariate table shows firms by ad spend (₹ lakh) and sales (₹ lakh). The cell 'ad spend 10–20, sales 200–300' shows 4. What does it mean?
st: Locate the row (ad spend 10–20) and column (sales 200–300).
The cell value counts firms that satisfy both conditions.
ex.a: 4 firms spend ₹10–20 lakh on ads and have sales of ₹200–300 lakh.

topics.rl: A frequency array of household size from survey data helps planners decide what sizes of homes to build under housing schemes.

topics.t: Forms of presentation and textual presentation
topics.h: A news anchor reading 'Of 120 crore Indians, about 69% live in villages' uses words. A table or a pie chart could say the same thing. Which works best depends on the data.
p: Data can be presented in three forms: textual (descriptive), tabular and diagrammatic.
Textual presentation describes data in sentences within the text, e.g. 'In a strike, 28 out of 140 workers stayed away'.
It suits small amounts of data and lets the writer emphasise certain points.
Its drawback: the reader must go through the whole passage to grasp the figures, and comparison is difficult when data are many.

ex.q: Which form suits this best: 'In a class of 40, 22 are girls and 18 are boys'?
st: The data have only two figures.
A sentence conveys them clearly without a table.
A table or diagram would add little.
ex.a: Textual presentation, because the data are small.

topics.rl: Budget speeches often use textual presentation for a few key figures ('fiscal deficit is estimated at x% of GDP'), while the detailed numbers go into annexure tables.

topics.t: Tabular presentation and classification in tables
topics.h: A single table in the Census can show literacy for men and women, in villages and cities, for every state. That's the power of rows and columns.
p: A table arranges data in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical). Each box where a row meets a column is a cell.
Qualitative classification in a table: by attributes, e.g. literacy rate by sex (male/female) and location (rural/urban).
Quantitative classification: by measurable classes, e.g. population by age group 0–14, 15–59, 60+.
Temporal classification: by time, e.g. India's exports for 2019, 2020, 2021.
Spatial classification: by place, e.g. share of India's exports going to different countries.

ex.q: A table has 3 rows (Rural, Urban, Total) and 3 columns (Male, Female, Total). How many cells does the body have, and what kind of classification is it?

topics.rl: RBI's Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy is mostly tables, organised by year (temporal) and by state (spatial).

topics.t: Parts of a table and rules of a good table
topics.h: A table without a title or unit is like a cricket scorecard without team names. You see numbers but can't tell what they mean.
p: One-way table: data classified by one characteristic; two-way: by two characteristics; three-way: by three characteristics.
Table number (for reference) and title (what, where, when, in brief, placed at the top).
Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings. The body holds the actual data.
Unit of measurement (e.g. ₹ crore, '000 tonnes) is stated, usually with the title or headings. Source says where the data came from; a note explains anything special, placed below the table.
Large figures are rounded and the unit stated (e.g. 12,34,56,789 written as 12.35 crore).

ex.q: Convert into a table: 'In 2011, literacy was 82% among males and 65% among females; in 2001 it was 75% among males and 54% among females.'
st: Title: Literacy rate in India by sex, 2001 and 2011 (in %)
ex.a: A two-way table with years as stubs and sex as captions.

topics.rl: Every table in the Economic Survey carries a title, unit, and a source line such as 'Source: NSO, MoSPI'.

topics.t: Bar diagrams: simple, multiple and component
topics.h: In one glance at a bar chart, you can see which state grows the most rice. That speed is why diagrams exist, even though tables are more exact.
p: Diagrams give a quick, attractive picture of data and help memory, but they are less exact than tables.
Simple bar diagram: bars of equal width with equal gaps; only the height (length) shows the value. Used for discrete variables, attributes, time series and non-frequency data.
Multiple bar diagram: two or more bars drawn side by side for each category to compare data sets, e.g. literacy in 2001 and 2011 for each state.
Component (sub-divided) bar diagram: each bar is split into parts showing components of a total, e.g. enrolment split into boys and girls.
Percentage component bar: every bar has height 100 and the parts show percentage shares.

ex.q: A school has 300 students: 120 in Science, 105 in Commerce, 75 in Arts. In a percentage component bar, what heights do the three parts have?

topics.rl: News channels on results day use multiple bar diagrams to compare seats won by parties in two elections, side by side.

topics.t: Pie diagrams
topics.h: Every rupee the Union Government spends can be shown as one pie: interest, defence, subsidies, states' share... Each slice's angle tells its share.
p: A pie diagram is a circle divided into sectors, each sector showing a component's share of the total.
Sector angle = (component value ÷ total) × 360°. If shares are already in percent, angle = percentage × 3.6°.
All the sector angles add up to 360° and all percentages to 100.

Pie diagrams suit data showing parts of a whole at one point of time (e.g. budget shares, religious or occupational composition). They do not suit time series like monthly rainfall, where a bar diagram or line graph is better.

ex.q: A family spends: food ₹8,000, rent ₹6,000, education ₹4,000, others ₹2,000. Find the sector angles.

topics.rl: The Budget at a Glance document shows 'Rupee comes from' and 'Rupee goes to' as pie charts every year.

topics.t: Histograms
topics.h: A histogram looks like a bar diagram with its bars squeezed together. But the missing gaps carry real meaning.
p: A histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles drawn on class intervals of a continuous variable; the area of each rectangle is proportional to the class frequency.
It is used only for continuous data (classes in exclusive form, so inclusive classes must first be adjusted). There are no gaps between rectangles.
With equal classes, heights can be the frequencies. With unequal classes, heights are frequency densities = frequency ÷ class width.

Mode can be located from a histogram: join the top-right corner of the tallest rectangle to the top-right corner of the rectangle before it, and its top-left corner to the top-left corner of the rectangle after it; the x-value directly below the point where these two lines cross is the mode.
Histogram vs bar diagram: in a histogram both width and height matter (area shows frequency); in a bar diagram only height matters, bars have equal width and gaps.

ex.q: Classes 0–10 (f = 5), 10–30 (f = 20), 30–35 (f = 10). Find the heights for a histogram.

topics.rl: Hospitals plot histograms of patients' waiting times to see where most patients wait, and to spot the modal waiting time.

topics.t: Frequency polygon, frequency curve and ogives
topics.h: Draw two ogives on the same graph and something magical happens: the point where they cross drops straight down to the median.
p: Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of histogram rectangles with straight lines, and close it by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes at both ends. Or plot frequency against class marks directly.
Frequency curve: a smooth freehand curve drawn through the points of the frequency polygon.
Less-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('less than' the upper limit) plotted against upper class limits; it rises from left to right.
More-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('more than' the lower limit) plotted against lower class limits; it falls from left to right.
The two ogives intersect at a point whose x-coordinate is the median.

ex.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 4, 6, 8, 2. Find the less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies.

topics.rl: Board result analysts use ogives to read off how many students scored below 33% or above 90% without listing every score.

topics.t: Arithmetic line graphs and choosing a diagram
topics.h: Plot India's exports and imports year by year on one graph and the widening gap between the two lines tells the trade deficit story without a single sentence.
p: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph) plots time on the x-axis and the value of the variable on the y-axis; points are joined by straight lines.
It shows trends, cycles and seasonal ups and downs, e.g. monthly vegetable prices or yearly GDP growth.
Multiple line graphs plot two or more series on the same axes for comparison, e.g. exports and imports, or growth rates of agriculture, industry and services.

Choosing a diagram: time series → line graph or bar diagram; parts of a whole → pie or component bar; continuous frequency distribution → histogram, polygon or ogive; categories → simple or multiple bar.

ex.q: Which diagram suits each? (a) monthly rainfall in Chennai, (b) share of food, rent and travel in a budget, (c) heights of 200 students in classes, (d) sectoral growth rates over 10 years.
st: (a) A time series: bar diagram or line graph.
(b) Parts of a whole: pie diagram.
(d) Several time series: multiple line graph.
ex.a: (a) bar/line graph, (b) pie, (c) histogram, (d) multiple line graph

topics.rl: RBI and MoSPI release charts of monthly CPI inflation as line graphs, making it easy to see if inflation is rising or easing.

topics.t: Averages and the arithmetic mean of ungrouped data
topics.h: A batter scores 12, 98, 45, 0 and 70 in five innings. One number, the average, sums up the whole series. But which way of computing it is fastest?
p: An average (measure of central tendency) is a single value that represents the whole data set. We study three: arithmetic mean, median and mode. (Geometric and harmonic means exist but are not studied here.)
Arithmetic mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations: X̄ = ΣX / N (direct method).
Assumed mean method: pick a convenient A, find deviations d = X − A, then X̄ = A + Σd / N.
Step deviation method: if deviations share a common factor c, use d′ = (X − A)/c, then X̄ = A + (Σd′ / N) × c.
All three methods give exactly the same answer; the short-cut methods only reduce arithmetic.

ex.q: Find the mean of 40, 50, 55, 78 and 58 by the direct and assumed mean (A = 55) methods.

topics.rl: Cricket's batting average and a city's average daily AQI reported by the CPCB are both arithmetic means.

topics.t: Mean of discrete and continuous series
topics.h: When 50 families report their sizes or 200 workers report wages in classes, you can't add values one by one. Frequencies and mid-points do the heavy lifting.
p: Discrete series: X̄ = ΣfX / Σf. Short cuts: X̄ = A + Σfd / Σf, or X̄ = A + (Σfd′ / Σf) × c.
Continuous series: replace each class by its mid-point m, then X̄ = Σfm / Σf (or the same short cuts with d = m − A).
Inclusive classes: mid-points are the same before and after adjustment, so the mean is unaffected. Unequal classes: just use each class's own mid-point.
Cumulative tables: first convert 'less than' or 'more than' cumulative frequencies back into simple class frequencies by subtraction, then find the mean.

ex.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have f = 5, 10, 20, 15. Find the mean by direct and step deviation methods.

topics.rl: Labour Bureau wage surveys group workers into wage classes; average wages are computed exactly this way using mid-points.

topics.t: Properties of the mean, weighted mean and missing frequencies
topics.h: If a billionaire walks into a village tea stall, the average wealth of the people inside jumps to thousands of crores. Nobody got richer. That is the mean's biggest weakness.
p: Property 1: the sum of deviations of observations from their arithmetic mean is always zero: Σ(X − X̄) = 0.
Property 2: the mean is affected by extreme values; one very large or small item can pull it a long way.
Weighted mean X̄w = ΣwX / Σw, where weights w reflect the relative importance of items (e.g. budget shares, credits of subjects).
Missing frequency: write ΣfX and Σf in terms of the unknown, set ΣfX / Σf equal to the given mean, and solve.
Changes: adding k to every value raises the mean by k; multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean by k; replacing one value changes the sum and hence the mean.

ex.q: X: 10, 20, 30, 40 with f: 5, f₁, 10, 5. The mean is 25. Find f₁.

topics.rl: Your CGPA is a weighted mean: a 4-credit subject counts twice as much as a 2-credit one.

topics.t: Median of ungrouped and discrete data
topics.h: Line up five friends by height. The one in the middle is the median, and she stays the middle even if the tallest friend is swapped for a basketball star.
p: The median is the middle value of data arranged in ascending or descending order; it divides the data into two equal halves. It is a positional average.
It is not affected by extreme values, since only position matters.
Ungrouped data: median = size of the ((N + 1)/2)th item. If N is even, it is the mean of the two middle items (N/2 and N/2 + 1).
Discrete series: arrange X in order, find cumulative frequencies (cf), locate the ((N + 1)/2)th item; the X whose cf first equals or exceeds this position is the median.

ex.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with f: 2, 5, 8, 6, 4. Find the median.
st: cf first reaches 13 or more at 15, where X = 3

topics.rl: Household income reports often quote the median income, because a few billionaires would distort the mean.

topics.t: Median of a continuous series
topics.h: With 10 lakh board candidates in mark classes, you can't line them up. One neat formula finds the median mark from the class table.
p: Find cumulative frequencies (cf) and N = Σf. The median class is the class containing the (N/2)th item (use N/2 for continuous series).
Median = L + ((N/2 − c.f.) / f) × h
L = lower limit of the median class; c.f. = cumulative frequency of the class just before the median class; f = frequency of the median class; h = width of the median class.
For less-than cumulative data, the given figures already are cf; find simple frequencies by subtraction. For inclusive classes, adjust first so L is the true lower limit (e.g. 19.5).
topics.rl: NSS reports on household consumption give the median monthly per capita expenditure in addition to the mean, from class-wise tables.

topics.t: Quartiles and percentiles
topics.h: 'You scored in the 98th percentile' does not mean you got 98 marks. It means you did better than (or as well as) about 98% of test takers.
p: Note: quartiles and percentiles are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.
Quartiles divide ordered data into four equal parts. There are three quartiles: Q1 (lower quartile), Q2 (the median) and Q3 (upper quartile).
For ungrouped data: Q1 = size of the ((N + 1)/4)th item; Q3 = size of the (3(N + 1)/4)th item.
Percentiles divide data into 100 equal parts (99 percentiles). P50 is the median, P25 = Q1, P75 = Q3.
Use: 25% of items lie below Q1 and 25% above Q3; e.g. if Q3 of incomes is ₹60,000, the top 25% earn more than ₹60,000.

ex.q: Data: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Find Q1, median and Q3.

topics.rl: Entrance exams like JEE Main report scores as percentiles, so candidates from different shifts can be compared fairly.

topics.t: Mode
topics.h: A shoe shop doesn't care about the average foot size. It wants the size most customers ask for. That's the mode.
p: Mode is the value that occurs most frequently. Data may be unimodal (one mode), bimodal (two), multimodal (more), or have no mode if all values occur equally.
Discrete series: the mode is the value with the highest frequency.
Continuous series: the modal class has the highest frequency. Mode = L + (D1 / (D1 + D2)) × h, where D1 = f1 − f0 and D2 = f1 − f2 (f1 = modal class frequency, f0 = previous class, f2 = next class).
The formula needs equal, exclusive class intervals; convert cumulative or inclusive data first.
Mode suits qualitative data and choices like the most popular shoe, garment or collar size. It can also be located graphically from a histogram.
topics.rl: Clothing brands decide how many M, L and XL shirts to stock using the modal size in each city.

topics.t: Comparing mean, median and mode
topics.h: A start-up says 'average salary ₹18 lakh'. The intern says 'most of us earn ₹4 lakh'. Both are telling the truth, using different averages.
p: In a symmetric distribution, mean = median = mode.
In an asymmetric (skewed) distribution, the median lies between the mean and the mode.
Mean: uses all values and suits further algebraic work, but is pulled by extremes and cannot be found with open-ended classes.
Median: unaffected by extremes, works with open-ended classes, suits qualitative ranking (e.g. intelligence) and income or wage data with a few very high values.
Mode: best for the most popular item or size (shoes, garments) and for qualitative data; may not be unique or may not exist.

ex.q: Choose the best average: (a) typical wage in a firm where the owner earns ₹50 lakh and 40 workers earn ₹2–3 lakh; (b) the most popular collar size; (c) average marks of a class for computing total marks.
st: (c) Need a value that relates to the total → mean

topics.rl: Real-estate portals often quote median home prices, because a few luxury homes would push the mean up.

topics.t: What correlation studies: types of relationship
topics.h: Ice-cream sales and drowning cases rise together every summer. Does ice-cream cause drowning? Of course not. Welcome to the trickiest idea in statistics.
p: Correlation studies whether two variables move together, in which direction, and how strongly.
Some relationships are cause and effect (a fall in price raises quantity demanded); others are coincidental.
Spurious correlation: two variables move together because both are driven by a third variable (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise with temperature).
Correlation measures covariation, not causation. The coefficient studied here measures linear (straight-line) relationships.
Positive correlation: both move in the same direction (income and consumption). Negative correlation: they move in opposite directions (price and quantity demanded).

ex.q: Classify: (a) height and weight of children, (b) price of a good and quantity demanded, (c) hours of practice and errors made in typing.
st: (a) Taller children tend to be heavier: same direction → positive.
(b) Higher price, lower quantity demanded: opposite → negative.
(c) More practice, fewer errors: opposite → negative.

topics.rl: When onion prices rise sharply, families buy fewer onions: a negative correlation between price and quantity demanded that markets see every year.

topics.t: Scatter diagrams
topics.h: Plot each student's study hours against marks as a dot. Before any formula, the cloud of dots already tells the story.
p: A scatter diagram plots each pair of values (X, Y) as a point on a graph, showing the relationship visually.
Points rising from lower left to upper right show positive correlation; falling from upper left to lower right show negative correlation.
Points scattered with no pattern show no (zero) correlation. Points lying exactly on a straight line show perfect correlation (+1 if rising, −1 if falling).
The closer the points lie to a straight line, the stronger the correlation.
A scatter diagram can reveal non-linear relationships (curves), but it does not give a numerical measure of correlation.

ex.q: Pairs (study hours, marks): (1, 40), (2, 50), (3, 60), (4, 70), (5, 80). What will the scatter diagram show?
st: Each extra hour adds exactly 10 marks.
All points lie on one rising straight line.

topics.rl: Economists plot inflation against interest rates for several years as a scatter to see if the two move together.

topics.t: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation
topics.h: One number between −1 and +1 sums up how tightly two variables move together. Karl Pearson gave us the formula that does it.
p: Karl Pearson's coefficient (product moment or simple correlation coefficient) r measures the degree of linear relationship between two variables.
Covariance: cov(X, Y) = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ)/N = Σxy/N, where x = X − X̄ and y = Y − Ȳ. Standard deviations: σx = √(Σx²/N), σy = √(Σy²/N).
r = Σxy / (N σx σy), which simplifies to r = Σxy / (√Σx² × √Σy²).
Direct (actual values) formula: r = [NΣXY − ΣXΣY] / [√(NΣX² − (ΣX)²) × √(NΣY² − (ΣY)²)].
Typical uses: years of schooling of farmers vs farm yield; price index vs money supply.
topics.rl: Studies of Indian farmers have used Pearson's r to check whether more years of schooling go along with higher crop yields.

topics.t: Properties and interpretation of r
topics.h: A student computes r = 1.4 and proudly calls it 'super strong correlation'. A strict examiner circles it in red, because it is impossible.
p: r is a pure number with no units, so relationships measured in different units can be compared. This is why it is preferred to covariance.
−1 ≤ r ≤ +1. Any value outside this range means a calculation error.
r is unaffected by a change of origin (adding or subtracting a constant) and of scale (multiplying or dividing by a positive constant).
r = +1: perfect positive; r = −1: perfect negative; r close to ±1: strong; r close to 0: weak; r = 0: no LINEAR relationship (a non-linear one may still exist, so it does not prove independence).
Use common sense: areas with more doctors may show more deaths during an epidemic (doctors are sent where the disease is), but doctors do not cause deaths.

ex.q: Heights in cm give r = 0.6 between brothers and sisters. If heights are converted to inches (÷ 2.54), what is r?
st: Converting units is a change of scale.
r is unaffected by change of scale.

topics.rl: Market analysts report r between rainfall and kharif output; a value of 0.7 means a fairly strong positive linear link, not that rain is the only cause.

topics.t: Step deviation method and computing r
topics.h: Big numbers like 1,20,000 and 3,40,000 make Pearson's formula painful. Shift and shrink them first: r won't even notice.
p: Because r is unaffected by change of origin and scale, define U = (X − A)/B and V = (Y − C)/D for convenient A, B, C, D (B, D > 0).
Compute r using U and V exactly as with X and Y: r_UV = r_XY.
Perfectly linear data (e.g. Y = 2X + 3) give r = +1; Y = −3X + 10 gives r = −1.
Symmetric data such as X: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 with Y = X² (4, 1, 0, 1, 4) give r = 0, although Y depends exactly on X (non-linear).
topics.rl: Analysts studying the price index and money supply (in lakh crore) shift and scale the figures first to make hand calculations manageable.

topics.t: Spearman's rank correlation
topics.h: Three judges at a college dance contest rank ten performers. Which two judges think most alike? You can't measure 'grace' in centimetres, but you can rank it.
p: Use rank correlation when attributes cannot be measured (beauty, honesty, intelligence), when only ranks are available, when data have extreme values, or when the relationship is monotonic but not linear.
Spearman's formula: r_s = 1 − 6ΣD² / (n³ − n), where D = difference between the two ranks of each item and n = number of pairs.
Case 1, ranks given: find D for each item, square, add, apply the formula.
Case 2, ranks not given: first rank each series (e.g. highest marks = rank 1), then proceed as in Case 1.
Comparing judges: compute r_s for each pair of judges; the pair with the highest r_s agree most.

ex.q: Two judges rank 5 dancers: Judge A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Judge B: 2, 1, 4, 3, 5. Find r_s.

topics.rl: Rankings such as NIRF college rankings can be compared year to year with rank correlation to see how stable the list is.

topics.t: Tied ranks and comparing the two measures
topics.h: Two students both score 60 and tie for 2nd place. Who gets rank 2 and who gets rank 3? Neither: both get 2.5.
p: Tied (repeated) ranks: give each tied item the average of the ranks they would have occupied. Two items tied for 2nd and 3rd place each get 2.5; three tied for 4th, 5th, 6th each get 5.
Correction: for each group of m tied items, add (m³ − m)/12 to ΣD².
Formula with ties: r_s = 1 − 6[ΣD² + Σ(m³ − m)/12] / (n³ − n).
Like r, the rank correlation coefficient lies between −1 and +1.
Rank correlation is generally less precise than Pearson's r because it uses ranks rather than actual values, and so uses less information.

ex.q: X marks: 50, 60, 60, 70, 80 (ranked ascending: 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4, 5); Y ranks: 2, 1, 3, 5, 4. Find r_s.

topics.rl: You can try it: rank the prices of 6 vegetables in two different markets of your city and compute rank correlation, handling equal prices as ties.

topics.t: What an index number measures
topics.h: Your nani says, 'In my day a cinema ticket cost one rupee!' An index number turns that kind of nostalgia into a precise measure of how much prices have really changed.
p: An index number is a statistical device for measuring the average change in a group of related variables over two different situations, such as two periods of time or two places.
The base period is the period of comparison; its index is set at 100. The current period is the one being compared.
Reading an index: 250 means the level is 2.5 times the base, i.e. a 150% rise over the base. An index of 80 means a 20% fall.

A price index measures changes in prices (e.g. CPI, WPI). A quantity index measures changes in physical volume, e.g. of production, employment or construction (e.g. the Index of Industrial Production).

ex.q: The price index of a basket is 180 with base 2012 = 100. Interpret it.
st: So prices on average are 1.8 times the base, 80% higher.
ex.a: Prices have risen on average by 80% since 2012.

topics.rl: When MoSPI reports that the CPI (base 2012 = 100) is around 190 or more, it means the consumer basket costs roughly double what it did in 2012.

topics.t: Aggregative price indices: simple, Laspeyres and Paasche
topics.h: If rice goes up ₹2 a kg and saffron goes up ₹2 a gram, an unweighted index treats them alike. Households certainly don't. Weights fix that.
p: Simple aggregative price index: P01 = (Σp1 / Σp0) × 100, where p0 and p1 are base and current prices.
Drawbacks of the simple index: prices in different units (kg, litre, dozen) are simply added, and every item gets equal importance.
Weighted aggregative index uses quantities as weights. Laspeyres: P01 = (Σp1q0 / Σp0q0) × 100, using base-year quantities q0.
Paasche: P01 = (Σp1q1 / Σp0q1) × 100, using current-year quantities q1.
The two differ only in the weights. Laspeyres asks how much more the base-year basket costs now; Paasche asks how much more the current basket costs compared with the base.

ex.q: Rice: p0 10, q0 10, p1 12, q1 10. Wheat: p0 5, q0 10, p1 7, q1 10. Dal: p0 25, q0 2, p1 30, q1 4. Find the simple aggregative, Laspeyres and Paasche indices.

topics.rl: Most official price indices in India, such as CPI and WPI, use fixed base-period weights, which is the Laspeyres idea in practice.

topics.t: Price relatives and the weighted relatives method
topics.h: Tomatoes up 50%, salt up 5%. Average them simply and you get 27.5%, which is fair only if a family spends equally on both. It doesn't.
p: Price relative of an item: R = (p1 / p0) × 100.
Simple average of price relatives: P01 = (1/n) Σ(p1/p0 × 100). It is unit-free, but gives every item equal weight.
Weighted average of price relatives: P01 = ΣWR / ΣW, where W is usually the base-year expenditure on each item (W = p0q0) or its share in the budget.
With W = p0q0, the weighted average of relatives gives the same answer as the Laspeyres index.

ex.q: Rice (p0 10, p1 12), wheat (p0 5, p1 7), dal (p0 25, p1 30), with base expenditures 100, 50, 50. Find the simple and weighted average of relatives.

topics.rl: The CPI is built as a weighted average of price relatives, with weights taken from household consumption expenditure surveys of NSO.

topics.t: Consumer Price Index
topics.h: Your monthly expenses on dal, rent, bus fare and mobile data all change at different rates. The CPI combines them into one number that even decides how much DA government employees get.
p: The Consumer Price Index (CPI), or cost of living index, measures the average change in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a target group.

CPI = ΣWR / ΣW, where W are weights (expenditure shares) and R are price relatives. If CPI is 140, a wage of ₹100 in the base must rise to ₹140; the 'excess over 100' (40%) is the compensation needed.

Different CPIs exist because baskets differ: CPI for industrial workers (CPI-IW), agricultural labourers (CPI-AL), rural labourers (CPI-RL), and CSO's CPI-Rural, CPI-Urban and CPI-Combined (base 2012 = 100 in the NCERT book).
In CPI-Combined (base 2012), the major groups are food and beverages (weight 45.86), pan, tobacco and intoxicants, clothing and footwear, housing, fuel and light, and miscellaneous.
The Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI) tracks retail food prices separately.

ex.q: Weights: food 50, clothing 10, housing 20, fuel 10, misc 10. Price relatives: 150, 120, 130, 140, 110. Find the CPI.
ex.a: CPI = 138: the cost of living has risen 38%

topics.rl: Dearness allowance for central government employees is revised using the All-India CPI for industrial workers compiled by the Labour Bureau.

topics.t: Wholesale Price Index and inflation measures
topics.h: Headlines often say 'WPI inflation turns negative' while 'CPI inflation is 5%' in the same month. How can both be true? They measure different baskets.
p: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures the general level of prices of goods traded in bulk (at the wholesale stage). It does not cover services.
WPI series used in the NCERT book: base 2011–12 = 100. Its three major groups and weights: primary articles 22.62, fuel and power 13.15, manufactured products 64.23.
WPI is used to track price movements in the goods economy and to deflate aggregates like national income.
Headline inflation is measured on the full index (all items). Core inflation excludes volatile items such as food and fuel, to show the underlying trend.
The RBI targets CPI (Combined) headline inflation under its inflation-targeting framework.

ex.q: WPI weights are 22.62 (primary), 13.15 (fuel and power) and 64.23 (manufactured). Check that they add up, and say which group dominates.
st: Manufactured products have the largest weight.

topics.rl: When global crude oil prices crash, WPI inflation can dip sharply because fuel and power and many manufactured products depend on oil.

topics.t: Index of Industrial Production, Sensex and other indices
topics.h: When the Sensex jumps 1,000 points, TV anchors cheer. When the IIP dips, economists worry. Both are index numbers telling different stories.
p: Index of Industrial Production (IIP): a quantity index of the volume of industrial output. The series used in the NCERT book has base 2011–12; it uses the Laspeyres formula with weights based on value added.

Sectoral weights in IIP: mining 14.37, manufacturing 77.63, electricity 7.99. Use-based groups include primary, capital, intermediate, infrastructure/construction goods, consumer durables and non-durables.
Eight core industries (coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity) carry about 40% of the weight in IIP.
Human Development Index (HDI, by UNDP): a composite index of health (life expectancy), education and income.
BSE Sensex: index of 30 large, actively traded shares on the Bombay Stock Exchange, base 1978–79 = 100; a benchmark of stock market movement. An index of agricultural production tracks farm output.

ex.q: IIP sector weights are mining 14.37, manufacturing 77.63 and electricity 7.99. Which sector dominates, and what does the index measure?
st: The weights add to 100 (99.99 after rounding).
Manufacturing has by far the largest weight, so factory output drives the IIP.
IIP measures changes in the volume (quantity) of industrial production, not prices.
ex.a: Manufacturing dominates (77.63); IIP is a quantity index.

topics.rl: A Sensex level of about 60,000 means its 30 shares, taken together, are worth roughly 600 times their 1978–79 level, because the base was set at 100.

topics.t: Issues in constructing an index number
topics.h: Choose 2020 as your base year and every index after it looks wild, because the pandemic made 2020 anything but normal.
p: Purpose: be clear what the index is for (e.g. cost of living of factory workers), since this decides the items and the formula.
Selection of items: choose items representative of the target group's consumption or production; the basket must not be too small or too large.

Base year: should be a normal year, free of extreme events like droughts, wars or pandemics, and not too distant. Bases are revised periodically as consumption patterns change (e.g. WPI moved to 2011–12).
Choice of formula: Laspeyres, Paasche or weighted relatives, depending on the question asked.
Data: prices must be collected from reliable, representative markets; poor data give a misleading index.

ex.q: A researcher considers 2009 (a severe drought year), 2016 (a normal year) and 1985 as base years for a food price index in 2025. Which is best?
st: 1985: too distant; consumption patterns have changed.

topics.rl: MoSPI periodically revises the CPI and WPI base years so that the baskets reflect what Indians actually buy today, such as mobile data and packaged foods.

topics.t: Using index numbers: inflation, real wages and purchasing power
topics.h: Your salary doubled in ten years. Celebrate? Only if prices didn't also double. Index numbers tell you what your rupees are really worth.
p: Uses of CPI: wage and DA negotiations, income and price policy, rent control, taxation. Uses of WPI: measuring inflation in goods, deflating aggregates such as national income.
Inflation rate = (X_t − X_{t−1}) / X_{t−1} × 100, where X is the price index in the current (t) and previous (t − 1) period.
Purchasing power of money = 1 / cost of living index (with the index expressed as a ratio, e.g. 125 → 1.25). If CPI = 125, ₹1 buys what ₹0.80 bought in the base.
Real wage = (money wage / CPI) × 100. Salary needed to keep the same standard of living = base salary × CPI / 100.
Indices with different base years cannot be compared directly; they must first be shifted to a common base.

ex.q: CPI rose from 160 to 168 in a year. Ravi's money wage is ₹33,600 and the CPI is 168. Find the inflation rate and his real wage.

topics.rl: When the government revises dearness allowance twice a year, it is using the CPI to protect the real wages of its employees.

topics.t: Starting a project: problem, objectives and target group
topics.h: Why do auto-rickshaws in your town overcharge at night? A good statistics project turns a question like this into data, findings and practical suggestions.
p: A project applies statistical tools to a real economic issue, studies it systematically and suggests improvements.
Step 1: identify the problem or area of study and set clear, specific objectives (what exactly do we want to find out?).
Step 2: choose the target group, i.e. the population whose members will be surveyed (e.g. auto drivers and commuters of a city, or households of a colony).
A precise objective decides what data are needed; a well-defined target group decides whom to ask and how to sample.

ex.q: A student wants to study 'saving habits'. Turn this into a clear objective and target group.
st: Specific objective: 'To find what share of monthly income households in Ward 12 save, and where they keep their savings.'
Target group: all households in Ward 12.
ex.a: Objective: share of income saved and savings instruments used; target group: households of Ward 12.

topics.rl: Before launching a new metro line, planners first define the objective (reduce travel time) and target group (daily commuters on the corridor) before collecting any data.

topics.t: Collecting data for a project
topics.h: You have two weeks and no budget. Do you knock on 500 doors or use the NSS report in the library? Smart projects choose their data sources deliberately.
p: Step 3: collect data. Primary data come from a questionnaire or interview schedule, through personal interviews, post, phone or email. Secondary data come from published sources such as the Census, NSS reports or RBI publications.
Decide census or sample; if sampling, choose a sampling method (random sampling is preferred to avoid bias).
A mailed questionnaire should carry a covering letter explaining the purpose of the survey, assuring confidentiality, and requesting a reply by a date.
When time or money is short, suitable secondary data are a sensible choice, but check that they match your purpose and are reliable.

ex.q: A student studying women's employment in her district has 10 days and no funds. How should she collect data?
st: A full primary survey of the district is too costly and slow.
Use secondary data (e.g. Census and PLFS reports) for the district picture.
Add a small random sample of households in her locality for primary insight, using a short questionnaire.
ex.a: Mainly secondary data, supplemented by a small random sample survey.

topics.rl: NGOs studying sanitation often combine Census data on toilets per household with a small sample survey of their own villages.

topics.t: Organising, analysing, concluding and the bibliography
topics.h: A pile of 200 filled questionnaires is not a project. It becomes one only after it is tabulated, graphed, analysed and turned into clear conclusions.
p: Step 4: organise and present the data in tables and suitable diagrams (bar diagrams, pie diagrams, histograms).
Step 5: analyse and interpret using averages (mean, median, mode) and correlation. (The NCERT book also mentions measures of dispersion, which are not part of the current syllabus.)
Step 6: draw conclusions from the analysis, forecast future prospects if relevant, and suggest policies or improvements.
Step 7: prepare a bibliography listing every secondary source used (books, reports, websites) so that readers can check them.

ex.q: A project finds that average monthly saving of 50 households is ₹4,500 and correlation between income and saving is 0.85. What conclusion and suggestion fit?
st: Average saving of ₹4,500 summarises saving levels.
r = 0.85 means higher-income households tend to save more (strong positive correlation).
Suggestion: savings schemes could target lower-income families with small, regular deposit options.
ex.a: Saving rises strongly with income; suggest small-saving schemes for lower-income households.

topics.rl: The Economic Survey ends many chapters with policy suggestions and lists its data sources, just like a well-written project report.

topics.t: Project ideas: playing an economic role
topics.h: Imagine you are the transport advisor to your district collector, or a bank officer judging a loan for a pickle-making unit. Projects are most fun when you play a role.
p: Transport advisor: study bus routes, waiting times and fares to suggest better services. Bank loan proposal: assess costs, sales and profits of a cottage unit. Advertising: study whether ad spending raises a firm's sales.

Literacy and dropouts: find why children leave school in a locality. Overcharging: check whether shops charge above MRP. Drinking water: survey availability and quality. Women's employment: study participation and wages.
Health and sanitation, food adulteration, immunisation coverage, household saving habits, and problems of farmers are other good areas.
Each role-based project still follows the same steps: problem, objectives, target group, data, presentation, analysis, conclusions, bibliography.

ex.q: As a bank officer, what data would you need to judge a loan proposal for a cottage unit making papads?
st: Costs: raw materials, labour, rent, machines.
Expected profit = revenue − cost, and ability to repay.
ex.a: Cost, sales, profit and repayment-capacity data.

topics.rl: Many schools encourage CBSE projects on local issues, such as checking whether packaged water is sold above MRP at railway stations.

topics.t: A consumer survey: questionnaire and presentation
topics.h: Which toothpaste do families in your colony use, and why? A consumer survey answers this the way real marketing teams do.
p: A consumer survey questionnaire covers: demographic details (age, sex, family size), income and occupation, brand used, satisfaction, preferences (taste, ingredients, price) and media that influenced the choice.

Present the age distribution of respondents with a table and a bar diagram. Family size and spending can be grouped into classes and shown with suitable diagrams: a bar diagram for counts of a discrete variable, a histogram for continuous classes.
Make a frequency distribution of income or monthly spending and find the mean, using the assumed mean or step deviation method to simplify arithmetic.
Show occupational status of respondents with a pie diagram; tabulate brand preferences and the reasons for choice as counts or percentages.

ex.q: In a survey of 120 respondents, 48 are salaried, 36 self-employed, 24 students and 12 retired. Find the pie angles.

topics.rl: FMCG companies like those selling toothpaste and soaps run such consumer surveys across Indian towns before launching new variants.

topics.t: Interpreting results and writing the conclusion
topics.h: Your survey shows 60% of users like Brand A, but only 30% are 'very satisfied'. What does that mean for the company? Interpretation turns numbers into insight.
p: Interpret satisfaction by brand: compare the share of 'satisfied' users across brands, not just the number of users.
Interpret preferences: e.g. if most respondents prefer herbal ingredients, products with such ingredients may gain share.
Interpret media influence: identify which medium (TV, social media, newspapers, word of mouth) influenced most buyers.
The concluding note summarises the main findings, states their limits (sample size, area covered) and gives practical suggestions.

ex.q: Brand A has 80 users, of whom 40 are very satisfied; Brand B has 40 users, of whom 30 are very satisfied. Which brand satisfies its users better?
st: Brand B has fewer users but a higher satisfaction rate.

topics.rl: Market research firms tell clients both 'reach' (how many use the product) and 'satisfaction rate' (how happy users are), because the two can differ.

topics.t: The economy and its central problems
topics.h: Every economy, from a village to India, must answer the same three questions every single day: what to make, how to make it, and who gets it.
p: In any society people produce goods and services, exchange them and consume them to meet their needs. But the resources available (land, labour, capital, raw materials) are limited.
Scarcity of resources relative to wants forces every society to choose how to allocate its resources among competing uses.
What to produce and in what quantities: more food or more clothes, more consumer goods or more capital goods, more public services like schools and hospitals?
How to produce: which technique to use. Labour-intensive techniques use more labour; capital-intensive techniques use more machines.
For whom to produce: how the output is distributed among people, i.e. who gets how much.

ex.q: A government must decide whether to build a dam using thousands of workers or a few huge machines, and whether its electricity will go to farms or factories. Identify the central problems.
st: Choosing workers versus machines is 'how to produce' (technique).
Choosing farms versus factories as users is 'for whom to produce'.
Deciding to build a dam rather than something else is 'what to produce'.
ex.a: All three: what, how and for whom to produce.

topics.rl: India's MGNREGA rural works often use labour-intensive techniques to create jobs, while metro rail projects use tunnel-boring machines: two different answers to 'how to produce'.

topics.t: Production possibility set and frontier
topics.h: With a fixed farm, a farmer can grow lots of corn, lots of cotton, or some of both. Draw all the best-possible combinations and you get a curve that sums up scarcity.
p: Production possibility set: all combinations of two goods that can be produced with the given resources and technology.
Production possibility frontier (PPF): the combinations obtained when resources are fully and efficiently used. Producing more of one good then means producing less of the other.
A point inside the PPF means resources are under-utilised or wasted (e.g. unemployment, idle factories).
A point outside the PPF is unattainable with the current resources and technology.
The PPF is drawn with one good on each axis and is usually concave (bowed out) to the origin.

ex.q: A PPF passes through (corn 2, cotton 7). Classify the points (2, 5) and (2, 9).
st: At corn = 2, the maximum cotton possible is 7.
(2, 5): less cotton than possible → inside the PPF → under-used resources.
(2, 9): more than possible → outside the PPF → unattainable.

topics.rl: During the 2020 lockdown, many factories and workers were idle, so India's output moved to a point well inside its PPF.

topics.t: Opportunity cost and the shape of the PPF
topics.h: Moving land from cotton to corn is easy at first, using land that is better for corn. Push further and you must give up ever more cotton for each extra unit of corn.
p: Opportunity cost of a good: the amount of the other good that must be given up to produce one more unit of it.
Marginal opportunity cost along a PPF is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT): MRT = units of good Y given up ÷ extra units of good X gained.
MRT usually increases as more of one good is produced, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Increasing opportunity cost (increasing MRT) makes the PPF concave (bowed out) to the origin. Constant opportunity cost would give a straight-line PPF.
The slope of the PPF (in absolute value) equals the MRT.

ex.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. Find the opportunity cost of each extra unit of corn.
ex.a: 1, 2, 3, 4 units of cotton: rising opportunity cost, so the PPF is concave

topics.rl: If India shifts land from rice to sugarcane in Maharashtra, the first hectares moved may be well suited to sugarcane, but later ones are better rice land, so each extra tonne of sugarcane costs more rice.

topics.t: Shifts and rotations of the PPF
topics.h: The Green Revolution let Indian farmland grow far more wheat and rice than before. In PPF language, it pushed the frontier outward.
p: The PPF is drawn for given resources and technology. If these change, the PPF moves.
Growth of resources (more labour, more capital, new mineral finds) or general improvement in technology shifts the whole PPF outward (to the right).
Loss of resources (war, earthquake, epidemic deaths) shifts the PPF inward (to the left).
If technology improves for only one good, the PPF rotates: its intercept on that good's axis moves out, while the intercept on the other axis stays the same.
An economy moving from inside the PPF to a point on it (e.g. reducing unemployment) is NOT a shift; the PPF itself is unchanged.

ex.q: A PPF between cloth and wheat. A new high-yield wheat seed is invented. What happens?
st: The maximum wheat (if all resources go to wheat) increases.
The maximum cloth stays the same.
ex.a: The PPF rotates outward along the wheat axis, pivoting on the cloth intercept.

topics.rl: ISRO's satellite-based weather forecasting helps farmers reduce crop losses; better technology like this can push the economy's PPF outward over time.

topics.t: Organisation of economic activities: planned, market and mixed
topics.h: In a market economy, no minister decides how many samosas a city needs, yet there are always enough. Prices do the coordinating.
p: Centrally planned economy: the government (central authority) makes the major decisions about what, how and for whom to produce, aiming at the society's overall welfare.
Market economy: economic activities are organised through the market. A market is any arrangement where people can freely buy and sell goods; it need not be a physical place (online platforms count).
In a market economy, prices act as signals: if demand for a good rises, its price tends to rise, which encourages producers to supply more of it.
Mixed economy: both the market and the government play important roles; the government steps in where markets fail (e.g. defence, public health, help for the poor). India is a mixed economy.

ex.q: Demand for electric scooters rises sharply in Bengaluru. How does a market economy respond, with no central order?
st: Higher demand pushes up the price and profits of e-scooters.
Firms are attracted to produce more and new firms enter.
Output rises to meet demand: prices have coordinated the decision.
ex.a: Price signals lead producers to supply more e-scooters.

topics.rl: In India, prices of most goods are set in markets, but the government runs the Public Distribution System, Indian Railways and public hospitals: a mixed economy at work.

topics.t: Positive vs normative economics, micro vs macro
topics.h: 'Petrol prices rose 5% last year' can be checked with data. 'Petrol should be cheaper' is a judgement. Economists keep the two apart.
p: Positive economics describes how economic mechanisms actually work: what is, was or will be. Its statements can be tested with facts.
Normative economics evaluates whether outcomes are desirable: what ought to be. Its statements involve value judgements (often using 'should', 'ought to').
Microeconomics studies individual economic agents (consumers, firms) and how prices and quantities are determined in individual markets.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: aggregate output, employment, the general price level, growth and inflation.

ex.q: Classify: (a) 'A rise in onion prices reduces quantity demanded.' (b) 'The government should give free electricity to farmers.' (c) 'India's GDP growth rate rose last year.'
st: (a) Testable cause and effect in one market: positive, micro.
(c) A testable fact about the whole economy: positive, macro.

topics.rl: The RBI's study of how a repo-rate change affects inflation is macroeconomics; a study of how a tomato price rise affects tomato demand is microeconomics.

topics.t: Utility, total utility and marginal utility
topics.h: The first golgappa after a long day is heaven. The tenth? Not so much. Economists measure that feeling with utility.
p: Two-good model: a consumer chooses between two goods; a consumption bundle is written (x1, x2), e.g. (3, 2) means 3 units of good 1 and 2 of good 2.
Utility is the want-satisfying power of a commodity. It is subjective and varies from person to person, place to place and time to time.
Cardinal utility approach: utility can be measured in numbers called utils (e.g. 10 utils).
Total utility (TU) is the total satisfaction from consuming a given quantity. Marginal utility (MU) is the change in TU from one more unit: MU_n = TU_n − TU_(n−1).
TU is the sum of marginal utilities: TU_n = MU_1 + MU_2 + … + MU_n.

ex.q: TU from 1, 2, 3, 4 chocolates is 12, 22, 28, 30 utils. Find MU of each.

topics.rl: A glass of water is worth very little to you at home but a lot to a runner at the end of the Mumbai Marathon: utility depends on person, place and time.

topics.t: Diminishing marginal utility and the consumer's equilibrium
topics.h: Why will you pay ₹20 for your first vada pav but not for your fifth? The answer explains why demand curves slope down.
p: Law of diminishing marginal utility: as consumption of a good increases (other things unchanged), the MU from each additional unit falls.
TU–MU relationship: TU rises while MU is positive; TU is maximum when MU = 0; TU falls when MU is negative.
One-good equilibrium: with utility measured in money terms, the consumer buys until MU of the good = its price.
Two-good equilibrium (law of equi-marginal utility): MU_x / P_x = MU_y / P_y, i.e. the last rupee spent on each good gives equal utility.
Deriving demand: if the price falls, MU > price at the old quantity, so the consumer buys more until MU falls to the new price. Diminishing MU thus gives a downward-sloping demand curve.

ex.q: MU (in ₹) of successive ice-creams: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10. The price is ₹30. How many does the consumer buy? What if price falls to ₹20?
st: At ₹30: buy while MU ≥ price → units 1, 2, 3 (MU 50, 40, 30).
Lower price → more quantity: law of demand.

topics.rl: Unlimited thali restaurants rely on diminishing MU: each extra roti gives less satisfaction, so diners stop after a few.

topics.t: Ordinal utility: indifference curves and MRS
topics.h: You can't say a samosa gives exactly 7 utils, but you can say 'I like this combo more than that one'. Ranking is all the ordinal approach needs.
p: Ordinal approach: the consumer cannot measure utility in numbers but can rank bundles (prefer, or be indifferent between them).
Indifference curve (IC): a curve joining all bundles that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. An indifference schedule lists such bundles in a table.
