Marginal rate of substitution (MRS): the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up good 2 for one more unit of good 1 while staying on the same IC. MRS = |Δx2 / Δx1|.
Diminishing MRS: as the consumer has more of good 1, she is willing to give up less and less of good 2 for each extra unit of good 1.

ex.q: Indifference schedule: (1, 15), (2, 11), (3, 8), (4, 6), (5, 5) for (x1, x2). Find MRS at each step.

topics.rl: A cricket fan indifferent between (2 match tickets, 5 pizzas) and (3 tickets, 3 pizzas) gives up 2 pizzas for the 3rd ticket: an MRS of 2.

topics.t: Properties of indifference curves and preferences
topics.h: Two indifference curves can never cross. Try to draw them crossing and you'll prove the consumer contradicts herself.
p: Indifference curves are usually convex to the origin because of diminishing MRS. For perfect substitutes (e.g. two brands of identical salt) the IC is a straight line with constant MRS.
Monotonic preferences: between two bundles, the consumer prefers the one with more of at least one good and no less of the other.
Indifference map: a family of ICs. With monotonic preferences, a higher IC (further from the origin) gives higher satisfaction.
Properties: (1) ICs slope downward from left to right; (2) a higher IC gives higher utility; (3) two ICs never intersect.

Proof that ICs cannot intersect: if IC1 and IC2 met at A, with B on IC1 and C on IC2 and C having more of both goods than B, then A ~ B and A ~ C imply B ~ C. But monotonicity says C is preferred to B: a contradiction.

ex.q: Bundles (5, 6) and (5, 8). Which does a consumer with monotonic preferences prefer, and why can they not lie on the same IC?
st: (5, 8) has more of good 2 and no less of good 1.
By monotonicity (5, 8) is preferred, so they cannot give equal satisfaction.
ex.a: (5, 8) is preferred; they lie on different ICs.

topics.rl: For a person who sees two brands of iodised salt as identical, the indifference curve between them is a straight line: perfect substitutes.

topics.t: The budget set and the budget line
topics.h: ₹100 of pocket money, pens at ₹5, notebooks at ₹10. Every combination you can afford forms your budget set, and its edge is the budget line.
p: Budget set: all bundles the consumer can buy with income M at prices p1 and p2: p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ M.
Budget line: bundles that cost exactly M: p1x1 + p2x2 = M.
Intercepts: if all income goes on good 1, x1 = M/p1; on good 2, x2 = M/p2. Slope of the budget line (good 1 on the horizontal axis) = −p1/p2.
The budget line slopes downward because, with fixed income, buying more of one good means buying less of the other.
The price ratio p1/p2 is the market rate of exchange: the amount of good 2 that must be given up to buy one more unit of good 1.

ex.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Write the budget equation, intercepts and slope. Is (6, 7) affordable?
st: (6, 7) costs 30 + 70 = 100 = M → on the budget line, affordable
ex.a: 5x1 + 10x2 = 100; intercepts 20 and 10; slope −0.5; (6, 7) is on the line.

topics.rl: A student with ₹300 for the week choosing between metro rides (₹30) and canteen meals (₹50) faces the budget line 30x1 + 50x2 = 300.

topics.t: Changes in the budget line
topics.h: Diwali bonus arrives: your budget line jumps outward. Petrol price rises: one end of it swings inward. Learn to predict each move.
p: Change in income (prices constant): the budget line shifts parallel. A rise in income shifts it outward; a fall shifts it inward. The slope −p1/p2 is unchanged.
Change in the price of good 1 only: the line rotates around the x2-intercept (M/p2 stays fixed). A fall in p1 rotates it outward (x1-intercept rises); a rise in p1 rotates it inward.
Change in the price of good 2 only: the line rotates around the x1-intercept.
If income and both prices change in the same proportion (e.g. all double), the budget line does not change at all.

ex.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. What happens if (a) M rises to ₹150; (b) p1 falls to ₹4?
st: (a) New intercepts: 150/5 = 30 and 150/10 = 15; slope still −0.5 → parallel outward shift.
(b) x1-intercept becomes 100/4 = 25; x2-intercept stays 10; slope becomes −0.4 → rotates outward about the x2-intercept.
ex.a: (a) parallel outward shift; (b) outward rotation with the x2-intercept fixed

topics.rl: When cooking-gas prices rise while incomes stay the same, a household's budget line between LPG and other goods rotates inward along the LPG axis.

topics.t: Consumer's equilibrium: indifference curve approach
topics.h: Your preferences say what you'd like; your budget says what you can afford. The best choice is where the two just touch.
p: The consumer chooses the bundle on the highest indifference curve she can reach with her budget.
At the optimum, the budget line is tangent to an IC: MRS = p1/p2 (the slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line).
The optimum lies on the budget line (she spends all income, given monotonic preferences).
If MRS > p1/p2, she values good 1 more than the market does, so she buys more of good 1 (and less of good 2), moving down the budget line until MRS falls to p1/p2.
If MRS < p1/p2, she buys less of good 1 and more of good 2 until MRS rises to p1/p2.

ex.q: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS = 3 while p1 = ₹4 and p2 = ₹2. Is she at the optimum? What should she do?
st: MRS = 3 > 2: she is willing to give up 3 units of good 2 for one unit of good 1, but the market asks only 2.
So buying more of good 1 makes her better off.
ex.a: Not optimal; she should buy more of good 1 and less of good 2 until MRS = 2.

topics.rl: An online shopper comparing earbuds and a speaker within a fixed budget is, without knowing it, trying to equate MRS with the price ratio.

topics.t: Demand: the demand curve and the law of demand
topics.h: Cut the price of off-peak metro tickets and more people ride. Lower price, more bought: the most famous law in economics.
p: Demand: the quantity of a good a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price, during a period. Demand function: q = d(p), with other factors (prices of related goods, income, tastes) held constant.
A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded; plotting it gives the demand curve, e.g. a linear demand curve q = a − bp.
Law of demand: other things remaining the same, quantity demanded rises when the price falls and falls when the price rises.

Deriving the demand curve: as p1 falls, the budget line rotates outward and the new optimum (tangency with a higher IC) usually has more of good 1. Plotting price against quantity gives the demand curve.
A price change has two effects: the substitution effect (the good is now relatively cheaper, so buy more of it) and the income effect (purchasing power rises, so demand rises for a normal good).

ex.q: Demand function q = 20 − 2p. Make a schedule for p = 2, 4, 6, 8 and state the law shown.
ex.a: q falls from 16 to 4 as p rises from 2 to 8: the law of demand.

topics.rl: Falling smartphone prices in India during the 2010s helped push sales up sharply: a lower price, a larger quantity demanded.

topics.t: Normal, inferior and related goods
topics.h: Get your first job and you might buy fewer bus rides and more cab rides. Same rise in income, opposite effects: that's normal versus inferior goods.
p: Normal good: demand rises when income rises (and falls when income falls), e.g. branded clothes, fruits.
Inferior good: demand falls when income rises, e.g. coarse cereals for some households. A good can be normal at low income levels and inferior at higher levels.
Giffen good: a special inferior good whose demand rises when its price rises, because the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect. It violates the law of demand.
Substitutes (tea and coffee): a rise in the price of one raises the demand for the other.
Complements (tea and sugar, cars and petrol): a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other.

ex.q: Income rises from ₹20,000 to ₹30,000. Demand for coarse grain falls from 30 kg to 20 kg; demand for fruit rises from 5 kg to 9 kg. Classify the goods.
ex.a: Coarse grain is inferior; fruit is normal for this household.

topics.rl: When petrol prices rise, demand for petrol cars tends to fall (complements), while demand for CNG and electric vehicles tends to rise (substitutes).

topics.t: Shifts vs movements, and market demand
topics.h: 'Demand for mangoes rose' and 'quantity demanded of mangoes rose' sound alike but mean different things on a graph. Examiners love this distinction.
p: Movement along the demand curve (change in quantity demanded): caused only by a change in the good's own price. Extension = more bought at a lower price; contraction = less at a higher price.
Shift of the demand curve (change in demand): caused by other factors: income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences. Rightward shift = increase in demand; leftward = decrease.
Rightward shift examples: rise in income (normal good), rise in price of a substitute, fall in price of a complement, favourable change in tastes.
Market demand is the horizontal summation of individual demands: at each price, add the quantities demanded by all consumers.
Example: d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. For p ≤ 10, market demand = 25 − 2p; for 10 < p ≤ 15, only consumer 2 buys: 15 − p; for p > 15, zero.

ex.q: d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. Find market demand at p = 4 and p = 12.

topics.rl: A viral health video about millets can shift the demand curve for millets to the right, even with no change in their price.

topics.t: Price elasticity of demand: meaning and the percentage method
topics.h: Raise the price of salt by 10% and people still buy almost the same amount. Raise the price of a particular brand of chips by 10% and sales crash. Elasticity measures this sensitivity.
p: Price elasticity of demand (e_D) = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Because price and quantity move oppositely, e_D is negative; we usually state its absolute value.
Percentage (proportionate) method: e_D = (ΔQ / Q) × (P / ΔP), using the original P and Q.
Elastic demand: |e_D| > 1. Inelastic: |e_D| < 1. Unitary elastic: |e_D| = 1.
Perfectly elastic (e_D = ∞): horizontal demand curve. Perfectly inelastic (e_D = 0): vertical demand curve.
Using a known elasticity: %ΔQ = e_D × %ΔP. With e_D = 2, a 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 20%.

ex.q: Price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity demanded falls from 50 to 45. Find e_D.

topics.rl: Demand for life-saving medicines like insulin is highly inelastic, which is one reason the government caps prices of essential drugs.

topics.t: Elasticity along a demand curve, its determinants and total expenditure
topics.h: On a single straight-line demand curve, elasticity changes at every point: zero at one end, infinity at the other, exactly 1 in the middle.
p: Linear demand q = a − bp: e_D = b × p / q (absolute value). It is 0 where the line meets the quantity axis, 1 at the mid-point, and ∞ where it meets the price axis.
Geometric (point) method: e_D at a point = lower segment ÷ upper segment of the demand line (lower = from the point to the quantity axis; upper = from the point to the price axis).
A demand curve shaped like a rectangular hyperbola (p × q = constant) has unitary elasticity at every point, because total expenditure never changes.
Determinants: nature of the good (necessities inelastic, luxuries elastic), availability of close substitutes (more substitutes → more elastic), share in the budget, habits, and time period.
Total expenditure (p × q) method: if price rises, expenditure rises when demand is inelastic, falls when elastic, and stays constant when unitary elastic.

ex.q: q = 20 − 2p. Find e_D at p = 5 and at p = 4.

topics.rl: Salt has few substitutes and takes a tiny share of the budget, so its demand is very inelastic; one brand of biscuits among dozens has elastic demand.

topics.t: The production function
topics.h: A dosa stall with 1 tawa and 2 cooks makes 60 dosas an hour; add a third cook and maybe 80. The production function is the recipe linking inputs to the maximum output.
p: A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, with a given technology: q = f(L, K), where L is labour and K is capital.
It is a technical relationship; improved technology changes the function itself.
An output table shows the output for different combinations of L and K; read across a row (K fixed) to see the effect of more labour.
Isoquant (in the NCERT book; check your syllabus): a curve showing all combinations of L and K that give the same output. Isoquants slope downward, and a higher isoquant means a higher output.

ex.q: An output table: with K = 2, output is 10, 24, 36 for L = 1, 2, 3; with K = 3, output is 14, 30, 45 for L = 1, 2, 3. What is the output with L = 2, K = 3? What happens if K rises from 2 to 3 with L = 2?
st: Read row K = 3, column L = 2: output = 30.
With L = 2, output rises from 24 (K = 2) to 30 (K = 3).
ex.a: Output = 30; it rises by 6 units when K rises from 2 to 3.

topics.rl: A textile mill in Surat can make the same 1,000 metres of cloth with many workers and old looms or with fewer workers and modern looms: two points on the same isoquant.

topics.t: Short run, long run, and TP, AP and MP
topics.h: A café can hire an extra waiter tomorrow, but building a bigger kitchen takes a year. That difference is the short run versus the long run.
p: Short run: at least one factor (e.g. capital, the building) is fixed; output changes only by varying the variable factor (e.g. labour). Long run: all factors can be varied.
These periods are defined by the flexibility of inputs, not by calendar time; the long run of a tea stall may be weeks, of a steel plant years.
Total product (TP): total output as one variable input (L) changes, other inputs fixed. Average product AP = TP / L.
Marginal product MP = ΔTP / ΔL, or with unit changes MP_L = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
TP is the sum of the MPs; AP at L units is the average of the MPs up to L.

ex.q: TP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4: 10, 24, 36, 44. Find AP and MP.

topics.rl: During festive rush, a sweet shop adds helpers (variable factor) in the same kitchen (fixed factor): a short-run decision.

topics.t: Numericals on TP, AP and MP
topics.h: Board papers love this: give any one of TP, AP or MP, and ask for the other two. Master the three links and these become free marks.
p: From TP: AP = TP/L; MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From AP: TP = AP × L; then MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From MP: TP = running sum of MPs; then AP = TP/L.
Always build the TP column first if it is missing; everything else follows.

ex.q: AP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 is 20, 18, 16, 14. Find TP and MP.

topics.rl: A garment unit manager uses these calculations to decide whether one more tailor on the shop floor adds enough shirts to justify the wage.

topics.t: Law of variable proportions (returns to a factor)
topics.h: Add workers to one small farm: first they help each other, then they get in each other's way, and finally they trample the crop. Output tells this whole story.
p: Law of variable proportions: when more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, the MP of the variable factor first rises, then falls, and may eventually become negative.
Phase I, increasing returns to a factor: MP rises, because the fixed factor is better utilised and workers can specialise.
Phase II, diminishing returns to a factor: MP falls but stays positive, because the fixed factor becomes relatively scarce (factor proportions worsen).
Phase III, negative returns: MP becomes negative and TP falls, because too many variable units crowd the fixed factor.
A rational producer operates in Phase II.

ex.q: MP of labour on a farm for L = 1 to 7: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, 0, −3. Identify the phases.
st: MP falls from 12 down to 0 (L = 3 to 6) without becoming negative: diminishing returns (TP is at its maximum when MP = 0)
ex.a: Phase I: L 1–2; Phase II: L 3–6; Phase III: L 7

topics.rl: In parts of rural India, many family members work on one small plot; the extra worker adds little or nothing to output, a sign of diminishing or even zero marginal product.

topics.t: Shapes of TP, MP and AP curves
topics.h: Three curves, one story. When you draw TP, AP and MP together, their key points line up exactly. Examiners check those alignments.
p: TP first rises at an increasing rate (MP rising), then at a diminishing rate (MP falling but positive), reaches its maximum when MP = 0, and falls when MP is negative.
MP and AP curves are both inverse-U shaped: they rise, reach a maximum and then fall.
MP cuts AP at the maximum point of AP.
When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum; when MP < AP, AP falls.
AP stays positive as long as TP is positive, but MP can become negative.

ex.q: TP for L = 1 to 6: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48. Where is AP maximum, and where is TP maximum?
st: TP maximum (48) where MP = 0, at L = 6
ex.a: AP max = 12 (where MP = AP); TP max = 48 (where MP = 0)

topics.rl: Factory managers who track output per worker (AP) and extra output of the last worker hired (MP) can see that hiring beyond the point where MP falls below AP lowers average productivity.

topics.t: Returns to scale and long-run costs
topics.h: Double every input of a pizza chain, ovens, chefs, outlets, and does output exactly double? That's the long-run question of returns to scale.
p: Note: returns to scale and long-run costs are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when ALL inputs increase in the same proportion: constant (output rises in the same proportion), increasing (more than proportionately) or decreasing (less than proportionately).
Cobb–Douglas production function: q = x1^a × x2^b. Returns to scale are constant if a + b = 1, increasing if a + b > 1, decreasing if a + b < 1.

In the long run all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is U-shaped: it falls under increasing returns to scale, is flat under constant returns, and rises under decreasing returns.
The long-run marginal cost (LRMC) curve cuts LRAC at LRAC's minimum point.

ex.q: q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5. Find output when x1 = 4, x2 = 9, and identify the returns to scale.
st: a + b = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 → constant returns to scale
Check: doubling inputs to (8, 18) gives √8 × √18 = √144 = 12, exactly double.

topics.rl: Large Indian car plants enjoy increasing returns to scale up to a point, which is why carmakers prefer big plants over many small ones.

topics.t: Cost concepts: fixed, variable, average and marginal
topics.h: A food truck pays ₹500 a day for parking whether it sells 0 or 300 rolls. The cost of ingredients rises with every roll. Two very different kinds of cost.
p: The cost function shows the least cost of producing each level of output, given input prices.

Total fixed cost (TFC): costs that do not change with output (rent, salaries of permanent staff, interest). Total variable cost (TVC): costs that vary with output (raw materials, wages of casual workers). TC = TFC + TVC.
AFC = TFC / q; AVC = TVC / q; AC (SAC) = TC / q = AFC + AVC.
Marginal cost (SMC) = ΔTC / Δq = ΔTVC / Δq (fixed cost does not change). With unit steps, MC_q = TC_q − TC_(q−1).
TVC = sum of MCs up to that output (TFC is not included).

ex.q: TFC = ₹100. TVC at q = 1, 2, 3: ₹40, ₹70, ₹90. Find TC, AFC, AVC, AC and MC at q = 3.

topics.rl: For Indian Railways, track maintenance is largely a fixed cost, while fuel for each additional train is a variable cost.

topics.t: Shapes of short-run cost curves
topics.h: Picture cost curves on a graph: one flat line, two rising ones running parallel, a curve that keeps falling, and three U-shapes. Each shape has a reason.
p: TFC is a horizontal straight line. TVC starts from the origin and rises; TC starts from the level of TFC and rises parallel to TVC (the vertical gap is always TFC).
AFC is a rectangular hyperbola: it falls continuously as output rises (AFC × q = TFC is constant) but never touches the x-axis.
SMC, AVC and SAC are U-shaped, because of the law of variable proportions: returns to the variable factor first increase (costs fall), then diminish (costs rise).
SMC cuts AVC and SAC from below at their minimum points. The minimum of SAC lies to the right of the minimum of AVC.
The vertical gap between SAC and AVC equals AFC; it narrows as output rises because AFC keeps falling.

ex.q: TFC = 100. At q = 4, AVC = 30 and at q = 5, AVC = 34. Find AFC and SAC at both outputs and the gap between SAC and AVC.
st: The gap (AFC) narrows as output rises.
ex.a: Gap = AFC: 25 at q = 4, 20 at q = 5

topics.rl: A newspaper's printing press is a big fixed cost; as circulation grows, the fixed cost per copy (AFC) keeps shrinking, which is why bigger print runs make each copy cheaper.

topics.t: Completing cost schedules
topics.h: Given a few numbers, an examiner expects you to fill an entire cost table. One golden rule: always find TC (or TVC) first.
p: From TC: TFC = TC at zero output; TVC = TC − TFC; MC = TC_q − TC_(q−1); AFC, AVC and AC by dividing by q.
From MC and TFC: TVC = running sum of MCs; TC = TFC + TVC; then the averages.
From AC: TC = AC × q; then the rest.
Check your table: MC should cut AVC and AC near their minimum values, and AC − AVC should equal AFC.

ex.q: TC at q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: 100, 140, 170, 190, 220. Find TFC, TVC, MC and AVC.

topics.rl: Small business owners in Indian MSME clusters use such tables to find the output where cost per unit is lowest.

topics.t: Revenue: TR, AR and MR
topics.h: A street vendor sells pens at a fixed ₹10 each. Every extra pen brings exactly ₹10 more. That simple fact gives three straight-line revenue curves.
p: Total revenue TR = price × quantity = p × q.
Average revenue AR = TR / q = p. AR is always equal to price.
Marginal revenue MR = ΔTR / Δq = change in TR from selling one more unit.
When price is constant (as for a price-taking firm), AR = MR = price at every output, and the AR/MR line is horizontal.
With a constant price, TR is a straight line from the origin with slope equal to the price.

ex.q: Price = ₹10. Complete TR, AR and MR for q = 1 to 4.
ex.a: AR = MR = ₹10 throughout; TR rises by ₹10 per unit.

topics.rl: A farmer selling wheat at the government's fixed procurement price earns the same price on every quintal: AR = MR = price.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Features of perfect competition
topics.h: Thousands of farmers sell the same variety of wheat at a mandi. If one farmer asks ₹50 more per quintal, buyers simply walk to the next heap. That is perfect competition.
p: Large number of buyers and sellers: each is too small to influence the market price.
Homogeneous product: every firm's output is identical, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
Free entry and exit: firms can enter or leave the industry without restrictions.
Perfect information: all buyers and sellers know the market price and product details.
Result: each firm is a price taker. It can sell any quantity at the market price, so it faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve.

ex.q: A wheat farmer finds the market price is ₹2,300 per quintal. What happens if she charges (a) ₹2,350, (b) ₹2,250?
st: (a) Buyers know the price and the wheat is identical, so they buy elsewhere: she sells nothing.
(b) She could sell all she wants at ₹2,300 anyway, so cutting price only lowers her revenue.
ex.a: She charges the market price of ₹2,300: she is a price taker.

topics.rl: Agricultural produce like wheat or potatoes sold through mandis comes close to perfect competition; most other markets fall short of the ideal.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Revenue of a price-taking firm
topics.h: A candle maker sells boxes at the market price of ₹10. Every box adds exactly ₹10 to revenue, so her revenue curves are as simple as they get.
p: TR = p × q. With a constant market price, TR is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals the price.
AR = TR/q = p and MR = ΔTR/Δq = p for a price taker.
So the firm's price line = AR = MR = its demand curve: one horizontal line at the market price.
If the market price rises, the TR line becomes steeper and the AR = MR line shifts up.

ex.q: Candle boxes sell at ₹10. Find TR and MR for 1 to 5 boxes.
ex.a: TR rises by ₹10 per box; AR = MR = ₹10.

topics.rl: A farmer selling tomatoes at a mandi where the day's price is ₹20 per kg earns ₹20 on every extra kg: her MR equals the price.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Conditions for profit maximisation
topics.h: Should a firm stop producing when price equals marginal cost? Only if three conditions hold, and the third tells it when to shut down altogether.
p: Profit (π) = TR − TC. A firm chooses output to make profit as large as possible.
Condition 1: price = marginal cost (p = MC, i.e. MR = MC). If p > MC, one more unit adds to profit; if p < MC, cutting output raises profit.
Condition 2: MC must be non-decreasing (rising) at that output. Where MC is falling and equals p, producing more would still raise profit.
Condition 3 (short run): price must be at least minimum AVC. If p < min AVC, the firm should shut down; its loss is then only the TFC.
Condition 3 (long run): price must be at least minimum LRAC; otherwise the firm exits the industry.

ex.q: A firm's MC equals the price of ₹20 at two outputs: 10 units (MC falling) and 40 units (MC rising). At 40 units AVC = ₹16. What output should it choose?
st: At 10 units MC is falling: Condition 2 fails.
At 40 units MC is rising: Condition 2 holds.

topics.rl: Sugar mills crush cane only when the sugar price covers their variable costs (cane, power, wages); otherwise they stay shut for the season.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Profit and loss: graphs and numericals
topics.h: On a graph, profit is literally a rectangle: its height is price minus average cost, and its width is output. Draw it right and you can read profit at a glance.
p: Graph: the firm produces q0 where the horizontal price line meets the rising SMC. Profit (or loss) = (p − SAC at q0) × q0.
If p > SAC at q0: super-normal profit, shown by the rectangle between price and SAC. If p < SAC but p ≥ AVC: a loss rectangle, but the firm still produces in the short run.
From a table: profit = TR − TC at each output; choose the output with the highest profit. Equivalently, keep producing while MC ≤ p.
Check: at the chosen output, MC of the next unit should exceed the price.

ex.q: Price ₹10. TC at q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. Find the profit-maximising output.
ex.a: q = 5, profit ₹14 (MC of the 6th unit, ₹11, exceeds the price).

topics.rl: A hand-pump manufacturer in Ludhiana that checks profit at each output level is doing exactly this table analysis.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: The firm's supply curve, shut-down point and normal profit
topics.h: Plot how much a firm produces at every price and you've drawn its supply curve. Surprise: it's just a piece of its marginal cost curve.
p: Short-run supply curve of a firm: the rising part of the SMC curve from minimum AVC upward. At prices below minimum AVC, output is zero.
Long-run supply curve: the rising part of the LRMC curve from minimum LRAC upward; below minimum LRAC, output is zero.
Shut-down point: in the short run, the point of minimum AVC (where SMC cuts AVC); in the long run, minimum LRAC.
Normal profit: the minimum profit needed to keep the firm in business. It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur (the return from the next best alternative) and is counted as part of cost.
Super-normal profit: profit above normal profit. Break-even point: where price = minimum AC, so the firm earns only normal profit (zero economic profit).

ex.q: A firm's minimum AVC is ₹20 and minimum AC is ₹30. What does it do at prices of ₹15, ₹25 and ₹40?
st: ₹25: between min AVC and min AC: produces where p = SMC, with a loss smaller than TFC.
₹40 > min AC: produces where p = SMC and earns super-normal profit.
ex.a: Shut down at ₹15; produce at a loss at ₹25; produce with super-normal profit at ₹40.

topics.rl: A software engineer who leaves a ₹15 lakh job to start a firm counts that ₹15 lakh as normal profit: her opportunity cost.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Determinants of a firm's supply
topics.h: A new drip-irrigation technique cuts a farmer's cost per kg; a hike in diesel prices raises it. Each pushes the supply curve in a different direction.
p: Supply schedule: quantities a firm is willing to sell at different prices. Law of supply: other things equal, quantity supplied rises with price.
Movement along the supply curve: caused by a change in the good's own price (extension or contraction of supply). Shift: caused by other factors.
Technological progress lowers MC, shifting the supply curve to the right.
A rise in input prices (wages, raw materials, fuel) raises MC, shifting supply to the left.
A unit (per-unit) tax raises the firm's MC by the amount of the tax, shifting supply to the left (upward by the tax).

ex.q: A firm supplies 100 units at ₹20. The government imposes a tax of ₹4 per unit. At what price will it now supply 100 units?
st: The tax raises MC by ₹4 at every output.
To supply 100 units it now needs ₹20 + ₹4.
ex.a: ₹24; the supply curve shifts up (left) by ₹4.

topics.rl: When CNG prices rise, auto-rickshaw operators' costs rise; at any given fare fewer rides are supplied: a leftward shift of supply.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Market supply
topics.h: Two dairy farms: one starts selling milk at ₹10 a litre, the other only at ₹15. Add their supplies and the market supply curve gets a kink at ₹15.
p: Market supply is the horizontal summation of the supply curves of all firms: at each price, add the quantities supplied.
If firms have different shut-down prices, the market supply curve has kinks where each new firm starts producing.
Example: s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10 (0 below); s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15 (0 below). Market: 0 for p < 10; p − 10 for 10 ≤ p < 15; 2p − 25 for p ≥ 15.
With n identical firms each supplying s(p), market supply = n × s(p).
An increase in the number of firms shifts the market supply curve to the right; a decrease shifts it to the left.

ex.q: s1 = p − 10 (p ≥ 10) and s2 = p − 15 (p ≥ 15). Find market supply at p = 12 and p = 20.

topics.rl: When many new solar-panel makers entered India's market, the market supply of panels shifted right at every price.

topics.ch: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
topics.t: Price elasticity of supply
topics.h: When the price of cricket balls doubles before the IPL season, how quickly can Meerut's workshops raise output? Elasticity of supply measures that response.
p: Price elasticity of supply e_S = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price. It is positive because price and quantity supplied move together.
Percentage method: e_S = (ΔQ/Q) × (P/ΔP). Use it both to compute e_S and to predict new quantities: %ΔQ = e_S × %ΔP.
Geometric method for a straight-line supply curve: if it meets the price axis (positive price intercept), e_S > 1; if it passes through the origin, e_S = 1; if it meets the quantity axis, e_S < 1.
Perfectly elastic supply (e_S = ∞): horizontal supply curve. Perfectly inelastic supply (e_S = 0): vertical supply curve (e.g. fixed stock of tickets for a match).

ex.q: Price of cricket balls rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 650. Find e_S.

topics.rl: The number of seats in a stadium for a World Cup final is fixed: supply of tickets is perfectly inelastic, whatever the price.

topics.t: Equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply
topics.h: At 6 a.m. the fish market is chaos; by 8 a.m. a price has settled at which almost every fish finds a buyer. Nobody announced it. The market found its equilibrium.
p: Market equilibrium: the situation where the plans of all buyers and sellers match, i.e. market demand = market supply.
Equilibrium price (p*) and equilibrium quantity (q*) are the price and quantity at which this happens.
Excess demand: at a price below p*, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage).
Excess supply: at a price above p*, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a surplus).
Invisible hand (Adam Smith): under excess demand, competing buyers bid the price up; under excess supply, sellers cut the price; this continues until equilibrium is reached.

ex.q: At ₹30, qD = 80 and qS = 50. At ₹40, qD = 60 and qS = 60. At ₹50, qD = 40 and qS = 70. Find p*, q* and the situation at ₹30 and ₹50.
ex.a: p* = ₹40, q* = 60; excess demand of 30 at ₹30; excess supply of 30 at ₹50.

topics.rl: When a new phone launches at a low introductory price, it sells out within minutes: excess demand, which often pushes resale prices up.

topics.t: Finding equilibrium with demand and supply functions
topics.h: Two straight lines, one equation: set qD = qS and the market's price falls out like a magic trick.
p: Graphically, equilibrium is where the market demand and supply curves intersect: their intersection gives p* and q*.
Algebraically, set qD = qS and solve for p*, then substitute to find q*.
Excess demand function: ED(p) = qD − qS; excess supply function: ES(p) = qS − qD. At p*, both are zero.
For the example: ED(p) = 80 − 4p, so ED(15) = 20 and ED(25) = −20 (i.e. excess supply of 20).

ex.q: qD = 200 − p and qS = 120 + p. Find p*, q* and the excess demand at p = 30.

topics.rl: Economists estimate demand and supply equations for crops like onions to predict how prices will settle after a good or bad harvest.

topics.t: Wage determination in a competitive labour market
topics.h: Why does a delivery app pay its riders what it does? In a competitive labour market, the wage settles where the value of the last worker's output equals the wage.
p: Note: wage determination is in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines it this year.

In a perfectly competitive labour market, firms are wage takers and hire labour up to the point where the wage equals the value of the marginal product of labour: w = VMP_L = p × MP_L (here also equal to MRP_L, the marginal revenue product).
Because MP_L diminishes, the demand curve for labour slopes downward: more workers are hired only at lower wages.
The supply curve of labour slopes upward: higher wages attract more hours of work or more workers.
The equilibrium wage is where market demand for labour equals market supply of labour.

ex.q: Output sells at ₹10 per unit. MP of the 4th worker is 30 units and of the 5th is 20 units. Wage is ₹250. How many workers will the firm hire?

topics.rl: During the festive season, demand for e-commerce delivery staff rises; the labour demand curve shifts right and wages for delivery jobs tend to rise.

topics.t: Shifts in demand or supply
topics.h: A good monsoon floods mandis with onions; a festival boosts demand for sweets. One shifts supply, the other shifts demand, and prices move in predictable ways.
p: Rightward shift of demand (supply unchanged): equilibrium price and quantity both rise. Leftward shift of demand: both fall.
Rightward shift of supply (demand unchanged): price falls and quantity rises. Leftward shift of supply: price rises and quantity falls.
Demand shifts due to: income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences, number of consumers.
Supply shifts due to: input prices, technology, number of firms, unit taxes.

Numerical: with qD = 100 − 2p, if supply rises from qS = 20 + 2p to qS = 40 + 2p, new p* = 15 and q* = 70 (from 20 and 60). A unit tax of ₹4 changes supply to qS = 20 + 2(p − 4) = 12 + 2p, giving p* = 22, q* = 56.

ex.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20, q* = 60). A bumper harvest changes supply to qS = 40 + 2p. Find the new equilibrium.
st: Price fell from 20 to 15, quantity rose from 60 to 70.

topics.rl: Tomato prices often crash after a bumper crop (supply shifts right) and spike after unseasonal rains damage crops (supply shifts left).

topics.t: Simultaneous shifts in demand and supply
topics.h: Diwali raises demand for sweets, while costlier milk cuts their supply. Will sweet prices rise? Certainly. Will more sweets be sold? That depends on which shift is bigger.
p: Both curves shift right: quantity definitely rises; price may rise, fall or stay the same (depends on the relative size of the shifts).
Both curves shift left: quantity definitely falls; price is ambiguous.
Demand shifts right and supply shifts left: price definitely rises; quantity is ambiguous.
Demand shifts left and supply shifts right: price definitely falls; quantity is ambiguous.
Drawing the diagram: draw the original D and S, then shift both. Draw versions where one shift is larger, then equal, to see which variable's change is certain.

ex.q: During a festival, demand for sweets rises and the price of milk rises at the same time. Predict the effect on sweets.
st: Both push price up: price definitely rises.
Quantity: demand pushes it up, supply pushes it down → ambiguous.
ex.a: Price rises; quantity may rise, fall or stay the same.

topics.rl: In a year with rising incomes (demand up) and a good harvest (supply up), the amount of rice sold surely rises, but whether its price rises depends on which effect is stronger.

topics.t: Free entry and exit: long-run equilibrium
topics.h: A new momo stall makes big profits; within months, five more stalls open on the same street. Profits shrink until no one else wants to join.
p: Note: this section is in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines it this year.
With free entry and exit, super-normal profits attract new firms (supply rises, price falls); losses make firms exit (supply falls, price rises).
In the long run, price settles at the minimum average cost (p = min AC), and each firm earns only normal profit.
Equilibrium number of firms = market quantity demanded at p = min AC ÷ output of each firm at min AC.
If demand shifts, the price returns to min AC; only the market quantity and the number of firms change.

ex.q: Each identical firm has min AC = ₹20 at 50 units. Market demand is qD = 1,000 − 10p. Find the long-run price, market quantity and number of firms.

topics.rl: As more cafés open in a busy college area, prices of a cup of coffee tend towards the level that just covers costs, including the owners' normal profit.

topics.t: Price ceiling
topics.h: If the government caps the price of wheat below the market price to help poor families, more people want wheat but farmers offer less. A shortage is born.
p: Price ceiling: a legal maximum price fixed by the government, below the equilibrium price, usually for essential goods (e.g. food grains, kerosene).
At the ceiling price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: excess demand (shortage).
Consequences: the government may need rationing (ration cards and fair price shops, as in the Public Distribution System), long queues, and black markets where goods sell above the ceiling.
A ceiling set above the equilibrium price has no effect, since the market price is already lower.
Case analysis, e.g. rent control: tenants gain lower rents, but fewer houses are offered for rent and maintenance suffers.

ex.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). The government fixes a ceiling of ₹15. Find the shortage.

topics.rl: India's Public Distribution System supplies rice and wheat through fair price shops at prices far below the market, with ration cards deciding who gets how much.

topics.t: Price floor
topics.h: Every season the government announces a minimum support price for wheat. If that price is above the market price, farmers grow more than buyers want, and someone has to buy the extra.
p: Price floor: a legal minimum price fixed by the government, above the equilibrium price.
At the floor price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: excess supply (surplus).
Examples: minimum support price (MSP) for crops, which protects farmers' incomes; minimum wage laws in the labour market, which protect workers.
To maintain the floor, the government may buy the surplus (e.g. procurement by the Food Corporation of India, building buffer stocks) or restrict supply.
A floor set below the equilibrium price has no effect, since the market price is already higher.

ex.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). The government fixes a floor of ₹25. Find the surplus the government must buy.

topics.rl: The Food Corporation of India procures wheat and rice at MSP and stores buffer stocks, which are later used for the Public Distribution System.

qa.q: Which one of these is an economic activity?
qa.a: A plumber repairing a pipe for a fee
qa.e: The plumber provides a service in return for payment, so it is done to earn a living.

qa.q: A doctor treating patients at a clinic for a fee is best described as a:
qa.a: Service producer
qa.e: The doctor produces a service (health care) that patients pay for.

qa.q: Raju works in a garment factory and receives ₹15,000 every month. In this role he is an:
qa.a: Employee
qa.e: Raju sells his labour to the factory owner for wages, so he is an employee.

qa.q: When the same Raju spends part of his wage on vegetables, he acts as a:
qa.a: Consumer
qa.e: Buying goods to satisfy his wants makes him a consumer. One person can play several economic roles.

qa.q: Which statement about economics is correct?
qa.a: It studies how people earn and spend to meet their needs in everyday life
qa.e: Economics begins with everyday activities: consumption, production, work, buying and selling.

qa.q: A taxi driver who drives his own car and charges passengers a fare is mainly a:
qa.a: Service provider
qa.e: He provides a transport service and earns income from it.

qa.q: At a market you observe four things. Which one is NOT an economic activity?
qa.a: A child feeding stray dogs out of kindness
qa.e: Feeding animals out of kindness earns no income and involves no buying or selling.

qa.q: A shopkeeper who employs two helpers is, at the same time, a:
qa.a: Seller and an employer
qa.e: He sells goods to customers (seller) and pays wages to helpers (employer).

qa.q: The basic economic problem arises because:
qa.a: Wants are unlimited and resources are limited
qa.e: The mismatch between unlimited wants and limited means is scarcity, the root of the economic problem.

qa.q: Which of these is the best example of a resource with alternative uses?
qa.a: A farm that can grow wheat or sugarcane
qa.e: The farm can be put to one use or another; choosing one means giving up the other.

qa.q: Meera has ₹1,000. A phone cover costs ₹300, earphones ₹800 and a book ₹400. Which set can she buy?
qa.a: Phone cover and book
qa.e: 300 + 400 = ₹700, which fits in ₹1,000. Every set with the earphones costs more than ₹1,000.

qa.q: A long queue outside a railway reservation counter during Diwali is mainly a sign of:
qa.a: Scarcity
qa.e: Many more people want tickets than there are seats, so seats are scarce.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Every society has to make choices about the use of its resources.
Reason (R): Resources are limited and have alternative uses.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Limited resources with alternative uses are exactly why choice becomes unavoidable.

qa.q: Which statement best expresses 'we cannot get something for nothing'?
qa.a: Everything we get has a cost in terms of money or something given up
qa.e: With limited means, getting one thing means paying for it or giving up something else.

qa.q: Rahul's income is ₹20,000 a month and the goods he wants cost ₹35,000. What is the shortfall he must manage by choosing?
qa.e: Wants exceed means by 35,000 − 20,000 = ₹15,000, so he must give up wants worth at least that much.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of scarcity?
qa.a: A shop with plenty of unsold stock and no buyers
qa.e: Unsold stock with no buyers is excess supply, the opposite of scarcity.

qa.q: The branch of economics that studies how national income is shared as wages, rent, interest and profit is:
qa.a: Distribution
qa.e: Distribution studies how income is divided among the factors of production.

qa.q: Interest is the reward for which factor of production?
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: Interest is paid to the owner of capital for its use.

qa.q: Which is the best definition of economics?
qa.a: The study of how society uses scarce resources with alternative uses to produce and distribute goods and services
qa.e: This definition captures scarcity, alternative uses, production and distribution.

qa.q: A mill's factor payments are wages ₹60 lakh, rent ₹15 lakh, interest ₹10 lakh and profit ₹25 lakh. What is the total income distributed (in ₹ lakh)?
qa.e: Total factor income = 60 + 15 + 10 + 25 = ₹110 lakh.

qa.q: Using the same mill (wages ₹60 lakh out of ₹110 lakh total), what percentage of the income goes to labour? (Round to two decimals.)
A producer deciding whether to make 100 or 200 bicycles a day, using more workers or more machines, is dealing with:
qa.a: Production
qa.e: Deciding how much to produce and with what inputs is the study of production.

qa.q: Why does modern economics need statistics more than ever?
qa.a: Because it studies issues like poverty, unemployment and inequality that must be measured with data
qa.e: Measuring and analysing these issues requires reliable numerical data.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Economics studies only the behaviour of producers.
Reason (R): Consumers do not face scarcity.
qa.a: Both A and R are false
qa.e: Economics studies consumers, producers and distribution, and consumers certainly face scarcity of income.

qa.q: Which of the following is an example of economic data?
qa.a: 'Wheat output was 112 million tonnes'
qa.e: Economic data are facts expressed as numbers.

qa.q: The correct sequence for tackling an economic problem is:
qa.a: Data → analysis → policy
qa.e: First collect data, then analyse causes, then design policy.

qa.q: Analysis of economic data mainly aims to:
qa.a: Find the causes of a problem
qa.e: Analysis identifies the causes, which then guide policy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Economic policy depends on statistical data.
Reason (R): Without data, the causes of a problem cannot be analysed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Policy needs analysis, and analysis needs data, so R explains A.

qa.q: A state finds from survey data that 30% of 2,000 sampled villages lack a primary health centre. How many sampled villages lack one?
Which is the best example of the government using statistical data for development policy?
qa.a: Using Census data on literacy to decide where to open new schools
qa.e: Literacy data show where schools are most needed, guiding the policy.

qa.q: After a new irrigation scheme, a district's crop yield rose from 2,000 kg to 2,500 kg per hectare. By what percentage did the yield rise?
qa.e: Rise = 500 kg on a base of 2,000 kg: 500/2,000 × 100 = 25%. Such numbers help evaluate a policy.

qa.q: Why is statistics called a tool of economics?
qa.a: It helps collect, organise and analyse economic data for theory and policy
qa.e: Statistics supplies and processes the data that economic analysis and policy need.

qa.q: In the sentence 'Statistics of rice production show a rising trend', the word statistics is used in the:
qa.a: Plural sense, meaning numerical data
qa.e: Here statistics refers to the numbers on rice production, i.e. data.

qa.q: Statistics in the singular sense refers to:
qa.a: Methods of collecting, presenting, analysing and interpreting data
qa.e: The singular sense is the science or set of methods for dealing with data.

qa.q: Which of these is qualitative data?
qa.a: Level of honesty of employees
qa.e: Honesty is an attribute and cannot be directly measured in numbers.

qa.q: Which of these is quantitative data?
qa.a: Rice output in million tonnes
qa.e: Output in million tonnes is measured in numbers with a unit.

qa.q: What is the correct order of the first three stages of a statistical study?
qa.a: Collection → organisation → presentation
qa.e: You must first collect data, then organise it, then present it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Statistics deals with both quantitative and qualitative data.
Reason (R): Attributes like gender can be counted, for example the number of females in a class.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Qualitative data become usable in statistics by counting how many units have each attribute.

qa.q: In a class of 40 students, 18 are girls. What percentage of the class are boys?
qa.e: Boys = 40 − 18 = 22. Percentage = 22/40 × 100 = 55%. A qualitative attribute (gender) turned into numbers by counting.

qa.q: Statement: 'Statistics can be used only for quantitative data and never for any attribute.' This statement is:
qa.a: False, because attributes can be counted and classified
qa.e: Qualitative characteristics can be classified and counted, so statistics handles them too.

qa.q: Which function of statistics is shown when the average income of 10 crore households is reported as one figure?
qa.a: Condensation
qa.e: Reducing a mass of data to one summary figure is condensation.

qa.q: An economist checks whether higher income leads to higher spending on food. Which use of statistics is this?
qa.a: Finding relationships between variables
qa.e: Testing how income and spending move together is finding a relationship.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of statistics?
qa.a: It studies aggregates and not individuals
qa.e: Statistics deals with groups; it cannot describe a single unit by itself.

qa.q: Five workers earn ₹8,000, ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹10,000 and ₹65,000. What is their average wage?
qa.e: Average = total / number = 1,00,000 / 5 = ₹20,000. Note how one high wage lifts the average far above most workers.

qa.q: In the previous data (₹8,000, ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹10,000, ₹65,000), how many workers earn LESS than the average of ₹20,000?
qa.e: Four of the five earn below ₹20,000; only one earns more. The average misleads about the typical worker.

qa.q: The 'average depth of a river' story is used to show that:
qa.a: Statistical methods are no substitute for common sense
qa.e: The average was correct but hid dangerous deep parts. Judgement is still needed.

qa.q: A ministry projects next year's crude oil imports from past data. Which use of statistics is this?
qa.a: Forecasting for planning
qa.e: Estimating future values from past data is forecasting, which supports planning.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Statistics can be misused.
Reason (R): Statistics is a precise science, so its results never depend on how data are chosen or presented.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Statistics can be misused precisely because results depend on how data are selected and presented, so R is false.

qa.q: Data collected by the investigator himself for the first time for a specific purpose are called:
qa.a: Primary data
qa.e: First-hand data collected for the enquiry are primary data.

qa.q: Which is an example of secondary data for a student project?
qa.a: Tables from the NSS report on household consumption
qa.e: The NSS report was collected by another agency, so it is secondary data for her.

qa.q: Census 2011 data are primary for:
qa.a: The office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, which collected them
qa.e: Data are primary for the agency that collected them first-hand.

qa.q: A main advantage of secondary data is that they:
qa.a: Save time and cost
qa.e: Someone else has already collected them, so you save time and money.

qa.q: A researcher has very little time and money but needs state-wise literacy rates. The most sensible choice is:
qa.a: Use published secondary data such as Census tables
qa.e: With limited time and money, reliable published data are the practical choice.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Before using secondary data, the investigator should check their reliability and suitability.
Reason (R): Secondary data were collected by someone else, possibly for a different purpose.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because they were gathered for another purpose, they may not fit or be reliable, so checking is needed.

qa.q: A survey records the monthly incomes of 25 households. How many observations of the variable 'income' does it have?
qa.e: Each household's recorded income is one observation, so there are 25.

qa.q: Which of these describes data as used in statistics?
qa.a: Values of variables, each recorded value being an observation
qa.e: Data are recorded values of variables; each value is an observation.

qa.q: Which of the following is a two-way question?
qa.a: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
qa.e: A two-way question offers exactly two possible answers, such as yes or no.

qa.q: 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best in the market?' is a poor question mainly because it is:
qa.a: Leading
qa.e: It pushes the respondent towards agreeing.

qa.q: A questionnaire should generally move from:
qa.a: General to specific questions
qa.e: Starting with general questions eases the respondent into the specific ones.

qa.q: The main disadvantage of open-ended questions is that the answers are:
qa.a: Difficult to compare and interpret
qa.e: Free answers vary widely in content and wording, so they are hard to tabulate and compare.

qa.q: Which question avoids ambiguity best?
qa.a: How many hours did you study yesterday?
qa.e: It asks for a precise, measurable answer about a fixed time.

qa.q: Which question should NOT be put in a questionnaire?
qa.a: If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
qa.e: Questions that require calculation burden the respondent and cause errors.

qa.q: A firm surveying the popularity of its noodles wants answers it can tabulate easily. It should mostly use:
qa.a: Closed-ended (multiple-choice) questions
qa.e: Closed-ended questions give fixed options that are quick to count and compare.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Closed-ended questions are easy to analyse.
Reason (R): Closed-ended questions are always easy to frame.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Closed questions are easy to analyse, but framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.

qa.q: Which method of data collection gives the highest response rate?
qa.a: Personal interview
qa.e: Face-to-face contact makes refusals less likely and lets the interviewer clarify questions.

qa.q: A major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire method is:
qa.a: Low response rate
qa.e: Many people do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.

qa.q: The telephone interview method cannot be used for people who:
qa.a: Do not have access to a phone
qa.e: Only people with phones can be reached.

qa.q: Which mode is most suitable for a survey of non-literate respondents?
qa.a: Personal interview
qa.e: An interviewer can read the questions aloud and record answers.

qa.q: A pilot survey is conducted:
qa.a: Before the main survey as a small trial
qa.e: It is a trial run to test the questionnaire and estimate cost and time.

qa.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey?
qa.a: Replacing the need for a main survey
qa.e: A pilot survey prepares for the main survey; it does not replace it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In a personal interview, the respondent's answers may be influenced by the interviewer.
Reason (R): The interviewer is physically present and may unintentionally suggest answers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers.

qa.q: A survey team mails 800 questionnaires and gets 200 back. What is the response rate?
qa.e: Response rate = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Low response is typical of mailed surveys.

qa.q: In statistics, 'population' means:
qa.a: All the units under study
qa.e: Population (universe) is the complete set of items being studied.

qa.q: Complete enumeration of every unit of the population is called:
qa.a: Census
qa.e: A census covers every unit.

qa.q: A study selects 300 households out of 6,000 households in a town. What percentage of the population is in the sample?
In a study of the monthly expenditure of 80 students chosen from a college of 1,600, the variable is:
qa.a: Monthly expenditure
qa.e: The variable is the characteristic being measured: monthly expenditure.

qa.q: Which situation requires a sample rather than a census?
qa.a: Testing matchsticks by striking them
qa.e: Testing destroys matchsticks, so only a sample can be tested.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A sample survey can collect more detailed information than a census with the same budget.
Reason (R): A sample covers fewer units, so more time and money can be spent on each unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: With fewer units, resources can go into detailed, careful questioning.

qa.q: A good sample should be:
qa.a: Representative of the population
qa.e: It must reflect the features of the population to give reliable estimates.

qa.q: India's population was about 23.8 crore in 1901 and about 121 crore in 2011. Roughly how many times did it grow?
qa.a: About 5 times
qa.e: 121 ÷ 23.8 ≈ 5.1, so about five times in 110 years.

qa.q: In random sampling:
qa.a: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
qa.e: Equal chance of selection is the defining feature of random sampling.

qa.q: How many different samples of 2 can be drawn from 6 households?
How many different samples of 3 students can be chosen from 10 students?
The list of all units of the population from which a sample is drawn is called the:
qa.a: Sampling frame
qa.e: A sampling frame is the full list, like a voters' list or school register.

qa.q: Choosing respondents simply because they are easy to reach is:
qa.a: Convenience sampling
qa.e: Convenience sampling picks easily accessible units, so bias is likely.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Non-random sampling may give biased results.
Reason (R): In non-random sampling, all units do not have an equal chance of being selected.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Unequal chances let the investigator's choice or convenience distort the sample.

qa.q: A lottery is drawn, but the slips for some names are folded differently and are easier to pick. Is the sample still random?
qa.a: No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
qa.e: A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed, giving each unit an equal chance.

qa.q: Why can an exit poll go wrong?
qa.a: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
qa.e: Unrepresentative booths or untruthful answers bias the estimate.

qa.q: Sampling error is the difference between:
qa.a: The sample estimate and the actual population value
qa.e: It is the gap between what the sample says and the true population value.

qa.q: Population of 5 incomes: ₹200, ₹300, ₹400, ₹500, ₹600. A sample picks ₹200 and ₹300. By how much does the sample mean underestimate the population mean?
qa.e: Population mean = 2,000/5 = ₹400. Sample mean = ₹250. The sample falls short by 400 − 250 = ₹150; this gap is the sampling error.

qa.q: Population of 4 marks: 40, 50, 60, 70. A sample picks 60 and 70. What is the sampling error of the sample mean?
qa.e: Population mean = 55, sample mean = 65, so error = 65 − 55 = 10 (an overestimate).

qa.q: Which of the following is a non-sampling error?
qa.a: An enumerator records the wrong age
qa.e: Recording mistakes are errors in data acquisition, a non-sampling error.

qa.q: Sampling error can be reduced by:
qa.a: Increasing the size of the sample
qa.e: Larger samples represent the population better.

qa.q: A telephone survey about internet use in a district misses all households without phones. This is:
qa.a: Sampling bias
qa.e: The method systematically excludes part of the population: sampling bias.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Non-sampling errors can occur even in a census.
Reason (R): A census covers every unit of the population.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but covering every unit does not explain the errors; they come from recording, non-response and similar problems.

qa.q: Why are non-sampling errors considered more serious than sampling errors?
qa.a: They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
qa.e: They arise from bias, non-response and recording errors, which a bigger sample does not remove.

qa.q: The Census of India has been conducted regularly every ten years since:
qa.e: Regular decennial census began in 1881.

qa.q: The first Census of independent India was held in:
qa.e: It was conducted in 1951.

qa.q: Which agency conducts large-scale sample surveys in 'rounds' on consumer expenditure and employment?
qa.a: NSSO
qa.e: NSSO runs nationwide sample surveys in rounds.

qa.q: The journal in which NSSO publishes its survey results is:
qa.a: Sarvekshana
qa.e: NSSO's journal is Sarvekshana.

qa.q: Data on India's foreign trade are compiled by:
qa.a: DGCIS
qa.e: The Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics compiles trade data.

qa.q: Census 2011 was the 7th Census after independence. If censuses are 10 years apart, in which year was the 1st post-independence census held?
qa.e: Counting back six gaps of 10 years from 2011 gives 2011 − 60 = 1951.

qa.q: Which of these is a secondary source of economic data published by the Ministry of Finance every year?
qa.a: Economic Survey
qa.e: The Economic Survey is released by the Ministry of Finance before the Union Budget.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Census is the most complete source of demographic data in India.
Reason (R): The Census covers every household through complete enumeration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because it enumerates everyone, it gives the fullest population data.

qa.q: Data in their original, unorganised form are called:
qa.a: Raw data
qa.e: Unprocessed data as collected are raw data.

qa.q: The main purpose of classification is to:
qa.a: Bring order to data so they can be analysed
qa.e: Classification organises data into groups for easy understanding and analysis.

qa.q: Which is a valid criterion for classifying a list of workers?
qa.a: Their monthly wages
qa.e: A classification needs a clear, relevant basis such as wage level.

qa.q: From the raw marks 34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38, how many are below 50?
qa.e: Below 50: 34, 45, 38, so 3 values.

qa.q: From the same raw marks (34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38), what is the difference between the highest and lowest value?
qa.e: Highest = 91, lowest = 34, difference = 57. With raw data you must scan every value to find them.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Classified data are more useful than raw data for analysis.
Reason (R): Classification groups similar items, making comparison and analysis easier.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Grouping makes patterns visible, which is why classified data aid analysis.

qa.q: Why is it tedious to find the average from a large mass of raw data?
qa.a: Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately
qa.e: Without grouping, every individual value must be processed.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an advantage of classification?
qa.a: It guarantees that data are free of errors
qa.e: Classification organises data; it cannot correct errors made during collection.

qa.q: Classification of data according to time is called:
qa.a: Chronological classification
qa.e: Classifying by years, months or days is chronological (temporal).

qa.q: Data on cotton production in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are an example of:
qa.a: Spatial classification
qa.e: Classifying by place (states) is spatial or geographical.

qa.q: Classifying a population first by sex, then each group by literate/illiterate, is called:
qa.a: Manifold classification
qa.e: Classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.

qa.q: Grouping workers by their daily wages into ₹200–300, ₹300–400 and so on is:
qa.a: Quantitative classification
qa.e: Wages are measurable, so this is quantitative classification.

qa.q: Out of 80 households, 20 fall in the income class ₹20,000–30,000. What is the relative frequency of this class?
In a survey of 200 people, 46 are in the 20–30 years age class. What percentage of people does this class hold?
A time series is produced by which type of classification?
qa.a: Chronological
qa.e: Arranging values by time gives a time series.

qa.q: The relative frequencies of all classes in a distribution add up to:
qa.e: Each is class frequency ÷ total, so together they sum to total ÷ total = 1 (or 100%).

qa.q: Which of the following is a continuous variable?
qa.a: Weight of a newborn baby
qa.e: Weight can take any value in a range, such as 2.85 kg.

qa.q: Which of these is a discrete variable?
qa.a: Number of tractors in a village
qa.e: Tractors are counted in whole numbers.

qa.q: A variable that can take any value, including fractions, within a range is called:
qa.a: Continuous
qa.e: That is the definition of a continuous variable.

qa.q: The number obtained on rolling a dice is:
qa.a: A discrete variable
qa.e: It can only be one of six whole numbers.

qa.q: How many possible values can the variable 'number on a standard dice' take?
qa.e: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: six values, which is why it is discrete.

qa.q: Which pair has one continuous and one discrete variable?
qa.a: Time taken and number of students
qa.e: Time is continuous; number of students is discrete.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Population of a city is a discrete variable.
Reason (R): Population can take any fractional value.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Population is a count of people, so it takes only whole numbers; R is false.

qa.q: What is the main difference between a variable and an attribute?
qa.a: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
qa.e: Variables (income, height) are quantitative; attributes (gender, honesty) are qualitative.

qa.q: The class mark of the class 30–50 is:
The class interval (width) of the class 15–25 is:
The lowest value in a data set is 18 and the highest is 96. What is the range?
The mid-point of a class is 45 and its lower limit is 40. What is the upper limit?
The class mark of a class is used in calculations because:
qa.a: It represents all the values in that class
qa.e: Once data are grouped, each value in a class is represented by the mid-point.

qa.q: A frequency curve is obtained by plotting:
qa.a: Frequencies against class marks and joining them by a smooth curve
qa.e: Frequencies are plotted against class marks and joined smoothly.

qa.q: The class marks of consecutive equal classes are 25, 35, 45. What is the class width?
qa.e: With equal classes, the gap between consecutive class marks equals the class width: 35 − 25 = 10.

qa.q: Consecutive class marks are 25, 35, 45 and the class width is 10. What are the limits of the first class?
Data range from 10 to 89. With a class width of 10, how many classes are needed?
qa.e: Range = 89 − 10 = 79, and 79/10 = 7.9, which is rounded up to 8 classes (10–20 up to 80–90).

qa.q: Which situation calls for unequal class intervals?
qa.a: Incomes ranging from ₹5,000 to ₹50 lakh with most below ₹50,000
qa.e: A huge range with bunching at one end is better shown with unequal classes.

qa.q: Open-ended classes such as 'Above 80' are generally avoided because:
qa.a: They have no defined mid-point
qa.e: Without an upper limit, the class mark cannot be found, which hampers calculations.

qa.q: In tally marking, the fifth observation is shown by:
qa.a: A stroke crossing the previous four
qa.e: The fifth stroke crosses the first four, making a bundle of five.

qa.q: If 4 complete tally groups and 3 extra strokes are marked against a class, its frequency is:
The values 21, 22, 23 and 28 fall in the class 20–30. After grouping, what single value represents each of them?
qa.e: Every value in the class is represented by the class mark (20 + 30)/2 = 25. This is the loss of information in grouping.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Grouping data into classes leads to some loss of information.
Reason (R): After grouping, individual values are replaced by the class mark.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Replacing actual values with the mid-point is exactly why detail is lost.

qa.q: Raw data: 5, 12, 18, 23, 7, 15, 28, 21, 9, 14. Using classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 (exclusive), what is the frequency of 10–20?
qa.e: Values from 10 up to but not including 20: 12, 18, 15, 14, so 4.

qa.q: In the exclusive method with classes 40–50 and 50–60, a value of exactly 50 goes into:
qa.e: The upper limit is excluded, so 50 goes into the class starting at 50.

qa.q: In the inclusive method, classes are written as:
qa.e: Both limits are included, so classes do not share limits.

qa.q: Adjust the inclusive class 60–69 (next class 70–79). The adjusted class is:
For inclusive classes 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, what is the correction (half the gap) to be applied?
qa.e: Gap = 15 − 14 = 1, half of it is 0.5.

qa.q: After adjusting 10–14 to 9.5–14.5, what is the true class width?
qa.e: 14.5 − 9.5 = 5. The unadjusted '14 − 10 = 4' understates the width.

qa.q: The class mark of the inclusive class 20–29 is:

Assertion (A): Inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram.
Reason (R): Inclusive classes have gaps between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: A histogram needs continuous classes, so the gaps must be removed by adjustment.

qa.q: Marks (whole numbers) are to be grouped by the inclusive method with class width 10, starting at 0. The third class is:
qa.e: Classes are 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, so the third is 20–29.

qa.q: A frequency array is used for:
qa.a: A discrete variable
qa.e: A frequency array lists each value of a discrete variable with its frequency.

qa.q: Household sizes from a survey: 3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3. What is the frequency of household size 4?
qa.e: Size 4 appears four times.

qa.q: Using the same data (3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3), how many households have more than 4 members?
qa.e: More than 4 means 5 or 6: one each, so 2 households.

qa.q: A distribution showing the joint frequencies of two variables is called:
qa.a: Bivariate
qa.e: Bivariate means two variables classified together.

qa.q: In a bivariate table of 20 firms, the cell for 'ad spend 5–10' and 'sales 100–200' is 3, and the row total for 'ad spend 5–10' is 8. How many firms with ad spend 5–10 have sales outside 100–200?
qa.e: 8 − 3 = 5 firms in that row lie in other sales classes.

qa.q: The row totals in a bivariate table give:
qa.a: The distribution of the row variable alone
qa.e: Adding across a row gives that variable's own frequency for each class.

qa.q: Count the letters in each word of the phrase 'DATA IS THE NEW OIL'. What is the frequency of 3-letter words?
qa.e: Word lengths: DATA 4, IS 2, THE 3, NEW 3, OIL 3. Three words have 3 letters.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A bivariate distribution can show whether two variables tend to move together.
Reason (R): It records how often each combination of classes of the two variables occurs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Seeing which combinations are common hints at how the variables are related.

qa.q: How many broad forms of data presentation are there?
qa.e: Textual, tabular and diagrammatic: three forms.

qa.q: Textual presentation is most suitable when:
qa.a: Data are small in quantity
qa.e: With only a few figures, sentences communicate them clearly.

qa.q: A major drawback of textual presentation is that:
qa.a: The reader must read the whole text to understand the data
qa.e: Figures are buried in sentences, making quick comprehension and comparison hard.

qa.q: 'Of the 50 workers in a factory, 35 joined the strike.' This is an example of:
qa.a: Textual presentation
qa.e: The data are described in a sentence.

qa.q: In the statement 'Of the 50 workers in a factory, 35 joined the strike', what percentage of workers did NOT join?
Which advantage does textual presentation have over a table?
qa.a: It allows emphasis on certain points
qa.e: A writer can stress key facts through sentences.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Large data are generally not presented in textual form.
Reason (R): In textual form, comparison of many figures is difficult.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because comparing many figures in sentences is hard, large data go into tables or diagrams.

qa.q: Which form gives the quickest visual impression of the data?
qa.a: Diagrammatic
qa.e: Diagrams convey patterns at a glance, though less exactly than tables.

qa.q: In a table, each box formed where a row and a column meet is called a:
qa.a: Cell
qa.e: That box is a cell.

qa.q: A table showing literacy rates for males and females in rural and urban areas uses:
qa.a: Qualitative classification
qa.e: Sex and location type are attributes, so this is qualitative.

qa.q: A table showing the share of India's exports to different countries uses:
qa.a: Spatial classification
qa.e: Classifying by country is spatial.

qa.q: A table showing population by age groups 0–14, 15–59 and 60 and above uses:
qa.a: Quantitative classification
qa.e: Age is measurable and grouped into classes.

qa.q: A table has 5 rows and 4 columns of data in its body. How many cells does the body have?
qa.e: 5 × 4 = 20 cells.

qa.q: Rows of a table are arranged:
qa.a: Horizontally
qa.e: Rows run horizontally; columns run vertically.

qa.q: A table gives sugar production for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The classification is:
qa.a: Temporal
qa.e: Classification by years is temporal (chronological).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Tables make comparison of data easier than text.
Reason (R): In a table, related figures are placed side by side in rows and columns.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Placing figures side by side is exactly what makes comparison easy.

qa.q: Column headings of a table are called:
qa.a: Captions
qa.e: Captions head the columns.

qa.q: Row headings of a table are called:
qa.a: Stubs
qa.e: Stubs head the rows.

qa.q: The part of a table that tells the reader where the data were obtained from is the:
qa.a: Source
qa.e: The source line names the origin of the data.

qa.q: A table classifies workers by gender and by location (rural/urban). It is a:
qa.a: Two-way table
qa.e: Two characteristics make it a two-way table.

qa.q: A table classifies students by gender, by stream (Science/Commerce/Arts) and by result (pass/fail). It is a:
qa.a: Three-way table
qa.e: Three characteristics make it a three-way table.

qa.q: ₹4,56,78,90,000 rounded to crore (one crore = 1,00,00,000) and to two decimals is how many crore?
Where is the title of a table normally placed?
qa.a: At the top
qa.e: The title sits at the top, after the table number.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A good table must state the unit of measurement.
Reason (R): Without the unit, the figures in the body cannot be correctly understood.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: '45' could mean ₹45 or 45 crore tonnes; the unit gives meaning.

qa.q: You convert this passage into a table: 'In 2011, literacy was 82% among males and 65% among females; in 2001 it was 75% among males and 54% among females.' If the years 2001 and 2011 are the stubs, what are the captions?
qa.a: Male and Female
qa.e: Stubs are the row headings (here the years), so the column headings (captions) are the other characteristic: Male and Female. The figures 75, 54, 82, 65 go in the body.

qa.q: In a simple bar diagram, the value of each item is shown by the bar's:
qa.a: Height (length)
qa.e: Only the height carries the value; all widths are equal.

qa.q: To compare literacy rates of males and females across five states, the best diagram is a:
qa.a: Multiple bar diagram
qa.e: Side-by-side bars for males and females compare two series per state.

qa.q: A component bar diagram is used to show:
qa.a: Parts of a total
qa.e: Each bar is divided into components of the total.

qa.q: A household spends ₹12,000 out of ₹40,000 on food. In a percentage component bar, the food portion has height:
In a percentage component bar for a firm, wages are 45 and raw materials are 35. If the rest is profit, what is the height of the profit portion?
Which is NOT a rule of a bar diagram?
qa.a: Bars should touch each other without gaps
qa.e: Bar diagrams have gaps between bars; touching bars belong to histograms.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Bar diagrams can be used for qualitative data such as religion or occupation.
Reason (R): A bar diagram needs a continuous variable on the x-axis.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Bar diagrams suit attributes and discrete data; it is the histogram that needs a continuous variable.

qa.q: Rice output (million tonnes): State A 16, State B 12, State C 8. If 1 cm represents 4 million tonnes, the bar for State B is how long?
qa.a: 3 cm

qa.q: In a pie diagram, the sector angle for a component that is 40% of the total is:
A sector of 54° represents what percentage of the total?
Out of ₹5,000 monthly expenses, a student spends ₹1,250 on books. The sector angle for books is:
In a pie diagram, the sum of all sector angles is:
qa.e: A full circle measures 360°.

qa.q: A pie diagram has three components. Two of them have angles of 150° and 120°. What is the angle of the third component?
Which data are LEAST suitable for a pie diagram?
qa.a: Monthly rainfall in Mumbai over a year
qa.e: Monthly rainfall is a time series, not parts of one whole; a bar diagram or line graph suits it.

qa.q: A town's population is 60% Hindi speakers, 25% Marathi speakers and the rest others. What is the sector angle for 'others'?

Assertion (A): A pie diagram is suitable for showing components of a whole.
Reason (R): The angles of all sectors together make up the full circle of 360°, representing the total.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because the circle stands for the total, its slices naturally show parts of the whole.

qa.q: A histogram can be drawn only for:
qa.a: Continuous data
qa.e: Its rectangles stand on continuous class intervals.

qa.q: In a histogram, the frequency of a class is proportional to the rectangle's:
qa.a: Area
qa.e: Area (width × height) represents frequency.

qa.q: Class 20–40 has frequency 30. If classes are unequal, the height of its rectangle (frequency density) is:
Classes 0–5 (f = 10) and 5–15 (f = 10). Which rectangle is taller in the histogram?
qa.a: 0–5, height 2 versus 1
qa.e: Densities: 10/5 = 2 and 10/10 = 1. Equal frequencies spread over a wider class give a shorter rectangle.

qa.q: Inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29 must be converted before drawing a histogram because:
qa.a: Histograms need continuous classes without gaps
qa.e: The gaps (19 to 20) must be removed: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.

qa.q: Which can be located graphically using a histogram?
qa.a: Mode
qa.e: The mode is found from the tallest rectangle and lines to its neighbours.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In a histogram, rectangles are drawn without gaps.
Reason (R): The class intervals of a continuous variable are continuous, with no breaks between them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Continuous classes run into each other, so the rectangles touch.

qa.q: A class 50–60 has frequency 12 and the next class 60–80 has frequency 12. What is the frequency density of 60–80?
qa.e: Width = 20, density = 12/20 = 0.6.

qa.q: A less-than ogive is drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against:
qa.a: Upper class limits
