qa.e: 'Less than' totals are measured up to the upper limit of each class.

qa.q: A more-than ogive generally:
qa.a: Falls from left to right
qa.e: 'More than' totals get smaller as the lower limit increases.

qa.q: The median of a distribution can be found graphically from:
qa.a: The intersection of less-than and more-than ogives
qa.e: The x-value of the meeting point of the two ogives is the median.

qa.q: Frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5 for classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40. What is the 'less than 30' cumulative frequency?
Same data (5, 8, 12, 5 for 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40). What is the 'more than 20' cumulative frequency?
A frequency polygon is closed at both ends by:
qa.a: Joining to the mid-points of imaginary zero-frequency classes
qa.e: Extending to zero-frequency classes on each side closes the polygon on the x-axis.

qa.q: Less-than and more-than ogives meet at a point where x = 34 and y = 25. What is the median?
qa.e: The median is the x-coordinate of the intersection: 34. (The y-value 25 is N/2.)

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A frequency curve is drawn as a smooth freehand curve.
Reason (R): It is drawn through the points of a frequency polygon to smooth out its sharp corners.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Smoothing the polygon's points gives the frequency curve.

qa.q: In an arithmetic line graph, the x-axis usually shows:
qa.a: Time
qa.e: It is a time series graph, so time goes on the horizontal axis.

qa.q: Which diagram best compares the growth rates of agriculture, industry and services over 10 years?
qa.a: Multiple line graph
qa.e: Three time series on the same axes are best compared with a multiple line graph.

qa.q: Exports were ₹400 crore and imports ₹550 crore in a year. If both are plotted on a multiple line graph, what is the vertical gap (trade deficit) that year, in ₹ crore?
qa.e: Deficit = imports − exports = 550 − 400 = ₹150 crore.

qa.q: A line graph mainly helps to show:
qa.a: Trends over time
qa.e: It reveals upward or downward movement over time.

qa.q: Which data are best shown by a histogram?
qa.a: Weights of 100 babies in classes 2–2.5 kg, 2.5–3 kg, etc.
qa.e: A continuous frequency distribution suits a histogram.

qa.q: Vegetable prices rise every summer and fall every winter, year after year. On a monthly line graph, this pattern is called:
qa.a: Seasonal variation
qa.e: Regular movements within a year are seasonal.

qa.q: A firm's sales were 100, 120, 150 and 180 units in four years. By how many units did sales rise from the first to the last year, as shown by the line graph?

Assertion (A): A multiple line graph is useful for comparing India's exports and imports over time.
Reason (R): Both series can be plotted on the same axes, showing their trends and the gap between them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Plotting both on common axes makes their comparison direct.

qa.q: Find the arithmetic mean of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24.
Using an assumed mean A = 50, the sum of deviations of 10 observations is 20. What is the mean?
By the step deviation method: A = 50, c = 10, Σd′ = −3, N = 6. Find the mean.
Marks: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Using A = 80 and c = 10, Σd′ equals:
qa.e: d′ = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, which sum to 0, so X̄ = 80.

qa.q: Daily earnings of 4 auto drivers are ₹600, ₹750, ₹820 and ₹830. What is their mean earning?
Which of the following is NOT one of the three averages studied in this chapter?
qa.a: Geometric mean
qa.e: Geometric and harmonic means exist but are outside this chapter.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The assumed mean and direct methods give the same arithmetic mean.
Reason (R): The assumed mean method simply shifts the origin to A and then adds A back.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Subtracting A and adding it back cannot change the mean; it only makes the arithmetic easier.

qa.q: What is the mean of the first 10 natural numbers?
X: 10, 20, 30 with f: 2, 3, 5. Find the mean.
Classes 0–20, 20–40, 40–60 have frequencies 4, 6, 10. Find the mean.
Using step deviation: A = 45, c = 10, Σfd′ = 6 and Σf = 30. What is the mean?
Less-than cumulative frequencies: <10: 3, <20: 8, <30: 15, <40: 20. What is the frequency of the class 20–30?
More-than cumulative frequencies: >0: 50, >10: 45, >20: 35, >30: 15, >40: 0. Find the mean (classes 0–10 to 30–40).
Unequal classes 0–10, 10–30, 30–60 have frequencies 5, 10, 5. Find the mean.
For inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, the mid-point used for the class 20–29 is:
qa.e: (20 + 29)/2 = 24.5, and adjustment to 19.5–29.5 gives the same 24.5.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Adjusting inclusive classes does not change the arithmetic mean.
Reason (R): Adjustment changes all class mid-points by half the gap.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Adjustment lowers each lower limit and raises each upper limit by the same amount, so mid-points do not change; R is false.

qa.q: For the data 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, what is the sum of deviations from the mean?
qa.e: Mean = 8; deviations −4, −2, 0, 2, 4 sum to 0. This always holds for the mean.

qa.q: A student scores 80 in Economics (weight 3), 70 in English (weight 2) and 40 in Hindi (weight 1). Find the weighted mean.
qa.e: ΣwX = 240 + 140 + 40 = 420; Σw = 6; weighted mean = 70.

qa.q: The mean of 10 observations is 15. Later it is found that one value 24 was wrongly recorded as 42. What is the correct mean?
qa.e: Wrong sum = 150; correct sum = 150 − 42 + 24 = 132; correct mean = 13.2.

qa.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4 with f: 4, f₁, 6, 4. The mean is 2.5. Find f₁.
qa.e: ΣfX = 4 + 2f₁ + 18 + 16 = 38 + 2f₁ and Σf = 14 + f₁. Then 2.5(14 + f₁) = 38 + 2f₁, so 35 + 2.5f₁ = 38 + 2f₁, giving 0.5f₁ = 3 and f₁ = 6.

qa.q: Five workers earn ₹10,000 each. A sixth worker who earns ₹70,000 joins. What happens to the mean wage?
qa.a: Rises to ₹20,000
qa.e: New total = 50,000 + 70,000 = ₹1,20,000; mean = 1,20,000/6 = ₹20,000. One extreme value doubles the mean.

qa.q: The mean of 6 observations is 40. If 5 is added to each observation, the new mean is:
qa.e: Adding a constant to every value raises the mean by that constant.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The arithmetic mean may not represent data with extreme values well.
Reason (R): The sum of deviations of items from the mean is zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the zero-sum property does not explain why extremes distort the mean; the reason is that every value enters the sum.

qa.q: A household index uses weights 50 for food, 30 for housing and 20 for others. Price relatives are 120, 110 and 130. Find the weighted mean relative.
X: 10, 20, 30 with f: 3, f₁, 4. The mean is 21. Find f₁ and then the median.
qa.e: ΣfX = 30 + 20f₁ + 120 = 150 + 20f₁ and Σf = 7 + f₁. 21(7 + f₁) = 150 + 20f₁ gives f₁ = 3. Then N = 10, cf = 3, 6, 10, and the 5th and 6th items are both 20, so the median is 20.

qa.q: Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.
qa.e: Ordered: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The 3rd item is 7.

qa.q: Find the median of 12, 5, 8, 20, 15, 10.
qa.e: Ordered: 5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20. Middle items are 10 and 12, so median = 11.

qa.q: In ungrouped data with N = 15 items arranged in order, the median is the:
qa.a: 8th item

qa.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with f: 2, 5, 8, 6, 4. What is the median?
qa.e: N = 25, cf = 2, 7, 15, 21, 25. The 13th item falls where cf = 15, at X = 3.

qa.q: X: 10, 20, 30, 40 with f: 3, 4, 5, 4. Find the median.
qa.e: N = 16; (N + 1)/2 = 8.5th item. cf: 3, 7, 12, 16. Both the 8th and 9th items are 30, so median = 30.

qa.q: Data: 3, 5, 7, 9, 1000. The median is:
qa.e: The median is the middle item, 7; the extreme value 1000 does not affect it. (The mean would be 204.8.)

qa.q: Why is the median called a positional average?
qa.a: Because its value depends on the position of the middle item in ordered data
qa.e: It is located by position, not computed from all values.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The median is not affected by extreme values.
Reason (R): The median depends only on the middle position of the ordered data.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since only the middle position matters, changing an extreme value does not move it.

qa.q: Classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, 40–50 have f = 5, 15, 20, 10. Find the median.
Given L = 40, N/2 = 50, c.f. = 38, f = 24 and h = 10, the median is:
Less than 10: 5, less than 20: 15, less than 30: 30, less than 40: 36, less than 50: 40. Find the median.
A distribution has N = 60. The median item for a continuous series is the:
qa.a: 30th item
qa.e: For a continuous series, the median position is N/2 = 30.

qa.q: cf of classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 are 8, 18, 34, 40. Which is the median class?
qa.e: N = 40, N/2 = 20. The first cf that equals or exceeds 20 is 34, in the class 20–30.

qa.q: In the median formula, c.f. stands for the cumulative frequency of:
qa.a: The class just before the median class
qa.e: c.f. is the cumulative frequency of the class preceding the median class.

qa.q: The median class is the inclusive class 30–39 (next class 40–49). Which value of L should be used?
qa.e: Adjust first: 30 − 0.5 = 29.5.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The median can be calculated even when the first and last classes are open-ended.
Reason (R): The median formula uses only the median class and the cumulative frequency before it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The end classes' limits are not needed unless one of them is the median class.

qa.q: How many quartiles divide a data set into four equal parts?
qa.e: Three cut points (Q1, Q2, Q3) make four parts.

qa.q: For N = 15 ordered items, Q1 is the size of which item?
qa.a: 4th

qa.q: P50 (the 50th percentile) is equal to:
qa.a: The median
qa.e: The 50th percentile splits data in half, like the median.

qa.q: A student is at the 85th percentile of a test. This means:
qa.a: About 85% of candidates scored at or below her
qa.e: A percentile rank tells the share of values at or below that score.

qa.q: The upper quartile (Q3) of monthly incomes in a town is ₹60,000. What can we say?
qa.a: 25% of people earn more than ₹60,000
qa.e: 75% lie below Q3, so the top 25% earn above it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Like the median, quartiles are positional measures.
Reason (R): Quartiles are located by the positions of items in ordered data.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Quartiles, like the median, depend on position, not on adding all values.

qa.q: Find the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 5.
qa.e: 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.

qa.q: The data 2, 2, 4, 4, 6 are:
qa.a: Bimodal
qa.e: Both 2 and 4 occur twice, so there are two modes.

qa.q: Given L = 40, D1 = 8, D2 = 4 and h = 6, the mode is:
X: 5, 10, 15, 20 with f: 3, 9, 6, 2. What is the mode?
qa.e: The value with the highest frequency (9) is X = 10.

qa.q: A shoe company wants to decide which size to produce in the largest quantity. Which average should it use?
qa.a: Mode
qa.e: The most frequently demanded size is the mode.

qa.q: Why must class intervals be equal before applying the mode formula?
qa.a: Because the formula compares frequencies of neighbouring classes, which is fair only when widths are equal
qa.e: Frequencies of classes of different widths are not comparable, so the modal class could be misjudged.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mode can be found for qualitative data such as the most popular colour.
Reason (R): Mode is based on frequency of occurrence, not on numerical values.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Counting which category occurs most needs no numbers, so mode works for attributes.

qa.q: In a perfectly symmetric distribution, the mean is 50. The median is:
qa.e: In a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode.

qa.q: In a skewed distribution, the mean is 40 and the mode is 30. Which value could be the median?
qa.e: The median lies between the mean and the mode, so only 35 fits.

qa.q: Which average is most suitable for the typical wage of workers when a few managers earn extremely high salaries?
qa.a: Median
qa.e: The median ignores the extreme salaries.

qa.q: Which average should a garment maker use to decide the size to produce most?
qa.a: Mode
qa.e: Mode identifies the most demanded size.

qa.q: For a distribution with open-ended classes like 'below 10' and '60 and above', the best average is generally the:
qa.a: Median
qa.e: The median can be found without knowing the open ends' limits.

qa.q: Five values have mean 12. Their sum of deviations from the mean is:
qa.e: The sum of deviations from the arithmetic mean is always zero.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: The mode may not be unique
qa.e: Data can be bimodal or multimodal, so the mode may not be unique.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The arithmetic mean is preferred when further algebraic treatment is needed.
Reason (R): The mean is based on all observations and has useful mathematical properties.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because it uses every value and is algebraically defined, the mean is easy to use in further calculations.

qa.q: Correlation analysis studies:
qa.a: Whether, in which direction and how strongly two variables move together
qa.e: Correlation measures the existence, direction and strength of covariation.

qa.q: Income and consumption expenditure usually show:
qa.a: Positive correlation
qa.e: As income rises, consumption tends to rise.

qa.q: The price of a good and its quantity demanded usually show:
qa.a: Negative correlation
qa.e: A higher price usually reduces quantity demanded.

qa.q: Sales of ice-cream and the number of drowning cases are found to be positively correlated. The best explanation is:
qa.a: Both rise because of a third factor, hot weather
qa.e: Hot weather increases both, giving a spurious correlation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A strong correlation between two variables proves that one causes the other.
Reason (R): Correlation measures how two variables vary together.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Correlation measures covariation (R is true) but does not prove causation (A is false).

qa.q: Which pair is most likely to show a cause-and-effect relationship?
qa.a: Price of a good and its quantity demanded
qa.e: A fall in price causes buyers to buy more; the others are coincidental or driven by a third factor (age, town size).

qa.q: The correlation coefficient studied in this chapter measures relationships that are:
qa.a: Linear
qa.e: It measures the degree of linear (straight-line) relationship.

qa.q: If one variable rises while the other falls, the correlation is:
qa.a: Negative
qa.e: Opposite movements mean negative correlation.

qa.q: In a scatter diagram, each point represents:
qa.a: A pair of values of X and Y
qa.e: Every observation pair (X, Y) is plotted as one point.

qa.q: Points in a scatter diagram fall from the upper left to the lower right in a narrow band. The correlation is:
qa.a: Strong negative
qa.e: A falling, tight pattern means a strong negative relationship.

qa.q: All points lie exactly on a straight line rising to the right. The correlation coefficient is:
qa.e: Points on a rising straight line indicate perfect positive correlation.

qa.q: Points are scattered all over the graph with no visible pattern. This suggests:
qa.a: No correlation
qa.e: No trend means no (linear) correlation.

qa.q: Pairs: (1, 10), (2, 8), (3, 6), (4, 4), (5, 2). What does the scatter diagram show?
qa.a: Perfect negative correlation
qa.e: Y falls by exactly 2 for each unit rise in X: all points on a falling straight line, r = −1.

qa.q: A main limitation of a scatter diagram is that it:
qa.a: Does not give a numerical measure of correlation
qa.e: It gives a visual idea only, not an exact figure.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A scatter diagram can reveal a non-linear relationship that the correlation coefficient may miss.
Reason (R): The correlation coefficient measures only linear relationships.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: A curve may give r close to 0, but the scatter clearly shows a pattern.

qa.q: Points form a U-shaped curve on a scatter diagram. The correct conclusion is:
qa.a: There is a non-linear relationship
qa.e: A U-shape is a clear curved relationship, even though linear correlation may be low.

qa.q: Given Σxy = 16, Σx² = 10 and Σy² = 40, find r.
Σxy = 30, N = 10, σx = 2, σy = 3. Find r.
For 5 pairs, Σxy = 16. What is the covariance of X and Y?
Covariance is 3.2, σx = √2 and σy = √8. Find r.
N = 5, ΣX = 15, ΣY = 50, ΣXY = 166, ΣX² = 55, ΣY² = 540. Find r by the direct method.
Karl Pearson's coefficient is also known as the:
qa.a: Product moment correlation coefficient
qa.e: It is also called the product moment or simple correlation coefficient.

qa.q: Σxy = −24, Σx² = 16 and Σy² = 64. Find r.

Assertion (A): Pearson's r is a better measure of the degree of relationship than covariance.
Reason (R): Covariance depends on the units of X and Y, while r is a pure number.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Dividing covariance by both standard deviations removes units, so r can be compared across data sets.

qa.q: The unit of the correlation coefficient is:
qa.a: It has no unit
qa.e: r is a pure number.

qa.q: Which of the following values of r is impossible?
qa.e: r must lie between −1 and +1; 1.05 indicates a calculation error.

qa.q: r between X and Y is 0.6. If every X is increased by 50 and every Y is divided by 10, the new r is:
qa.e: r is unaffected by change of origin and (positive) scale.

qa.q: r = 0 between two variables means:
qa.a: There is no linear relationship between them
qa.e: There could still be a non-linear relationship.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Correlation coefficient r is preferred to covariance for measuring the degree of relationship.
Reason (R): r can lie outside the range −1 to +1.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: r is preferred because it is unit-free, but it always lies between −1 and +1; R is false.

qa.q: During an epidemic, districts with more doctors record more deaths. The correct interpretation is:
qa.a: More doctors were sent to districts where the disease was worse
qa.e: The epidemic's severity drives both; common sense rejects a causal reading.

qa.q: Which value of r shows the strongest relationship?
qa.e: Strength depends on the absolute value; |−0.90| is the largest.

qa.q: A positive value of r indicates that:
qa.a: X and Y tend to move in the same direction
qa.e: Positive r means both tend to rise or fall together.

qa.q: U = (X − 30)/10 and V = (Y − 100)/20. If r between U and V is 0.8, then r between X and Y is:
qa.e: Change of origin and scale (positive factors) does not alter r.

qa.q: U: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and V: −1, −2, 1, 0, 2 (both means zero). Find r.

qa.e: Y = 2X + 3 exactly, a rising straight line, so r = +1.
Y = 16 − 3X exactly, a falling straight line, so r = −1.
x = X (mean 0), y = Y − 2 = 2, −1, −2, −1, 2. Σxy = −4 + 1 + 0 − 1 + 4 = 0, so r = 0, even though Y depends on X.

qa.q: Why is the step deviation method used for computing r?
qa.a: To simplify calculations with large numbers, without changing r
qa.e: Shifting and scaling makes numbers small; r stays the same.

qa.q: Σuv = 12, Σu² = 16 and Σv² = 25, where u and v are deviations from their means. Find r.

Assertion (A): The Y = X² data with X symmetric around zero give r = 0.
Reason (R): r measures only the linear relationship between variables.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The relation is perfect but curved, and r captures only linear relationships.

qa.q: Two judges rank 5 items; ΣD² = 10. Find Spearman's rank correlation.
For 10 pairs of ranks, ΣD² = 33. Find r_s.
Ranks by two judges for 4 contestants: A: 1, 2, 3, 4 and B: 4, 3, 2, 1. Find r_s.
qa.e: D = −3, −1, 1, 3; ΣD² = 20; n³ − n = 60; r_s = 1 − 120/60 = −1. Complete disagreement.

qa.q: Marks of 5 students in Economics: 85, 70, 92, 60, 78. If the highest marks get rank 1, what is the rank of the student who scored 78?
Spearman's rank correlation is most appropriate when:
qa.a: Variables are qualitative attributes like honesty that can only be ranked
qa.e: Attributes that cannot be measured can still be ranked.

qa.q: Judges P and Q have r_s = 0.62, Q and R have 0.35, P and R have 0.81. Which pair of judges agree most?
qa.a: P and R
qa.e: The highest rank correlation (0.81) shows the closest agreement.

qa.q: Ranks of 5 items by two judges are identical (D = 0 for all). Find r_s.
qa.e: ΣD² = 0, so r_s = 1 − 0 = 1: perfect agreement.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rank correlation can be used when data contain extreme values.
Reason (R): Ranks are not affected by how extreme a value is, only by its order.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: An extreme value just becomes rank 1 or rank n, so it does not distort the measure.

qa.q: Marks 45, 52, 52, 60 are ranked in ascending order. What rank does each 52 receive?
qa.e: They would occupy ranks 2 and 3, so each gets (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5.

qa.q: Three items tie for ranks 5, 6 and 7. Each gets the rank:
What is the correction factor added to ΣD² for one tie of 3 items?
n = 5, ΣD² = 5.5 and there is one tie of 2 items. Find r_s.
n = 6, ΣD² = 12, with one tie of 2 items and another tie of 3 items. Find r_s.
Rank correlation, like Pearson's r, always lies between:
qa.a: −1 and +1
qa.e: Both coefficients lie in the range −1 to +1.

qa.q: Why is rank correlation generally less precise than Pearson's r for measurable data?
qa.a: It ignores the actual size of differences between values and uses only their order
qa.e: Converting values to ranks discards information about magnitudes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When ranks are tied, a correction is added to ΣD².
Reason (R): Averaging tied ranks alters the sum of squares of ranks, so the formula needs adjusting.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The correction (m³ − m)/12 compensates for the effect of averaged ranks.

qa.q: An index number measures:
qa.a: The average change in a group of related variables between two situations
qa.e: It summarises the average relative change in a group of related items.

qa.q: The index for the base period is always taken as:
qa.e: The base period value is set at 100 for comparison.

qa.q: A price index of 250 means prices are how many times the base-period level?
qa.e: 250/100 = 2.5 times the base.

qa.q: A price index of 250 shows a rise of what percentage over the base period?
A production index fell to 85. By what percentage has production fallen from the base?
Which of these is a quantity index?
qa.a: Index of Industrial Production
qa.e: IIP measures changes in the volume of industrial output.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Index numbers are expressed in percentages but the % sign is not written.
Reason (R): The base period value is taken as 100 and other values are expressed relative to it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because values are relative to a base of 100, they are effectively percentages.

qa.q: Index numbers can compare situations across:
qa.a: Time or places
qa.e: They can compare two time periods or two places (e.g. cost of living in two cities).

qa.q: Prices of three items in the base year: ₹10, ₹5, ₹25; in the current year: ₹12, ₹7, ₹30. Find the simple aggregative price index.
Σp1q0 = 250 and Σp0q0 = 200. Find the Laspeyres price index.
Σp1q1 = 310 and Σp0q1 = 250. Find the Paasche price index.
Which index uses base-year quantities as weights?
qa.a: Laspeyres
qa.e: Laspeyres weights prices by q0.

qa.q: Two items: A (p0 = 4, p1 = 6, q0 = 10) and B (p0 = 10, p1 = 12, q0 = 5). Find the Laspeyres index.
A main drawback of the simple aggregative price index is that:
qa.a: It ignores the relative importance of items and adds prices in different units
qa.e: All items count equally and prices per kg, litre or dozen are just added.

qa.q: Interpret a Laspeyres price index of 140 for a family's basket.
qa.a: The base-year basket of goods now costs 40% more
qa.e: Laspeyres compares the cost of the same base-year basket at current and base prices.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Laspeyres and Paasche indices may give different values for the same data.
Reason (R): They use different quantity weights.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Base-year versus current-year quantity weights lead to different results.

qa.q: The price of sugar rose from ₹40 to ₹50 per kg. What is its price relative?
Price relatives of three items are 120, 140 and 120. Find the simple average of relatives.
Relatives 120, 140, 120 with weights 100, 50, 50. Find the weighted average of relatives.
Weights 40 and 60 with price relatives 150 and 110. Find the weighted index.
In the weighted relatives method for a price index, the weights are usually:
qa.a: Base-year expenditure (value) on each item
qa.e: W = p0q0, the base-year expenditure, reflects each item's importance.

qa.q: The price of an item fell from ₹80 to ₹60. Its price relative is:
qa.e: 60/80 × 100 = 75, showing a 25% fall.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The weighted average of relatives with base-year values as weights equals the Laspeyres index.
Reason (R): Σ(p0q0 × p1/p0) = Σp1q0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Multiplying each weight p0q0 by p1/p0 gives p1q0, so the two formulas coincide.

qa.q: Why is the simple average of relatives an improvement over the simple aggregative index?
qa.a: It is unaffected by the units in which prices are quoted
qa.e: Relatives are percentages, so kg, litre or dozen units no longer matter.

qa.q: The CPI is also known as the:
qa.a: Cost of living index
qa.e: It measures changes in the cost of the consumption basket of a group.

qa.q: Weights 50, 10, 20, 10, 10 and price relatives 150, 120, 130, 140, 110. Find the CPI.
Weights: food 60, others 40. Price relatives: food 150, others 100. Find the CPI.
Why are different CPIs constructed for industrial workers, agricultural labourers and urban households?
qa.a: Their consumption baskets and spending patterns differ
qa.e: Each group buys different items in different proportions, so separate baskets are needed.

qa.q: In CPI-Combined with base 2012, which group has the largest weight?
qa.a: Food and beverages
qa.e: Food and beverages carries a weight of 45.86 out of 100.

qa.q: The CPI rises from 100 to 140. By how much must a wage of ₹15,000 (base period) rise to keep the same standard of living?
qa.e: The excess over 100 is 40%, and 40% of ₹15,000 = ₹6,000 (new wage ₹21,000).

qa.q: The CPI for agricultural labourers and rural labourers is compiled by the:
qa.a: Labour Bureau
qa.e: The Labour Bureau compiles CPI-IW, CPI-AL and CPI-RL.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): CPI weights are based on the consumption pattern of the target group.
Reason (R): The CPI measures changes in the cost of a fixed basket bought by that group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since the CPI tracks that group's basket, weights must reflect what the group actually buys.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT covered by the WPI?
qa.a: Services such as transport fares and school fees
qa.e: WPI covers goods only.

qa.q: In the WPI series used in the NCERT book, the base year is:
qa.e: That WPI series uses base 2011–12 = 100.

qa.q: Which major group has the highest weight in the WPI (2011–12 series)?
qa.a: Manufactured products
qa.e: Manufactured products carry a weight of 64.23.

qa.q: Weights in WPI: primary articles 22.62 and fuel and power 13.15. What is the weight of manufactured products?
Core inflation is measured by excluding:
qa.a: Volatile items such as food and fuel
qa.e: Removing volatile food and fuel prices shows the underlying trend.

qa.q: Headline inflation refers to inflation measured on:
qa.a: All items in the price index
qa.e: Headline includes every item in the basket.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): WPI and CPI inflation can move in different directions in the same month.
Reason (R): They cover different baskets, and WPI excludes services.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Different items and weights mean the two indices can diverge.

qa.q: The WPI is used mainly to:
qa.a: Track price movements of goods and deflate aggregates like national income
qa.e: WPI reflects the goods economy and helps deflate nominal aggregates.

qa.q: The Index of Industrial Production is a:
qa.a: Quantity index
qa.e: It measures changes in the physical volume of industrial output.

qa.q: Which sector has the largest weight in the IIP (base 2011–12)?
qa.a: Manufacturing
qa.e: Manufacturing carries 77.63 out of 100.

qa.q: In the IIP (base 2011–12), which weight belongs to manufacturing?
qa.e: Manufacturing 77.63, mining 14.37, electricity 7.99. (40.27 is roughly the combined weight of the eight core industries.)

qa.q: How many companies' shares make up the BSE Sensex?
qa.e: The Sensex is based on 30 shares.

qa.q: The base year of the Sensex is:
qa.e: Sensex base = 1978–79 = 100.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight core industries?
qa.a: Automobiles
qa.e: The eight are coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity.

qa.q: The Human Development Index combines indicators of:
qa.a: Health, education and income
qa.e: HDI is a composite of life expectancy, education and per capita income.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Sensex is regarded as a benchmark of the Indian stock market.
Reason (R): It reflects the average movement in prices of large, actively traded shares.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Because it tracks major shares, its movement represents the market's general direction.

qa.q: Which is the best choice of base year?
qa.a: A normal year that is not too distant
qa.e: A normal, recent year allows meaningful comparison.

qa.q: Why should the items in a CPI be representative of the target group?
qa.a: So that the index reflects the group's actual cost of living
qa.e: If the basket differs from what the group buys, the index misrepresents its cost of living.

qa.q: Why are base years of index numbers revised from time to time?
qa.a: Consumption patterns and products change over time
qa.e: New products and changing spending shares make old weights outdated.

qa.q: The first step in constructing an index number is to:
qa.a: Decide its purpose
qa.e: The purpose decides the items, base and formula.

qa.q: Why do we need index numbers at all?
qa.a: To measure average changes in groups of related variables such as prices or production
qa.e: Index numbers summarise changes in many related items at once.

qa.q: A price index and a quantity index differ in that:
qa.a: A price index tracks prices; a quantity index tracks physical volumes
qa.e: One measures changes in prices, the other in quantities produced or consumed.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An index number based on unreliable price data may mislead policy makers.
Reason (R): The accuracy of an index depends on the quality of data used.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Poor data feed directly into a misleading index.

qa.q: Which is NOT an issue to consider while constructing an index number?
qa.a: The favourite colour of the statistician
qa.e: Purpose, items, base, formula and data quality matter; personal preferences do not.

qa.q: A price index rose from 200 to 230. What is the rate of inflation?
Money wage ₹45,000 and CPI 150. What is the real wage?
The cost of living index is 250. What is the purchasing power of a rupee compared with the base period?
qa.e: 1/2.5 = 0.40, so ₹1 now buys what 40 paise bought in the base.

qa.q: A worker earned ₹20,000 when the CPI was 100. The CPI is now 138. What salary keeps her standard of living the same?
The general CPI is 135; the food index is 150 and the non-food index is 120. What is the weight of food (out of 100)?
GST rates of 5%, 12% and 18% apply to items with weights 50, 30 and 20. What is the weighted average tax rate?
Which index is most suitable for fixing dearness allowance?
qa.a: CPI
qa.e: DA protects consumers' living standards, so the CPI is used.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An IIP with base 2004–05 and one with base 2011–12 cannot be compared directly.
Reason (R): Index values relative to different base years refer to different reference levels and baskets.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Each series is 100 in a different year with different weights, so values must be linked or shifted first.

qa.q: The first step in a statistical project is to:
qa.a: Identify the problem and set objectives
qa.e: Without a defined problem and objectives, the study has no direction.

qa.q: The 'target group' in a project refers to:
qa.a: The population whose members are to be surveyed
qa.e: It is the population relevant to the problem being studied.

qa.q: A student studies overcharging by bus conductors in her city. A suitable target group is:
qa.a: All bus commuters and conductors on city routes
qa.e: Those who use or operate city buses are directly connected to the issue.

qa.q: Which is the best objective for a project?
qa.a: To find the share of income spent on food by 100 households in our colony
qa.e: It is specific, measurable and tied to a clear group.

qa.q: A project aims to apply statistical tools to an economic issue in order to:
qa.a: Understand the issue and suggest improvements
qa.e: The goal is to study a problem systematically and suggest solutions.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A clearly defined objective helps decide what data must be collected.
Reason (R): The objective states exactly what the study wants to find out.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Knowing exactly what we want to find tells us which data are needed.

qa.q: A study of 'drinking water availability in Ward 7' has 1,200 households. If 10% are surveyed, how many households are in the sample?
Which of these is NOT part of the first two steps of a project?
qa.a: Writing the bibliography
qa.e: The bibliography comes at the very end of the report.

qa.q: A covering letter sent with a postal questionnaire mainly aims to:
qa.a: Explain the purpose of the survey and request cooperation
qa.e: It introduces the survey, assures confidentiality and asks for a reply.

qa.q: A student has very little time and money for her project. The most practical source of data is:
qa.a: Reliable secondary data
qa.e: Published data save time and cost, if they suit the purpose.

qa.q: Which method of primary data collection is most suitable when respondents are spread far apart and literate?
qa.a: Mailed or emailed questionnaire
qa.e: It is cheap and covers a wide area.

qa.q: Out of 400 questionnaires mailed for a project, 100 were returned. What is the response rate?
An interview schedule differs from a questionnaire because it is:
qa.a: Filled in by the interviewer while asking the questions
qa.e: The enumerator asks questions and records the answers.

qa.q: Why should a project use random sampling where possible?
qa.a: To give every unit an equal chance and reduce bias
qa.e: Random selection makes the sample more representative.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Secondary data should be used with caution in a project.
Reason (R): They may have been collected for a different purpose or with different definitions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Mismatched purpose or definitions can make secondary data unsuitable.

qa.q: Which is an example of secondary data a project on employment could use?
qa.a: Periodic Labour Force Survey reports
qa.e: PLFS reports are published by NSO, so they are secondary data for the student.

qa.q: Which step comes immediately after collecting data in a project?
qa.a: Organising and presenting the data
qa.e: Raw data must first be organised and presented before analysis.

qa.q: Which statistical tools are mainly used for analysis in a Class 11 project?
qa.a: Averages and correlation
qa.e: Mean, median, mode and correlation help analyse the data.

qa.q: A bibliography in a project report lists:
qa.a: All secondary sources used
qa.e: It records books, reports and websites consulted.

qa.q: A project on household spending finds food takes 45% of income. Which diagram best shows the full split of spending?
qa.a: Pie diagram
qa.e: Shares of a total are best shown as a pie diagram.

qa.q: A project finds r = −0.7 between price of vegetables and quantity bought per family. The correct interpretation is:
qa.a: Families tend to buy less when prices are higher
qa.e: A fairly strong negative correlation means quantity bought tends to fall as price rises.

qa.q: Which of the following belongs in the conclusion of a project report?
qa.a: Main findings and suggested policies
qa.e: The conclusion summarises findings and gives suggestions.

qa.q: The mean monthly income of 40 sampled families is ₹25,000. What is the total income of the sample?

Assertion (A): A project report should end with suggestions.
Reason (R): The purpose of a project is to study an issue and suggest ways to improve the situation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Suggestions fulfil the project's aim of improving the situation studied.

qa.q: A student acting as 'transport advisor' to the collector would most need data on:
qa.a: Bus routes, frequency, waiting times and fares
qa.e: These variables relate directly to improving public transport.

qa.q: To study whether advertising increases sales, the most useful statistical tool is:
qa.a: Correlation between ad spending and sales
qa.e: Correlation measures how ad spending and sales move together.

qa.q: A papad-making unit's monthly costs are ₹40,000 and expected sales revenue is ₹55,000. What is its expected monthly profit?
qa.e: Profit = revenue − cost = 55,000 − 40,000 = ₹15,000.

qa.q: A volunteer finds that 18 of 60 shops charged above MRP for bottled water. What percentage overcharged?
Which of these is a suitable project on social welfare?
qa.a: Immunisation coverage of children in a village
qa.e: It is a local welfare issue that can be studied with a survey.

qa.q: A survey of 80 school-age children in a slum finds 12 have dropped out. What is the dropout rate?

Assertion (A): Role-based projects still follow the standard steps of a statistical study.
Reason (R): Every project needs a problem, data, analysis and conclusions, whatever role the student plays.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The role sets the context; the method stays the same.

qa.q: Which data would best help a project on household saving habits?
qa.a: Monthly income, monthly saving and where savings are kept
qa.e: These variables directly describe saving behaviour.

qa.q: Which of these is a demographic question in a consumer survey?
qa.a: What is your age?
qa.e: Age is a demographic characteristic of the respondent.

qa.q: Out of 200 respondents, 70 use Brand X. What percentage use Brand X?
Occupational status of respondents is best shown by a:
qa.a: Pie diagram
qa.e: Categories that make up a whole suit a pie diagram.

qa.q: In a pie chart of 120 respondents, the sector for students is 72°. How many respondents are students?
Monthly spending classes ₹300–500, ₹500–700, ₹700–900 have frequencies 10, 25, 15. Find the mean spending.
Monthly spending of respondents is grouped into continuous classes ₹0–500, ₹500–1,000, ₹1,000–1,500. Which diagram suits it best?
qa.a: Histogram
qa.e: A frequency distribution with continuous classes is shown by adjacent rectangles: a histogram.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A consumer survey questionnaire should ask about media that influenced the purchase.
Reason (R): Such information helps the company judge which advertising channels work.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Knowing media influence helps companies plan advertising.

qa.q: Using A = 600 and c = 200, Σfd′ = 10 and Σf = 50 for monthly spending, the mean is:
Brand A: 80 users, 40 very satisfied. Brand B: 40 users, 30 very satisfied. What percentage of Brand B's users are very satisfied?
In the same data (A: 40 of 80, B: 30 of 40 very satisfied), which conclusion is correct?
qa.a: Brand B satisfies its users better because its satisfaction rate is higher
qa.e: 75% for B versus 50% for A.

qa.q: Out of 150 respondents, 90 say TV advertisements influenced their choice. What percentage is this?
A concluding note of a project should include:
qa.a: Main findings, limitations and suggestions
qa.e: It summarises results, admits limits and suggests action.

qa.q: A survey of only 30 households in one street concludes about the whole city. What is the main limitation?
qa.a: The sample may not represent the city
qa.e: A tiny sample from one street may not reflect the whole city.

qa.q: 72 of 120 respondents prefer toothpaste with herbal ingredients. What fraction is this?

Assertion (A): Interpretation of data should be supported by the findings.
Reason (R): Unsupported conclusions can mislead decision makers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Conclusions that go beyond the evidence can lead to wrong decisions.

qa.q: Which is the best suggestion from a finding that most young buyers were influenced by social media?
qa.a: Spend more of the advertising budget on social media aimed at young buyers
qa.e: The suggestion follows directly from the finding.

qa.q: The central problems of an economy arise mainly because of:
qa.a: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses
qa.e: Limited resources that can be used in many ways force choices.

qa.q: Deciding between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques is the problem of:
qa.a: How to produce
qa.e: Choice of technique is 'how to produce'.

qa.q: Deciding how national output is distributed among households is the problem of:
qa.a: For whom to produce
qa.e: Distribution of output is 'for whom'.

qa.q: A country deciding whether to produce more consumer goods or more capital goods faces the problem of:
qa.a: What to produce
qa.e: Choosing the mix of goods is 'what to produce'.

qa.q: A road can be built by 200 workers in 50 days, or by 40 workers with machines in 25 days. How many worker-days does the labour-intensive method use?
qa.e: 200 workers × 50 days = 10,000 worker-days (the machine method uses 40 × 25 = 1,000).

qa.q: Which is an example of a capital-intensive technique?
qa.a: Harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
qa.e: A combine harvester replaces a lot of labour with machinery.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Reason (R): Resources are limited relative to wants in every economy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Universal scarcity is why every economy faces these problems.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the central problems of an economy?
qa.a: Which festival to celebrate
qa.e: The three central problems concern production and distribution of goods.

qa.q: The production possibility frontier shows combinations of two goods when:
qa.a: Resources are fully and efficiently used
qa.e: Each point on the PPF uses all resources efficiently.

qa.q: A point inside the PPF indicates:
qa.a: Under-utilisation or wastage of resources
qa.e: More of one or both goods could be produced with the same resources.

qa.q: A point lying outside the PPF is:
qa.a: Unattainable with current resources and technology
qa.e: It needs more resources or better technology.

qa.q: A PPF passes through (4, 0), (3, 4), (2, 7), (1, 9) and (0, 10), where the first number is corn and the second is cotton. Is (2, 6) inside, on or outside the frontier?
qa.a: Inside the frontier
qa.e: With corn = 2, up to 7 cotton is possible; producing only 6 means resources are under-used.

qa.q: Using the same PPF, how much cotton is lost if production moves from (2, 7) to (2, 6)?
qa.e: Cotton falls from 7 to 6 while corn stays at 2: 1 unit of cotton is wasted.

qa.q: Which situation would place an economy inside its PPF?
qa.a: A long strike that shuts many factories
qa.e: Idle resources mean actual output is below potential.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An economy cannot produce at a point outside its PPF.
Reason (R): The PPF shows the maximum output possible with given resources and technology.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since the PPF is the maximum, anything beyond it cannot be produced right now.

qa.q: The production possibility set consists of:
qa.a: All points on and inside the PPF
qa.e: Every combination that can be produced, efficiently or not.

qa.q: Opportunity cost of producing one more unit of corn is:
qa.a: The amount of cotton given up to produce it
qa.e: It is measured by the alternative output forgone.

qa.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. What is the opportunity cost of the 3rd unit of corn?
qa.e: Moving from 2 to 3 corn reduces cotton from 7 to 4: 3 units of cotton.

qa.q: In the same table (Corn 0–4, Cotton 10, 9, 7, 4, 0), what is the MRT when corn rises from 3 to 4 units?
qa.e: Cotton falls from 4 to 0, so MRT = 4.

qa.q: Increasing marginal opportunity cost makes the PPF:
qa.a: Concave to the origin
qa.e: A rising MRT means the curve bows outward.

qa.q: If the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other were constant, the PPF would be:
qa.a: A downward-sloping straight line
qa.e: A constant slope gives a straight line.

qa.q: When good X rises from 5 to 7 units, good Y falls from 30 to 20 units. Find the MRT.
qa.e: MRT = ΔY/ΔX = 10/2 = 5.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A PPF is usually concave to the origin.
Reason (R): As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be used, so MRT rises.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Rising MRT due to imperfectly adaptable resources gives the bowed-out shape.

qa.q: The slope of the PPF at any point measures:
qa.a: The marginal rate of transformation
qa.e: Its (absolute) slope is the MRT, the rate at which one good is converted into the other.

qa.q: An increase in the stock of capital and labour in an economy will:
qa.a: Shift the PPF outward
qa.e: More resources raise the maximum possible output of both goods.

qa.q: A severe earthquake destroys many factories. The PPF will:
qa.a: Shift inward
qa.e: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.

qa.q: New technology improves only the production of wheat (on the x-axis). The PPF will:
qa.a: Rotate outward on the wheat axis, keeping the other intercept fixed
qa.e: Only the maximum wheat output increases.

qa.q: Government schemes put unemployed workers back to work. On a PPF diagram, this is shown as:
qa.a: A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the PPF
qa.e: The resources already existed; they are now being used.

qa.q: A PPF has maximum outputs of 100 cloth or 50 wheat. A wheat-only technology raises maximum wheat by 20%. What is the new maximum wheat output?
qa.e: 50 × 1.2 = 60; maximum cloth stays at 100.

qa.q: Which event shifts the PPF outward?
qa.a: Discovery of large oil reserves
qa.e: New resources raise potential output.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Economic growth is shown by an outward shift of the PPF.
Reason (R): Growth increases the economy's capacity to produce goods and services.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Higher productive capacity means a bigger set of attainable combinations.

qa.q: Which of these does NOT shift the PPF?
qa.a: Moving resources from wheat to cloth production
qa.e: Re-allocating existing resources only moves the economy along the same PPF.

qa.q: In a centrally planned economy, the central problems are solved by:
qa.a: The government or central authority
qa.e: The central authority decides what, how and for whom.

qa.q: In a market economy, the main coordinating mechanism is:
qa.a: The price mechanism
qa.e: Prices signal what buyers want and guide producers.

qa.q: A market, in economics, means:
qa.a: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers can freely exchange goods
qa.e: It need not be a place; online platforms are markets too.

qa.q: If demand for a good increases in a market economy, its price tends to:
qa.a: Rise, encouraging more supply
qa.e: Rising price raises profitability and induces producers to supply more.

qa.q: India's economy is best described as a:
qa.a: Mixed economy
qa.e: Both the market and the government have significant roles.

qa.q: Which is a role of the government in a mixed economy?
qa.a: Providing defence and public health
qa.e: The state supplies public goods and corrects market failures, while markets handle most goods.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Prices act as signals in a market economy.
Reason (R): A rise in the price of a good indicates greater scarcity or demand, guiding producers to supply more.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Price changes carry information that steers production decisions.

qa.q: Online shopping platforms where buyers and sellers never meet face to face are:
qa.a: Markets, because buyers and sellers can freely exchange
qa.e: The economic meaning of a market does not require a physical place.

qa.q: Positive economics deals with:
qa.a: What is, was or will be
qa.e: It describes actual economic mechanisms and can be tested.

qa.q: Which statement is normative?
qa.a: The government should provide free education to all
qa.e: 'Should' signals a value judgement.

qa.q: Which statement is positive?
qa.a: The price of petrol rose by ₹2 per litre last month
qa.e: It is a factual claim that can be checked.

qa.q: Microeconomics studies:
qa.a: Individual consumers, firms and markets
qa.e: It focuses on individual agents and individual markets.

qa.q: Which of these is a macroeconomic topic?
qa.a: India's unemployment rate
qa.e: Unemployment in the whole economy is an aggregate.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): 'A rise in income increases demand for normal goods' is a positive statement.
Reason (R): It can be tested against facts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Testability with data makes it positive.

qa.q: Of 10 statements in a test, 4 use 'should' or 'ought' and the rest are factual. How many are positive statements?
qa.e: 10 − 4 = 6 factual (positive) statements.

qa.q: The study of how the price of rice is determined in a market is part of:
qa.a: Microeconomics
qa.e: Price determination in an individual market is a microeconomic topic.

qa.q: Utility of a commodity means its:
qa.a: Want-satisfying power
qa.e: Utility is the capacity to satisfy a want, whether or not the good is 'useful'.

qa.q: TU from 2 units is 22 utils and from 3 units is 28 utils. What is the MU of the 3rd unit?
MUs of the first four units are 20, 15, 10 and 5. What is the TU of 4 units?
TU from 4 units is 30 and the MU of the 5th unit is −4. What is the TU from 5 units?
In the cardinal approach, utility is:
qa.a: Measured in numbers called utils
qa.e: The cardinal approach assumes utility can be expressed numerically.

qa.q: The bundle (4, 1) in the two-good model means:
qa.a: 4 units of good 1 and 1 unit of good 2
qa.e: The first number is x1 (good 1), the second x2 (good 2).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Utility of a woollen sweater is higher in Shimla in winter than in Chennai in summer.
Reason (R): Utility depends on place and time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The same good satisfies wants differently in different places and seasons.

qa.q: TU from 1, 2, 3 units of tea is 10, 18 and 24 utils. What is the MU of the 2nd cup?
The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, as more units of a good are consumed:
qa.a: MU from each additional unit falls
qa.e: Each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the previous one.

qa.q: When MU is zero, TU is:
qa.a: At its maximum
qa.e: TU stops rising exactly when MU = 0.

qa.q: When MU becomes negative, TU:
qa.a: Falls
qa.e: Each extra unit now reduces total satisfaction.

qa.q: MU (in ₹) of successive units of a good: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10. At a price of ₹20, how many units will the consumer buy?
qa.e: She buys while MU ≥ price: units 1–4 (MU 50, 40, 30, 20).

qa.q: MU_x = 40, P_x = ₹10, MU_y = 30, P_y = ₹5. What should the consumer do?
qa.a: Buy more Y and less X
qa.e: MU_x/P_x = 4 and MU_y/P_y = 6. A rupee on Y gives more utility, so shift spending to Y.

qa.q: A consumer is in equilibrium with MU_x = 24 and P_x = ₹8. If P_y = ₹5, what must MU_y be?

Assertion (A): Diminishing marginal utility leads to a downward-sloping demand curve.
Reason (R): A consumer buys more only when the price falls to match the lower MU of extra units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Extra units are worth less, so they are bought only at lower prices.

qa.q: TU from 1 to 5 units: 10, 18, 24, 24, 20. At which unit is MU zero?
qa.a: 4th

qa.q: The ordinal approach assumes that the consumer can:
qa.a: Rank bundles in order of preference
qa.e: Only rankings (more, less or equal satisfaction) are needed.

qa.q: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that:
qa.a: Give the same level of satisfaction
qa.e: All points on an IC are equally preferred.

qa.q: On an IC, a consumer moves from (2, 11) to (3, 8). What is the MRS?
qa.e: She gives up 3 units of good 2 for 1 more unit of good 1: MRS = 3.

qa.q: On an IC, a consumer moves from (2, 20) to (4, 14). What is the MRS?
Diminishing MRS means that as the consumer gets more of good 1, she is willing to give up:
qa.a: Less and less of good 2
qa.e: Each extra unit of good 1 is worth less in terms of good 2.

qa.q: MRS is defined as:
qa.a: |Δx2 / Δx1| along an IC
qa.e: It is the absolute slope of the indifference curve.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): MRS usually diminishes along an indifference curve.
Reason (R): As a consumer has more of good 1 and less of good 2, good 2 becomes relatively more valuable to her.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Scarcer good 2 is valued more, so she gives up less of it for each extra unit of good 1.

qa.q: Indifference schedule: (1, 12), (2, 7), (3, 4), (4, 2). What is the MRS when moving from the 3rd to the 4th bundle?
qa.e: x2 falls from 4 to 2 as x1 rises by 1: MRS = 2.

qa.q: Indifference curves are convex to the origin because of:
qa.a: Diminishing MRS
qa.e: As MRS falls, the curve flattens, giving a convex shape.

qa.q: For two perfect substitutes, the indifference curve is:
qa.a: A straight line
qa.e: The consumer swaps them at a constant rate, so MRS is constant.

qa.q: With monotonic preferences, which bundle is preferred: (4, 6) or (4, 9)?
qa.e: (4, 9) has more of good 2 and the same good 1.

qa.q: Why do indifference curves slope downward?
qa.a: To keep satisfaction constant, more of one good must be balanced by less of the other
qa.e: With monotonic preferences, getting more of both would raise satisfaction, so one must fall.

qa.q: An indifference map is:
qa.a: A family of ICs, with higher ones giving higher satisfaction
qa.e: It shows the consumer's whole preference pattern.

qa.q: Which of these bundles lies on a higher IC than (3, 3) for a consumer with monotonic preferences?
qa.e: (4, 3) has more of good 1 and the same good 2.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two indifference curves cannot intersect.
Reason (R): If they did, one bundle with more of both goods would give the same satisfaction as another, violating monotonic preferences.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: That contradiction is exactly the proof.

qa.q: A consumer is indifferent between (1, 10) and (2, 8), and between (2, 8) and (3, 6). Is the MRS diminishing along this curve?
qa.a: No, it is constant at 2
qa.e: Both steps give up 2 units of good 2 for 1 of good 1: MRS is constant at 2, so this part is a straight line.

qa.q: A consumer has ₹120. p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10. The budget equation is:
qa.e: Spending on each good = price × quantity, and the total equals income.

qa.q: M = ₹120, p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10. What is the maximum quantity of good 1 she can buy?
p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10 (good 1 on the x-axis). The slope of the budget line is:
A bundle (4, 6) lies on the budget line with p1 = ₹5 and p2 = ₹10. What is the consumer's income?
M = ₹10, p1 = p2 = ₹5, and goods come in whole units only. How many bundles (including (0, 0)) are in the budget set?
The budget line slopes downward because:
qa.a: With fixed income, buying more of one good requires buying less of the other
qa.e: Spending on one good can rise only if spending on the other falls.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The absolute slope of the budget line equals the price ratio p1/p2.
Reason (R): To buy one more unit of good 1, the consumer must give up p1/p2 units of good 2.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: The price ratio is the market rate of exchange between the goods.

qa.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Which bundle is NOT affordable?
A rise in the consumer's income, with prices unchanged, causes the budget line to:
qa.a: Shift parallel outward
qa.e: Both intercepts rise in proportion and the slope stays −p1/p2.

qa.q: A fall in the price of good 1 (on the x-axis), with income and p2 unchanged, makes the budget line:
qa.a: Rotate outward, keeping the x2-intercept fixed
qa.e: Only the x1-intercept M/p1 increases.

qa.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5. If p1 falls to ₹4, the new maximum quantity of good 1 is:
M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Income rises to ₹150. What is the new x2-intercept?
Income doubles and both prices also double. The budget line will:
qa.a: Not change
qa.e: M/p1 and M/p2 are unchanged, and so is p1/p2.

qa.q: p1 rises from ₹5 to ₹10, p2 = ₹10, M = ₹100. The slope of the new budget line is:
qa.e: Slope = −p1/p2 = −10/10 = −1, steeper than before.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A change in income does not change the slope of the budget line.
Reason (R): The slope depends only on the price ratio p1/p2.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Income affects the intercepts, not the price ratio.

qa.q: The price of good 2 rises while M and p1 stay the same. Which intercept stays fixed?
qa.a: x1-intercept (M/p1)
qa.e: Only M/p2 falls; M/p1 is unchanged, so the line rotates around the x1-intercept.

qa.q: Under the IC approach, the consumer is in equilibrium where:
qa.a: The budget line is tangent to the highest attainable IC
qa.e: Tangency gives the highest satisfaction possible within the budget.

qa.q: The condition for consumer's equilibrium in the IC approach is:
qa.a: MRS = p1/p2
qa.e: The slope of the IC (MRS) equals the slope of the budget line (p1/p2).

qa.q: p1 = ₹6 and p2 = ₹3. At the optimum, the MRS must be:
MRS = 4 and p1/p2 = 2 at the current bundle. The consumer should:
qa.a: Buy more of good 1
qa.e: She values good 1 more than the market rate, so more good 1 raises her satisfaction.

qa.q: MRS = 1 and p1 = ₹3, p2 = ₹1 at the current bundle. The consumer should:
qa.a: Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2
qa.e: MRS (1) < p1/p2 (3): good 1 is worth less to her than its market cost in terms of good 2.

qa.q: Why does the optimal bundle lie on (not inside) the budget line?
qa.a: Because with monotonic preferences, spending leftover income on more goods raises satisfaction
qa.e: Any bundle inside leaves money unspent that could buy more and raise utility.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At the consumer's optimum, the rate at which she is willing to substitute equals the rate at which the market allows her to substitute.
Reason (R): At the optimum, MRS = p1/p2.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: MRS is her willingness; p1/p2 is the market rate; equality is the tangency condition.

qa.q: A consumer's MRS = 2.5 at her chosen bundle, and p2 = ₹4. If she is at the optimum, what is p1?
Demand for a good means the quantity a consumer is:
qa.a: Willing and able to buy at a given price
qa.e: Desire must be backed by ability to pay at that price.

qa.q: The law of demand states that, other things remaining the same:
qa.a: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
qa.e: A fall in price raises quantity demanded, and vice versa.

qa.q: q = 50 − 5p. What is the quantity demanded at p = ₹6?
q = 100 − 4p. At what price is quantity demanded 40?
When the price of a good falls, the substitution effect makes the consumer:
qa.a: Buy more of it, since it is now relatively cheaper
qa.e: The good becomes cheaper relative to others, so she substitutes towards it.

qa.q: For a normal good, when its price falls, the income effect:
qa.a: Increases quantity demanded
qa.e: Higher purchasing power raises demand for a normal good, reinforcing the substitution effect.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The demand curve can be derived from indifference curves and budget lines.
Reason (R): As price falls, the budget line rotates outward and the new optimum usually contains more of the good.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Tracing optimum quantities at different prices gives the demand curve.

qa.q: q = 30 − 3p. What is the maximum price at which any quantity is demanded?
qa.e: q = 0 when p = 10, so at any price above ₹10 nothing is demanded.

qa.q: A good whose demand falls when the consumer's income rises is:
qa.a: An inferior good
qa.e: Inferior goods have an inverse relation with income.

qa.q: If the price of coffee rises, the demand for tea will:
qa.a: Rise
qa.e: Tea and coffee are substitutes.

qa.q: If the price of petrol rises sharply, the demand for petrol cars will tend to:
qa.a: Fall
qa.e: Cars and petrol are complements; costlier petrol reduces demand for petrol cars.

qa.q: A Giffen good is a good whose demand:
qa.a: Rises when its price rises, because a strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect
qa.e: It is an inferior good with an unusually strong negative income effect.

qa.q: Income rises from ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 and demand for a good rises from 5 kg to 9 kg. By what percentage did demand rise?
qa.e: (9 − 5)/5 × 100 = 80%. It is a normal good.

qa.q: Pen and ink are an example of:
qa.a: Complements
qa.e: They are used together.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For an inferior good, the income effect of a price fall reduces quantity demanded.
Reason (R): A price fall raises real income, and demand for an inferior good falls as real income rises.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Higher real income leads to less demand for inferior goods.

qa.q: The price of sugar rises. What happens to the demand for tea (a complement of sugar)?
qa.a: Demand for tea falls
qa.e: Costlier sugar makes the tea-plus-sugar combination costlier, reducing tea demand.

qa.q: A change in the good's own price causes:
qa.a: A movement along the demand curve
qa.e: Own-price changes move us along a given demand curve.

qa.q: A rise in consumers' income (normal good) causes the demand curve to:
qa.a: Shift to the right
qa.e: At every price, more is demanded.

qa.q: Which causes a leftward shift of the demand curve for tea?
qa.a: A fall in the price of coffee
qa.e: Cheaper coffee (a substitute) draws buyers away from tea.

qa.q: Market demand is obtained by:
qa.a: Adding quantities demanded by all consumers at each price
qa.e: It is the horizontal summation of individual demands.

qa.q: d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. What is the market demand at p = ₹4?
d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. What is the market demand at p = ₹12?
qa.e: Consumer 1 buys nothing at p > 10 (quantity cannot be negative); consumer 2 buys 3.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A fall in the price of a good leads to an increase in demand.
Reason (R): A fall in own price causes an extension (movement down) along the demand curve.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: A own-price fall raises quantity demanded (extension), not demand; A misuses the term.

qa.q: Three identical consumers each have demand q = 20 − 2p. What is the market demand at p = ₹5?
qa.e: Each demands 20 − 10 = 10; three consumers demand 30.

qa.q: Price falls from ₹5 to ₹4 and quantity demanded rises from 100 to 130 units. Find the price elasticity of demand (absolute value).
Price rises from ₹20 to ₹25 and quantity demanded falls from 80 to 70. Find |e_D|.
e_D = 2 and the price of a good rises by 10%. Quantity demanded was 500 units. What is the new quantity demanded?
qa.e: Quantity falls by 2 × 10% = 20%, i.e. by 100 units: 500 − 100 = 400.

qa.q: Demand for a good is called elastic when:
qa.e: Quantity changes by a larger percentage than price.

qa.q: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is:
qa.a: Vertical
qa.e: Quantity demanded does not change at all with price (e_D = 0).

qa.q: Price falls by 10% and quantity demanded rises by 10%. The demand is:
qa.a: Unitary elastic

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The price elasticity of demand is usually negative.
Reason (R): Price and quantity demanded generally move in opposite directions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Opposite signs of ΔQ and ΔP make the ratio negative; we often drop the sign.

qa.q: Quantity demanded falls by 12% when price rises. If e_D = 0.8, by what percentage did price rise?
At the mid-point of a straight-line demand curve, price elasticity is:
qa.e: Lower and upper segments are equal, so e_D = 1.

qa.q: q = 100 − 5p. Find |e_D| at p = 12.
On a straight-line demand curve, a point divides it so that the lower segment is 6 cm and the upper segment is 3 cm. Find e_D at that point.
qa.e: e_D = lower/upper = 6/3 = 2.

qa.q: Where a straight-line demand curve meets the quantity axis, e_D is:
qa.e: At that point price is zero, so the upper segment is the whole line and the lower segment is zero.

qa.q: Price of a good rises from ₹10 to ₹12, and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 90. What happens to total expenditure, and what does it show?
qa.a: Rises from ₹1,000 to ₹1,080; inelastic demand
qa.e: Expenditure = 10 × 100 = 1,000 before and 12 × 90 = 1,080 after. A price rise that raises expenditure means inelastic demand.

qa.q: A demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, with p × q = 600 throughout. If price is ₹20, how much is demanded, and what is e_D?
qa.a: 30 units, e_D = 1
qa.e: q = 600/20 = 30. Expenditure is constant along the curve, so e_D = 1 everywhere.

qa.q: Demand for a good is more elastic when:
qa.a: It has many close substitutes
qa.e: Buyers can easily switch, so they respond strongly to price changes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Demand for salt is inelastic.
Reason (R): Salt is a necessity with few close substitutes and takes a very small share of the budget.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Each factor in R makes demand less responsive to price.

qa.q: A production function shows the relationship between:
qa.a: Inputs and the maximum output
qa.e: It is a technical relation between inputs used and the maximum output.

qa.q: In q = f(L, K), K stands for:
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: L is labour and K is capital.

qa.q: Output table (K = 2): L = 1 → 10, L = 2 → 24, L = 3 → 36. How much does output rise when L goes from 2 to 3?
An isoquant is a curve showing:
qa.a: Combinations of inputs that produce the same output
qa.e: 'Iso' means equal: equal quantity of output.

qa.q: A production function assumes that technology is:
qa.a: Given (constant)
qa.e: For a given technology it shows the maximum output possible.

qa.q: Output table: with L = 2, output is 24 when K = 2 and 30 when K = 3. By what percentage did output rise?

Assertion (A): Two different combinations of labour and capital can produce the same output.
Reason (R): Labour and capital can, to some extent, be substituted for each other.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Substitutability of inputs is why isoquants contain many combinations.

qa.q: Why does an isoquant slope downward?
qa.a: If one input increases, the other must decrease to keep output unchanged
qa.e: More of one input with the same amount of the other would raise output.

qa.q: In the short run:
qa.a: At least one factor is fixed
qa.e: Some inputs, like the plant, cannot be changed quickly.

qa.q: The distinction between short run and long run is based on:
qa.a: Whether all inputs can be varied
qa.e: It depends on input flexibility, not a fixed number of months.

qa.q: TP of 4 workers is 44 units. What is the AP?
TP rises from 36 to 44 when the 4th worker is hired. What is MP of the 4th worker?
MPs of the first four workers are 10, 14, 12 and 8. What is the TP of 4 workers?
qa.e: TP = sum of MPs = 44.

qa.q: TP rises from 40 to 52 when labour rises from 4 to 6 units. What is the MP per unit of labour?
qa.e: MP = ΔTP/ΔL = 12/2 = 6.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The long run of a tea stall may be much shorter than that of a steel plant.
Reason (R): Short and long run are defined by input flexibility, not calendar time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: A tea stall can change all inputs quickly; a steel plant cannot.

qa.q: Average product of labour is defined as:
qa.a: TP / L
qa.e: Output per unit of the variable input.

qa.q: AP of labour at L = 3 is 16. What is TP at L = 3?
AP is 20 at L = 1 and 18 at L = 2. What is MP of the 2nd worker?
MPs for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 are 5, 7, 9, 6. What is TP at L = 4?
MPs for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 are 5, 7, 9, 6. What is AP at L = 4?
TP for L = 1 to 5 is 8, 20, 30, 36, 40. What is MP of the 5th worker?
TP for L = 1 to 5 is 8, 20, 27, 32, 35. At which level of labour is AP the highest?
qa.e: AP = 8, 10, 9, 8, 7. It peaks at 10 when L = 2.

qa.q: AP at L = 4 is 14 and at L = 5 is 12. What is MP of the 5th worker?
qa.e: TP4 = 56, TP5 = 60, MP5 = 4. AP falls because MP (4) is below AP.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): If MP of the next worker is less than the current AP, AP will fall.
Reason (R): Adding a value below the average pulls the average down.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: This is ordinary averaging logic applied to products.

qa.q: The law of variable proportions applies when:
qa.a: One factor is varied while others are fixed
qa.e: It is a short-run law with a fixed factor.

qa.q: In the phase of increasing returns to a factor:
qa.a: MP rises
qa.e: Each extra unit adds more than the previous one.

qa.q: Diminishing returns to a factor set in mainly because:
qa.a: The fixed factor becomes relatively scarce compared with the variable factor
qa.e: Factor proportions worsen as more variable input shares the fixed input.

qa.q: MP of labour for L = 1 to 6 is 6, 9, 7, 4, 0, −2. At which L do negative returns begin?
qa.e: MP first becomes negative at L = 6.

qa.q: Using MPs 6, 9, 7, 4, 0, −2 (L = 1 to 6), what is the maximum TP?
qa.e: TP peaks when MP = 0 (at L = 5): 6 + 9 + 7 + 4 + 0 = 26.

qa.q: In Phase III of the law of variable proportions:
qa.a: TP falls and MP is negative
qa.e: Too many variable inputs reduce total output.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A rational producer never operates in the stage of negative returns.
Reason (R): In that stage, extra units of the variable factor reduce total output.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Paying for inputs that cut output makes no sense.

qa.q: Increasing returns to a factor in the early phase are mainly due to:
qa.a: Better utilisation of the fixed factor and specialisation
qa.e: A few workers cannot use a big fixed input fully; more workers use it better.

qa.q: TP is at its maximum when MP is:
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: TP stops rising when the last unit adds nothing.

qa.q: When MP is greater than AP, AP:
qa.a: Rises
qa.e: Adding a value above the average raises it.

qa.q: MP cuts AP at:
qa.a: The maximum of AP
qa.e: AP stops rising exactly when MP falls to equal it.

qa.q: TP for L = 1 to 4 is 10, 24, 36, 44. At L = 3, MP = 12. What is AP at L = 3, and what does the comparison show?
qa.a: 12; AP is at its maximum since MP = AP
qa.e: AP3 = 36/3 = 12 = MP3, so AP is at its peak.

qa.q: When TP rises at an increasing rate, MP is:
qa.a: Rising
qa.e: Bigger increments mean rising MP.

qa.q: TP for L = 4, 5, 6 is 44, 48, 48. What is MP of the 6th worker?
qa.e: 48 − 48 = 0, so TP is at its maximum.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): AP falls whenever MP falls.
Reason (R): AP rises as long as MP is above AP, even if MP itself is falling.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: AP can still rise while MP falls, as long as MP > AP; so A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Which curve can go below the x-axis?
qa.a: MP
qa.e: MP becomes negative in the third phase; AP stays positive while TP is positive.

qa.q: Returns to scale refer to the change in output when:
qa.a: All inputs change in the same proportion
qa.e: It is a long-run concept with all inputs varying together.

qa.q: If all inputs are doubled and output more than doubles, there are:
qa.a: Increasing returns to scale
qa.e: Output rises more than proportionately.

qa.q: For q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5, what is the output when x1 = 4 and x2 = 9?
For q = 5L × K, what is the output when L = 2 and K = 3?

qa.a: Decreasing returns to scale

qa.q: The long-run average cost curve is U-shaped because of:
qa.a: Increasing, then constant, then decreasing returns to scale
qa.e: In the long run, returns to scale determine the shape.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): There are no fixed costs in the long run.
Reason (R): In the long run all inputs can be varied.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Fixed costs arise only from fixed inputs, which do not exist in the long run.

qa.q: q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5. If x1 = 16 and x2 = 4, what is q?
Which of these is a fixed cost?
qa.a: Rent of the factory
qa.e: Rent does not change with the level of output in the short run.

qa.q: TFC = ₹200 and TVC = ₹300 at q = 10. What is AC?
TC at q = 4 is ₹220 and at q = 5 is ₹270. What is MC of the 5th unit?
TFC = ₹100. What is AFC at q = 8?
MC of successive units is ₹40, ₹30, ₹20 and TFC is ₹100. What is TC at q = 3?
Which relation is correct?
qa.a: AC = AFC + AVC
qa.e: AC = TC/q = (TFC + TVC)/q = AFC + AVC.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Marginal cost is not affected by fixed cost.
Reason (R): Fixed cost does not change when output changes, so ΔTC = ΔTVC.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Only variable cost changes with output, so MC depends on TVC alone.

qa.q: AVC at q = 5 is ₹34 and AFC is ₹20. What is TC at q = 5?
The shape of the TFC curve is:
qa.a: A horizontal straight line
qa.e: Fixed cost does not change with output.

qa.q: The AFC curve is a:
qa.a: Rectangular hyperbola
qa.e: AFC × q = TFC, a constant.

qa.q: SMC cuts the AVC curve at:
qa.a: The minimum point of AVC
qa.e: AVC falls while SMC < AVC and rises when SMC > AVC, so they meet at AVC's minimum.

qa.q: TFC = ₹120. What is the vertical gap between SAC and AVC at q = 8?
Why are SAC, AVC and SMC curves U-shaped in the short run?
qa.a: Because of the law of variable proportions
qa.e: Increasing then diminishing returns to the variable factor make costs fall, then rise.

qa.q: Why does the gap between SAC and AVC narrow as output rises?
qa.a: Because AFC keeps falling
qa.e: The gap is AFC, which falls as fixed cost is spread over more units.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The minimum point of SAC lies to the right of the minimum point of AVC.
Reason (R): After AVC starts rising, SAC continues to fall for a while because the fall in AFC outweighs the rise in AVC.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Falling AFC keeps pulling SAC down a little beyond AVC's minimum.

qa.q: TFC = ₹100. At what output is AFC equal to ₹4?
TC at zero output is ₹150. What is TFC?
qa.e: At zero output there is no variable cost, so TC = TFC.

qa.q: TC: q = 0 → 100, q = 1 → 140, q = 2 → 170. What is AVC at q = 2?
TC: q = 2 → 170, q = 3 → 190. What is MC of the 3rd unit?
TFC = ₹60; MC of units 1 to 4 is ₹20, ₹15, ₹15, ₹30. What is AC at q = 4?
AC at q = 6 is ₹40 and TFC is ₹60. What is AVC at q = 6?
AC at q = 4 is ₹55 and at q = 5 is ₹54. What is MC of the 5th unit?

Assertion (A): TVC can be found by adding up the marginal costs.
Reason (R): Each MC is the addition to variable cost from one more unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Summing the increments in variable cost gives total variable cost.

qa.q: TC at q = 0, 1, 2, 3 is ₹50, ₹80, ₹100, ₹130. At which output is AVC lowest?
Average revenue is always equal to:
qa.a: Price
qa.e: AR = TR/q = p.

qa.q: A firm sells 25 units at ₹8 each. What is its TR?
TR at q = 4 is ₹60 and at q = 5 is ₹75. What is MR of the 5th unit?
TR = ₹300 at q = 20. What is the price?
When price is constant at all levels of output:
qa.a: MR = AR
qa.e: Each extra unit adds exactly the constant price.

qa.q: With a constant price, the TR curve is:
qa.a: A straight line through the origin
qa.e: TR = p × q rises proportionally with q.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For a firm selling at a constant price, AR and MR curves are the same horizontal line.
Reason (R): Each additional unit sold adds an amount equal to the price to TR.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Constant MR equal to price means AR = MR = p, a horizontal line.

qa.q: Price is ₹12 per unit. TR at q = 9 minus TR at q = 8 equals:
qa.e: 108 − 96 = 12, which is the MR and equals the price.

qa.q: Under perfect competition, an individual firm is a:
qa.a: Price taker
qa.e: It is too small to influence price, so it accepts the market price.

qa.q: The demand curve faced by a perfectly competitive firm is:
qa.a: Horizontal (perfectly elastic)
qa.e: At the market price it can sell any quantity; at a higher price, nothing.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of perfect competition?
qa.a: Heavy advertising by each firm
qa.e: With identical products and perfect information, advertising serves no purpose.

qa.q: If a perfectly competitive firm raises its price above the market price, it will:
qa.a: Sell nothing
qa.e: Buyers can buy the identical product elsewhere at the market price.

qa.q: The price elasticity of demand facing a perfectly competitive firm is:
qa.a: Infinite
qa.e: A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker.
Reason (R): Each firm supplies a very small share of total market output of a homogeneous product.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Being tiny and identical to others, a firm cannot influence price.

qa.q: Free entry and exit under perfect competition ensures that in the long run firms earn:
qa.a: Only normal profit
qa.e: New entrants wipe out extra profits; exits remove losses.

qa.q: A market price of ₹40 prevails. A perfectly competitive firm sells 150 units. What is its total revenue?
For a perfectly competitive firm, the TR curve is:
qa.a: A straight line through the origin with slope equal to price
qa.e: TR = p × q with constant p.

qa.q: For a price-taking firm, which of these is equal to the market price?
qa.a: Both AR and MR
qa.e: Every unit sells at p, so AR = MR = p.

qa.q: Candle boxes sell at ₹10 each. What is TR from 7 boxes?
A firm's TR rises from ₹150 to ₹165 when it sells one more unit. If it is a price taker, what is the market price?
qa.e: MR = 165 − 150 = 15, and for a price taker MR = p.

qa.q: The slope of the TR curve of a price-taking firm when the price is ₹25 is:
qa.e: TR rises by ₹25 per unit sold.

qa.q: The firm's demand curve under perfect competition is the same as its:
qa.a: AR and MR curve (the price line)
qa.e: All are the horizontal line at the market price.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For a price-taking firm, MR equals AR.
Reason (R): Selling an extra unit does not require lowering the price on any unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: With a fixed price, each extra unit adds exactly p to revenue.

qa.q: The market price rises from ₹10 to ₹12. What happens to a price taker's TR at 50 units?
qa.a: Rises by ₹100
qa.e: TR rises from 500 to 600, an increase of ₹100.

qa.q: The first condition for profit maximisation of a price-taking firm is:
qa.a: p = MC
qa.e: Output is set where the price equals marginal cost.

qa.q: Why must MC be rising at the profit-maximising output?
qa.a: If MC is falling where p = MC, producing a little more would add to profit
qa.e: Beyond that point p > MC, so profit is not yet maximised.

qa.q: In the short run, a firm should shut down if the price is less than:
qa.a: Minimum AVC
qa.e: Below minimum AVC, it cannot even cover variable costs.

qa.q: A firm with TFC = ₹500 shuts down in the short run. What is its loss?
qa.e: With zero output, TR = 0 and TC = TFC, so the loss equals TFC.

qa.q: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm stays in the industry only if price is at least:
qa.a: Minimum LRAC
qa.e: In the long run all costs must be covered.
