qa.q: At the current output, p = ₹50 and MC = ₹42 (MC rising). To raise profit the firm should:
qa.a: Increase output
qa.e: Each extra unit adds ₹50 of revenue but only about ₹42 of cost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A firm may continue producing in the short run even when it makes a loss.
Reason (R): If the price covers AVC, producing keeps the loss smaller than TFC.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Covering variable cost and part of fixed cost beats losing all of TFC.

qa.q: p = ₹30, and at the output where p = MC (MC rising), AVC = ₹28 and AC = ₹33. In the short run the firm should:
qa.a: Produce, since p ≥ AVC, accepting a small loss
qa.e: Price covers AVC (₹30 > ₹28), so producing minimises the loss.

qa.q: Price = ₹20, output = 100 units, SAC at that output = ₹15. What is the profit?
Price = ₹12, output = 80, SAC = ₹15, AVC = ₹10. What is the loss, and should the firm produce in the short run?
qa.a: Loss ₹240; yes, since price covers AVC
qa.e: Loss = (15 − 12) × 80 = ₹240. Price (₹12) > AVC (₹10), so producing is better than shutting down.

qa.q: Price ₹10. TC for q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is the profit-maximising output?
Using the same table (p = ₹10; TC 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47 for q = 0–6), what is the maximum profit?
qa.e: At q = 5: TR = 50, TC = 36, profit = ₹14.

qa.q: Price ₹10; TC for q = 0 to 6 is 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is MC of the 6th unit, and why does the firm not produce it?
qa.a: ₹11; it exceeds the price of ₹10
qa.e: MC6 = 47 − 36 = 11 > 10, so the 6th unit reduces profit.

qa.q: On a cost–revenue diagram, the profit of a firm is shown by a rectangle whose height is:
qa.a: Price minus SAC at the chosen output
qa.e: Profit per unit (p − SAC) times output gives the rectangle's area.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When price equals SAC at the chosen output, the firm earns zero economic profit.
Reason (R): TR then exactly equals TC, which already includes normal profit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: p = SAC means TR = TC, so only normal profit is earned.

qa.q: A firm sells 60 units at ₹25. TC is ₹1,350. What is its profit?
The short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is:
qa.a: The rising part of SMC above minimum AVC
qa.e: At each price above minimum AVC, the firm produces where p = rising SMC.

qa.q: The short-run shut-down point of a firm is where price equals:
qa.a: Minimum AVC
qa.e: Below minimum AVC, producing loses more than shutting down.

qa.q: Normal profit is:
qa.a: The minimum profit needed to keep the firm in the industry
qa.e: It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur, counted as cost.

qa.q: The break-even point is where:
qa.a: Price = minimum AC
qa.e: TR = TC, so the firm earns only normal profit.

qa.q: Minimum AVC is ₹20 and minimum AC is ₹30. At a price of ₹25, the firm in the short run will:
qa.a: Produce at a loss smaller than TFC
qa.e: Price covers AVC but not AC, so it produces and limits its loss.

qa.q: A teacher earning ₹60,000 a month quits to open a coaching centre. The opportunity cost of her own time is:
qa.a: ₹60,000 a month
qa.e: The salary she gives up is her next best alternative.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A firm earning only normal profit will remain in the industry.
Reason (R): Normal profit covers the entrepreneur's opportunity cost.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Since she earns as much as in her next best option, she has no reason to leave.

qa.q: Price is ₹45 and minimum AC is ₹30. At the profit-maximising output the firm earns:
qa.a: Super-normal profit
qa.e: Price above minimum AC means profit above normal.

qa.q: Technological progress in production will:
qa.a: Shift the supply curve to the right
qa.e: Lower MC means more is supplied at every price.

qa.q: A rise in the price of an input used by a firm will:
qa.a: Shift supply to the left
qa.e: Higher MC reduces the quantity supplied at every price.

qa.q: A unit tax of ₹5 is imposed. A firm previously supplied 200 units at ₹30. At what price will it supply 200 units now?
qa.e: MC rises by ₹5 at every output, so it needs ₹35.

qa.q: A rise in the good's own price leads to:
qa.a: An extension (movement up) along the supply curve
qa.e: Own-price changes move along the curve.

qa.q: Which of these causes a leftward shift of a firm's supply curve?
qa.a: Imposition of a unit tax
qa.e: A unit tax raises the firm's marginal cost.

qa.q: Supply schedule: p = ₹10 → 40 units, ₹12 → 50 units, ₹14 → 60 units. How many extra units are supplied for each ₹2 rise in price?
qa.e: Quantity rises by 10 units for each ₹2 increase.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A unit tax shifts the supply curve upward by the amount of the tax.
Reason (R): The tax adds a fixed amount to the cost of producing every unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: MC at every output rises by the tax, so the curve moves up by that amount.

qa.q: 'Increase in supply' refers to:
qa.a: A rightward shift of the supply curve
qa.e: More is supplied at every price due to a non-price factor.

qa.q: Market supply is the:
qa.a: Horizontal summation of firms' supply curves
qa.e: At each price, quantities supplied by all firms are added.

qa.q: s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10 (0 otherwise) and s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15 (0 otherwise). What is market supply at p = ₹20?
Using the same firms, what is market supply at p = ₹12?
qa.e: s1 = 2; firm 2 does not produce below ₹15, so s2 = 0.

qa.q: Why does the market supply curve of these two firms have a kink at ₹15?
qa.a: Firm 2 starts producing only at ₹15, so above ₹15 quantity rises twice as fast as price rises
qa.e: Beyond ₹15 both firms respond to price, so quantity rises twice as fast.

qa.q: There are 50 identical firms, each with supply s = 2p − 10 for p ≥ 5. What is market supply at p = ₹10?
qa.e: Each firm supplies 2 × 10 − 10 = 10; 50 firms supply 500.

qa.q: An increase in the number of firms in a market will:
qa.a: Shift the market supply curve to the right
qa.e: More firms supply more at every price.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The market supply curve is flatter than each firm's supply curve when firms are identical.
Reason (R): At each price, market quantity is the sum of all firms' quantities, so it responds more in quantity to a price change.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Adding n identical curves horizontally multiplies the quantity response by n.

qa.q: Three firms supply 20, 35 and 45 units at ₹50. What is the market supply at ₹50?
Price rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 650. Find e_S.
Price of cricket balls rises from ₹10 to ₹30 and supply rises from 200 to 1,000. Find e_S.
e_S = 0.5. Price rises by 20% and the current supply is 400 units. What is the new quantity supplied?
A straight-line supply curve passes through the origin. Its price elasticity at every point is:
qa.e: For q = bp, e_S = bp/q = 1.

qa.q: A straight-line supply curve meets the price axis above the origin. Its elasticity is:
qa.a: Greater than 1
qa.e: For q = −a + bp with a > 0, e_S = bp/(bp − a) > 1.

qa.q: The supply of tickets for a cricket final in a stadium with fixed seats is:
qa.a: Perfectly inelastic
qa.e: Quantity cannot change whatever the price, so e_S = 0.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Price elasticity of supply is generally positive.
Reason (R): Price and quantity supplied usually move in the same direction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Same-direction movement makes the ratio positive.

qa.q: Supply q = 20 + p. Find e_S at p = 20.
qa.e: q = 40; e_S = (Δq/Δp) × p/q = 1 × 20/40 = 0.5 (line meets the quantity axis, so e_S < 1).

qa.q: Market equilibrium occurs where:
qa.a: Market demand equals market supply
qa.e: Plans of buyers and sellers match at that price.

qa.q: At a price below the equilibrium price, there is:
qa.a: Excess demand
qa.e: Lower price raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied.

qa.q: At ₹30, qD = 80 and qS = 50. What is the excess demand?
When there is excess supply in a perfectly competitive market, the price tends to:
qa.a: Fall
qa.e: Sellers with unsold stock cut prices.

qa.q: Price ₹50: qD = 40, qS = 70. What is the excess supply?
The 'invisible hand' refers to:
qa.a: The automatic adjustment of price that brings the market to equilibrium
qa.e: Self-interested buyers and sellers push prices towards equilibrium without central direction.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): At equilibrium there is neither excess demand nor excess supply.
Reason (R): At the equilibrium price, the quantity buyers wish to buy equals the quantity sellers wish to sell.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Equality of planned purchases and sales leaves no gap.

qa.q: At which price below is the market in equilibrium? (₹30: qD 80, qS 50; ₹40: qD 60, qS 60; ₹50: qD 40, qS 70)
qa.e: At ₹40, qD = qS = 60.

qa.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. What is the equilibrium price?
qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. What is the equilibrium quantity?
qD = 200 − p and qS = 120 + p. What is the equilibrium price?
qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. What is the excess demand at p = 15?
qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. What is the excess supply at p = 25?
qD = 50 − p and qS = 2p − 10. Find the equilibrium quantity.

Assertion (A): The excess demand function equals zero at the equilibrium price.
Reason (R): At equilibrium, qD = qS.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: ED = qD − qS = 0 when they are equal.

qa.q: The excess demand function for qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p is:
A competitive firm hires labour up to the point where:
qa.a: Wage = value of marginal product of labour
qa.e: Hiring stops when the extra worker's output value equals the wage.

qa.q: Price of output = ₹10 and MP of a worker = 30 units. What is the VMP of that worker?
Output price ₹10. MP of the 4th worker is 30 and of the 5th is 20. If the wage is ₹250, how many workers are hired?
qa.e: VMP4 = 300 ≥ 250 but VMP5 = 200 < 250, so 4 workers.

qa.q: Why does the demand curve for labour slope downward?
qa.a: Because MP of labour diminishes as more workers are hired
qa.e: Lower VMP for extra workers means they are hired only at lower wages.

qa.q: The equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market is determined by:
qa.a: Intersection of labour demand and labour supply
qa.e: As in other competitive markets, demand and supply set the price of labour.

qa.q: Output price ₹20 and wage ₹600. At what MP of labour will the firm stop hiring?

Assertion (A): If the price of the good produced rises, a competitive firm demands more labour at each wage.
Reason (R): VMP_L = p × MP_L rises when p rises.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Higher VMP makes more workers worth hiring at any given wage.

qa.q: The supply curve of labour usually:
qa.a: Slopes upward
qa.e: Higher wages draw out more labour.

qa.q: If demand increases (shifts right) and supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity:
qa.a: Both rise
qa.e: Higher demand at every price pushes up both.

qa.q: If supply increases (shifts right) and demand is unchanged:
qa.a: Price falls and quantity rises
qa.e: More is offered at each price, so price falls and more is bought.

qa.q: A rise in the price of a key input will lead to:
qa.a: Higher equilibrium price and lower quantity
qa.e: Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls.

qa.q: qD = 100 − 2p. Supply changes from qS = 20 + 2p to qS = 40 + 2p. What is the new equilibrium price?
With qD = 100 − 2p and new supply qS = 40 + 2p, what is the new equilibrium quantity?
qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p. A unit tax of ₹4 is imposed on sellers, so supply becomes qS = 20 + 2(p − 4). What is the new equilibrium price paid by buyers?
qa.e: 100 − 2p = 12 + 2p → 4p = 88 → p = 22. Buyers pay ₹2 more; sellers keep 22 − 4 = ₹18.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A fall in consumers' incomes lowers both the equilibrium price and quantity of a normal good.
Reason (R): Demand for a normal good falls when income falls, shifting the demand curve left.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: A leftward demand shift with unchanged supply lowers both p and q.

qa.q: Which event shifts the demand curve for cars to the right?
qa.a: A fall in petrol prices
qa.e: Cheaper petrol (a complement) raises demand for cars; the others affect supply or cause movements.

qa.q: Demand and supply both increase. Which is certain?
qa.a: Quantity rises
qa.e: Both shifts raise quantity; their effects on price oppose each other.

qa.q: Demand increases and supply decreases. Which is certain?
qa.a: Price rises
qa.e: Both shifts push price up; their effects on quantity oppose.

qa.q: Demand falls and supply rises. The equilibrium price will:
qa.a: Fall
qa.e: Both shifts lower the price.

qa.q: Both demand and supply decrease. The equilibrium quantity will:
qa.a: Fall
qa.e: Both shifts reduce quantity.

qa.q: Demand and supply both increase, and the increase in demand is greater than the increase in supply. The price will:
qa.a: Rise
qa.e: A bigger demand shift dominates the price effect.

qa.q: Demand decreases and supply increases by equal amounts. What happens?
qa.a: Price falls; quantity unchanged
qa.e: Price falls for sure; with equal-sized opposite shifts, quantity stays the same.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): When demand rises and supply falls, the change in equilibrium quantity cannot be predicted without more information.
Reason (R): The demand shift tends to raise quantity while the supply shift tends to lower it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Opposing pressures make the net quantity effect depend on the size of the shifts.

qa.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). Demand becomes 120 − 2p and supply becomes 40 + 2p. What is the new equilibrium price?
qa.e: 120 − 2p = 40 + 2p → 4p = 80 → p = 20. Equal shifts leave the price unchanged; quantity rises to 80.

qa.q: With free entry and exit, the long-run price in a perfectly competitive market equals:
qa.a: Minimum AC
qa.e: Entry and exit push price to the lowest average cost.

qa.q: In long-run equilibrium under free entry, firms earn:
qa.a: Only normal profit
qa.e: Any extra profit attracts entry until it disappears.

qa.q: Min AC = ₹20 at 50 units per firm, and qD = 1,000 − 10p. What is the equilibrium number of firms?
Demand rises to qD = 1,200 − 10p in the same market (min AC = ₹20 at 50 units). In the long run, how many firms will there be?
qa.e: Price stays ₹20; q = 1,000; firms = 1,000/50 = 20.

qa.q: Under free entry, after an increase in demand, the long-run equilibrium price:
qa.a: Remains at min AC
qa.e: Entry of firms brings price back to min AC.

qa.q: If firms in an industry are making losses, in the long run:
qa.a: Some firms exit, supply falls and price rises to min AC
qa.e: Exit continues until the remaining firms earn normal profit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In the long run, the number of firms changes but the price stays at min AC when demand changes.
Reason (R): Free entry and exit remove any super-normal profit or loss.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Entry or exit adjusts supply until price is back at min AC.

qa.q: Min AC = ₹15 at 30 units per firm, and qD = 600 − 20p. How many firms are there in long-run equilibrium?
A price ceiling is:
qa.a: A maximum price fixed below equilibrium
qa.e: It caps the price below the market level.

qa.q: An effective price ceiling leads to:
qa.a: Excess demand (shortage)
qa.e: At the low price, buyers want more than sellers offer.

qa.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. A ceiling of ₹15 is fixed. What is the shortage?
qa.e: qD = 70, qS = 50, shortage = 20.

qa.q: Using qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p, a ceiling of ₹25 is fixed. What happens?
qa.a: No effect, since ₹25 is above the equilibrium price of ₹20
qa.e: A ceiling above equilibrium does not bind; the price stays at ₹20.

qa.q: Which is a likely consequence of a price ceiling?
qa.a: Black marketing
qa.e: With shortages, some sellers sell illegally at higher prices.

qa.q: Ration cards and fair price shops are used under a price ceiling to:
qa.a: Ration the limited supply fairly among consumers
qa.e: They distribute scarce goods when price cannot rise.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rent control can reduce the number of houses offered for rent.
Reason (R): A rent ceiling below equilibrium lowers the return to landlords, so quantity supplied falls.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Lower returns discourage landlords from renting out or maintaining houses.

qa.q: qD = 200 − p and qS = 120 + p (p* = 40). A ceiling of ₹30 is fixed. What is the shortage?
qa.e: qD = 170, qS = 150, shortage = 20.

qa.q: A price floor is:
qa.a: A minimum price set above equilibrium
qa.e: It guarantees sellers at least this price.

qa.q: An effective price floor results in:
qa.a: Excess supply (surplus)
qa.e: At the higher price, sellers offer more than buyers want.

qa.q: Minimum support price for wheat is an example of:
qa.a: A price floor
qa.e: It sets a minimum price for farmers above the market level.

qa.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. A floor of ₹25 is set. What is the surplus?
qa.e: qS = 70, qD = 50, surplus = 20.

qa.q: With the same functions and a floor of ₹30, how much must the government spend to buy the entire surplus at the floor price?
A minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage in a labour market may cause:
qa.a: Excess supply of labour (some unemployment)
qa.e: At the higher wage, more people want work than firms want to hire.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The government often buys and stores grain when it fixes MSP above the market price.
Reason (R): A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus that must be absorbed to keep the price from falling.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
qa.e: Without government purchases, the surplus would push the price below the floor.

qa.q: A floor of ₹15 is set when the equilibrium price is ₹20. What happens?
qa.a: No effect; the market price stays ₹20
qa.e: A floor below equilibrium does not bind.
